procedures.title: Front-of-Neck Rescue Airway in CICO
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The decision framework that sits above the individual techniques — recognizing CICO fast, and choosing the right front-of-neck approach without hesitation.
procedures.description: The decision framework above the individual techniques.

blocks.html:
• Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate — confirmed after optimized, and failed, attempts at all three of: face mask ventilation, supraglottic airway, and tracheal intubation
  • Progressive desaturation despite those optimized attempts
  • Any situation where the algorithm is exhausted and oxygenation cannot be achieved by any other route

This entry is the decision layer; the Cricothyrotomy entry is the technique layer. Knowing how to cut is necessary and not sufficient. Almost every published CICO disaster is a story about a team that could have performed the procedure competently and didn't start it soon enough.

None. If the diagnosis of CICO is correct, a front-of-neck airway is indicated. The only meaningful error in the other direction is misdiagnosing CICO when a further optimized attempt at mask, supraglottic, or tube would still have worked — which is why the section below is about what "optimized" actually means.

sections.title: Recognizing CICO — The Part That Actually Fails

blocks.html: You are diagnosing a failure of oxygenation, not collecting failed attempts

“Optimized” has a specific meaning. Before you can call an attempt failed, it has to have been a real attempt:

  • Face mask: two-person technique, oral and nasal adjuncts in, jaw thrust, head position corrected, seal checked.
  • Supraglottic airway: correct size, a second attempt or a different device — not one hurried insertion that didn't seat.
  • Intubation: best operator available, best device available, external laryngeal manipulation, patient repositioned. A maximum of three attempts plus one by a more experienced operator is the commonly taught ceiling; the exact number matters less than the principle that repeating an identical failing attempt is not a new attempt.

Once all three limbs have genuinely failed and the saturation is falling, the diagnosis is made. There is no fourth category to try.

blocks.title: The clock you are actually racing
blocks.html: By the time saturations fall below roughly 90% they drop precipitously, not linearly — the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve's steep segment means you go from 90% to profound hypoxia in well under a minute in a patient with no reserve. Any plan that assumes you will have several minutes of gentle decline to make up your mind is wrong. Obese, pregnant, pediatric, and critically ill patients have essentially no reserve at all.

The human-factors failure modes, by name. These are what the audit data actually describes:

  • Task fixation — the operator who keeps re-attempting laryngoscopy because this time it will work. The strongest predictor of it is having just felt close to success.
  • Loss of situational awareness — nobody is watching the saturation trend because everybody is watching the mouth.
  • Diffusion of responsibility — several senior people present, none of whom believes it is their call to escalate.
  • Hierarchy — the person who first recognized CICO is the most junior in the room and raises it as a question rather than a statement.
  • Sunk cost — "we've come this far with this plan."

sections.title: Declaring It — The Steps That Matter

steps.title: Say the words out loud
steps.html: “This is CICO. We are performing a front-of-neck airway.” Said as a declaration, not a question. Verbalizing the diagnosis is the single act that shifts the whole team out of intubation mode — without it, everyone continues optimizing the thing that has already failed. This is the step that is most often skipped and it costs more lives than any technical error.

steps.title: Name people, not roles
steps.html: “Sarah, get the CICO cart. James, you're on the neck with me. Priya, keep the saturation and the time out loud.” Unaddressed requests in a crowded room are absorbed by everybody and actioned by nobody. Assign a timekeeper explicitly — time perception collapses in these events.

steps.title: Keep oxygen going through the front door
steps.html: Do not abandon upper-airway oxygenation because you have declared CICO. Leave the supraglottic device or mask in place with high-flow oxygen and continue attempts at passive or active oxygenation while the neck is being prepared. Any residual patency buys seconds, and — importantly — it is also the exhalation route if you end up using a needle technique.

steps.title: Default to scalpel–bougie–tube in adults
steps.html: Decide this before the emergency, as an institutional default, so it is not debated at the bedside. Adults: scalpel technique. Children below roughly 8–12 years, or an adult neck where open technique is genuinely impossible: needle. Do not pick up a Seldinger kit because it feels familiar — see the Cricothyrotomy entry for why speed decides this.

steps.title: Stop going back
steps.html: Once the decision is made, further attempts at oral intubation or mask ventilation by the same operator are a distraction that consumes the only resource that matters. A second person may continue upper-airway oxygenation; the person doing the neck does the neck.

steps.title: Confirm oxygenation, then stop and reassess everything
steps.html: A rising saturation through the front-of-neck airway ends the emergency, not the episode. Secure the tube, get imaging, manage bleeding, sedate, and plan the definitive airway.

blocks.title: Rehearse the sentence, not just the procedure
blocks.html: Teams that have said “this is CICO, we are moving to a surgical airway” out loud in simulation say it faster in reality. It sounds trivial. It is the single highest-yield thing you can rehearse, because the barrier in the real event is almost never manual dexterity — it is the social and cognitive cost of being the person who declares that the plan has failed.

sections.title: What Should Already Be True Before the Emergency

blocks.html:
• A CICO cart with a known location that every anesthetist, intensivist, and emergency clinician can find without asking.
  • One agreed default technique, institution-wide. Debate it at a governance meeting, never at a bedside.
  • A cognitive aid on the cart — a single laminated card. Working memory is the first thing hypoxic-patient stress takes away from you.
  • An airway assessment habit that flags the high-risk neck before induction: previous difficult airway, radiotherapy, neck mass, obesity, limited mouth opening, short thyromental distance, prior surgery.
  • A pre-induction verbalized plan for anyone flagged: “Plan A is videolaryngoscopy, plan B is a supraglottic, plan C is front-of-neck and the cart is in that corner.” Naming plan C out loud before you need it dramatically lowers the threshold to reach it.
  • Landmarks identified in advance in the high-risk patient — marking the cricothyroid membrane with a skin pen before induction takes fifteen seconds and removes the hardest step from the worst moment.

sections.title: When the Decision Is the Hard Part

rows: Third or fourth identical laryngoscopy attempt
Task fixation
Change something or stop. An unchanged attempt is not a new attempt
Nobody has said a number out loud in two minutes
Lost situational awareness
Assign a timekeeper to call saturation and elapsed time aloud every 30 seconds
Several seniors present, no decision being made
Diffusion of responsibility
One person names themselves team leader out loud and takes the decision
You think it's CICO but you're junior in the room
Hierarchy gradient
State it as an observation with a number: “Sat is 82 and falling, we've failed mask, SGA and tube — I think this is CICO.” Data is harder to wave away than a question
“Let's just try once more” after the diagnosis is made
Sunk cost
The declaration ends the debate. Someone else may oxygenate from above; the neck proceeds
Can't find the cart / unfamiliar kit
System failure, surfacing now
Scalpel, bougie, 6.0 tube is sufficient. Don't wait for a kit — that is the whole point of the default technique
Saturation briefly improves mid-preparation
The most dangerous moment in the event
Keep going unless oxygenation is genuinely restored and sustained. Transient improvement has repeatedly seduced teams into standing down too early

blocks.html:
• Delayed declaration — the dominant failure mode, by a wide margin
  • Choosing the slower technique (Seldinger, or an unfamiliar commercial kit) when speed was the deciding variable
  • Standing down on transient improvement, then having to restart the decision from scratch with less reserve than before
  • Abandoning upper-airway oxygenation the moment CICO is declared — it still buys time, and it is the exhalation route for needle techniques
  • Communication breakdown — if CICO isn't said out loud, help doesn't mobilize and the room stays in intubation mode
  • No pre-agreed default, producing a bedside debate about technique while the patient desaturates

The hard part is the decision, not the scalpel. Every element of preparation should be aimed at lowering the threshold to that decision.

Say it as a statement. “This is CICO, we are moving to a surgical airway” — not “do you think maybe we should…”

Name people, not roles. Unaddressed instructions are executed by nobody.

Mark the membrane before induction in a high-risk neck. Fifteen seconds then; the hardest step removed later.

Transient improvement is a trap. It is the most common reason a correctly-made decision gets reversed.

Rehearse it out loud. The team that has practiced the sentence moves faster than the individual who has only practiced the procedure.

procedures.title: Cricothyrotomy — Surgical, Percutaneous & Needle
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: Three techniques for one problem: Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate. Adapted from the author's original “Introduction to Surgical Airways” teaching deck, used with permission.
procedures.description: Surgical, percutaneous, and needle techniques for CICO.

blocks.html:
• Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate (CICO) — the only indication that matters in the moment
  • Artificial airway obstruction (device failure, blocked ETT or tracheostomy tube) that cannot be cleared
  • Pathologic airway obstruction — angioedema, trauma, burns, tumor, abscess, distorted anatomy — not amenable to oral or nasal intubation
  • Failure of primary and rescue airway techniques when oxygenation cannot be achieved by any other route

The indication is oxygenation, not intubation. A patient you cannot intubate but can oxygenate by mask or supraglottic airway is not a CICO patient — that is a difficult airway, and you have time to think. The front-of-neck decision belongs to the patient who is desaturating despite optimized attempts at all three of mask, supraglottic, and tube. See the Front-of-Neck Rescue Airway entry for the decision framework that sits above this one.

• In true CICO there are no absolute contraindications. The alternative to a front-of-neck airway in that situation is a hypoxic death.
  • A viable, faster alternative airway exists (relative) — if one more optimized laryngoscopy attempt or a supraglottic device will work, do that instead
  • Children under roughly 8–12 years — the cricothyroid membrane is tiny, soft, and hard to identify; needle technique is the default here and the age threshold varies between guidelines, so know which one your institution follows
  • Coagulopathy, overlying infection, or anterior neck tumor — all relative, and none of them outrank hypoxia

sections.title: Equipment — What Should Be on the CICO Cart

blocks.html:
Scalpel-bougie-tube (the adult default — this is the set that matters)

  • #10 scalpel — the broad belly is deliberate; a #11 point is easy to bury and harder to control
  • Bougie, ideally coudé-tipped
  • Cuffed tube, size 6.0 — a standard 7.0–8.0 ETT will often not pass a cricothyroid membrane. Have the 6.0 pre-identified, not hunted for mid-procedure.
  • Syringe for the cuff, tube tie or suture, capnography

Needle cricothyrotomy (pediatric default, adult fallback)

  • Large-bore cannula, 12–14 ga in adults, smaller in children
  • Syringe (saline-filled, so aspirated air shows as bubbles)
  • A purpose-built ventilation device with a pressure-limited source and an exhalation route — not an improvised setup assembled for the first time under pressure. A 3 mm ETT connector or a 3-way stopcock arrangement works, but know which one is on your cart and how it assembles.

Percutaneous (Seldinger) kit — and the things people forget

  • Introducer needle, guidewire, dilator, airway catheter (commercial kits vary — open yours once in daylight before you need it at 3 a.m.)
  • Ultrasound with a linear probe — the single most useful addition to a difficult-neck CICO cart
  • Suction, working and within reach — the field will bleed
  • Gloves you can actually feel through. This is a tactile procedure.

blocks.title: Know which kit is on your cart before the emergency
blocks.html: The most common equipment failure in a real CICO event is not a missing item — it is an operator meeting an unfamiliar commercial kit for the first time while a patient desaturates. Open your institution's kit once, lay the parts out, and assemble it. That fifteen-minute exercise is worth more than any amount of reading.

blocks.html: This is where the procedure is actually won or lost

The laryngeal handshake. Stand at the patient's side. With your non-dominant hand, grasp the larynx between thumb and middle finger and walk down the midline: the hyoid first, then the thyroid cartilage (the broad shield, with the notch superiorly), then the soft depression immediately below it — that is the cricothyroid membrane — and then the firm ring of the cricoid cartilage below that. Rock the larynx gently side to side as you go; the whole assembly moves as a unit, which is how you distinguish it from surrounding soft tissue.

In an adult the membrane sits roughly a finger's breadth below the thyroid notch and is about 1 cm tall and 2–3 cm wide — a small target, and smaller still in women.

When you cannot feel anything — obesity, edema, hematoma, burns. This is common and it is the situation that kills.

  • Ultrasound, if it is already in the room and someone can drive it. Linear probe transverse across the anterior neck: the tracheal rings appear as a row of hypoechoic arcs, and sliding cephalad the cricoid is the largest and most prominent. Do not go looking for the machine mid-arrest.
  • If there is no ultrasound, the incision is the assessment. Make a long vertical midline incision — 8–10 cm if you have no landmarks at all — and dissect bluntly with your finger down to the larynx. Midline is relatively avascular; this is precisely why vertical is the correct choice when you are unsure.
  • Then palpate inside the wound. Your finger, not your eye, finds the membrane in a bleeding neck.

blocks.title: Never let go of the larynx
blocks.html: Once your non-dominant hand has the larynx, it stays there until the tube is in. Every time you release to reposition, adjust a glove, or take an instrument, you lose the anatomy and start again — in a neck that is now bleeding. Hand off instruments, accept awkward angles, but do not let go.
Fastest, most reliable, and the technique to default to when seconds matter

steps.title: Position and expose
steps.html: Extend the neck if not contraindicated — it brings the larynx forward and makes everything easier. Stand at the patient's side, not the head. Get the neck exposed properly; do not operate through a gown collar or a cervical collar's front panel (open it, and have someone hold manual in-line stabilization if the spine is a concern).

steps.title: Stabilize the larynx and choose your incision
steps.html: Laryngeal handshake with the non-dominant hand. If you can confidently palpate the membrane, a transverse stab through it is reasonable. If you cannot, make a long vertical midline skin incision first — it stays out of the anterior jugular veins, it can be extended in either direction, and it lets you feel your way down. When in doubt, vertical.

steps.title: Stab through the membrane, then turn the blade
steps.html: With the membrane identified, insert the scalpel through it transversely. Then rotate the blade so the sharp edge points caudally (toward the feet). This orients the opening and, critically, gives the bougie a surface to slide along. Keep the blade in place — it is now your guide, and removing it means finding the hole again.

steps.title: Slide the bougie along the blade, angled caudally
steps.html: Pass the bougie into the trachea alongside the scalpel blade, directed toward the carina. Some operators substitute a finger for the blade at this point to hold the tract open — the finger-and-bougie combination is what confirms you are in the trachea in a dark, bloody field. You are looking for tracheal clicks as the coudé tip runs over the cartilage rings, and hold-up at 20–30 cm. Soft, endless advancement with neither clicks nor hold-up means you are in tissue or esophagus.

steps.title: Railroad a 6.0 cuffed tube
steps.html: Remove the scalpel, keeping the bougie and your stabilizing hand exactly where they are. Railroad the tube over the bougie with a gentle rotating motion — if it catches at the membrane, twisting usually walks it through where pushing will not. Advance only about 5–6 cm past the membrane. This is not an oral intubation; pushing to a normal 22 cm mark puts you in the right mainstem or through the carina.

steps.title: Remove bougie, inflate cuff, confirm, secure
steps.html: Withdraw the bougie, inflate the cuff, ventilate, and confirm (see below). Then secure the tube immediately and obsessively — a surgical airway sits in a short, slippery tract with nothing anatomical holding it, and it will fall out during the first transfer if it is only being held by the person who placed it.

blocks.title: Bleeding is expected. Keep going.
blocks.html: The anterior neck bleeds, mostly venous, and it will obscure your view almost immediately. This is not a complication to stop and fix — it is the normal appearance of the procedure. In CICO the bleeding does not kill the patient in the next two minutes and the hypoxia does. Work by feel, keep the larynx stabilized, and deal with hemostasis once the airway is secured.

sections.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy — And Why Exhalation Is the Whole Problem

blocks.html: The pediatric default, and an adult temporizing measure only

steps.title: Puncture caudally, aspirating as you go
steps.html: Stabilize the larynx. Insert the cannula through the membrane angled caudally at about 45°, with a saline-filled syringe on the hub, aspirating continuously. Free bubbling of air confirms tracheal entry — the saline is what makes that unmistakable.

steps.title: Advance the cannula, withdraw the needle, hold on
steps.html: Slide the cannula off the needle into the trachea and remove the needle. Hold the cannula continuously by hand — it kinks and dislodges with almost no provocation, and it is the only airway the patient has.

steps.title: Connect the ventilation device you already know
steps.html: Attach your pressure-limited oxygen source or the 3 mm connector/stopcock arrangement from your cart. A standard bag-valve will generate almost no flow through a 14 ga cannula — this needs a high-pressure source to work at all.

steps.title: Ventilate with a long expiratory phase and watch the chest fall
steps.html: Short insufflation, then a markedly prolonged expiratory phase — think in the region of 1:4 or longer. Watch the chest actually come back down between breaths. If it does not, stop insufflating. Stacking breaths into a chest that cannot empty is how this technique kills people.

blocks.alt: Why needle cricothyrotomy depends on the upper airway. In the left panel the upper airway is partly patent, so gas insufflated through the narrow cannula can escape upward past the obstruction and the chest falls between breaths. In the right panel the obstruction is complete, gas enters through the cannula but cannot leave, intrathoracic pressure rises with every breath, and the result is barotrauma, pneumothorax and circulatory collapse.
blocks.caption: If the chest does not come back down between insufflations, stop. Stacking breaths into a chest that cannot empty is how this technique kills people — and it is the reason a needle cricothyrotomy is a bridge, never the answer to a completely obstructed airway.

blocks.title: Gas goes in through the cannula; it comes out through the upper airway
blocks.html: A 14 ga cannula is an inadequate exhalation route. Expiration depends on the patient's own upper airway being at least partially patent. If the obstruction is complete — total supraglottic obstruction, severe angioedema, a foreign body — insufflated gas has nowhere to go, intrathoracic pressure climbs with every breath, and you produce barotrauma, pneumothorax, and circulatory collapse. In complete obstruction a needle technique is the wrong answer; you need a cuffed surgical airway.

Needle cricothyrotomy is a bridge, not a destination. Ventilation through a narrow cannula does not clear CO2 adequately, so hypercarbia climbs steadily — usable for roughly 30–45 minutes. Start arranging the definitive airway the moment the cannula is working, not when the gas goes bad.
Familiar sequence, but it costs time you may not have

steps.title: Puncture and confirm
steps.html: Stabilize the larynx; introducer needle through the membrane angled caudally, aspirating a saline-filled syringe until air bubbles freely.

steps.title: Wire in, needle out
steps.html: Thread the guidewire caudally into the trachea and remove the needle over it. From this point the wire is the airway — never let go of it, and never pull it back through the needle.

steps.title: Nick the skin, then dilate
steps.html: Small vertical skin incision at the wire to let the dilator through, then advance the dilator-and-airway assembly over the wire with a firm, steady, rotating push. The resistance at the membrane is real and expected; it is also exactly where a false passage gets created if your angle has drifted.

steps.title: Airway in, dilator and wire out, confirm
steps.html: Slide the airway off the dilator into the trachea, remove dilator and wire together, inflate the cuff if present, confirm and secure.

blocks.title: Right sequence, wrong emergency
blocks.html: Seldinger technique is elegant and most clinicians are fluent in it from central lines — which is exactly why it is tempting under stress. It is also measurably slower than scalpel–bougie–tube, has more steps to drop, and depends on fine motor control that degrades badly with adrenaline. In a true CICO, reach for the scalpel. Keep this technique for the semi-elective, better-lit, slightly-more-time situation.

sections.title: Confirming You Are in the Trachea

blocks.html:
• Waveform capnography is the standard — but read the caveat below before you rely on its absence.
  • Bougie feel, at the time of insertion: tracheal clicks and hold-up at 20–30 cm. Soft endless passage is a red flag you get before committing the tube.
  • Chest rise, bilateral breath sounds, absence of gastric insufflation.
  • Bedside ultrasound — tracheal widening on tube passage, or lung sliding bilaterally.
  • Rising SpO2, allowing for the lag in a profoundly hypoxic patient.

blocks.title: Absent capnography in an arrested patient does not mean you missed
blocks.html: End-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> depends on pulmonary blood flow. In cardiac arrest, or in a patient who has been profoundly hypoxic with a failing circulation, the trace may be flat or minimal even with a perfectly placed tube. Do not pull a correctly sited surgical airway because the capnograph is unconvincing during arrest — corroborate with bougie feel, chest rise, and ultrasound instead.

Rotate rather than push. Drop to a 6.0 (or smaller) if you started bigger. Consider extending the incision
Tube passes but no capnography

Check bougie feel, chest rise, ultrasound. Do not reflexively pull a tube that felt right during arrest

Stop ventilating through it. Reassess position directly; be prepared to start again
Needle technique: chest not falling between breaths

Stop insufflating. Convert to a cuffed surgical airway. Expect and look for pneumothorax

blocks.html:
• Delayed recognition of CICO — consistently the biggest driver of bad outcomes, ahead of any technical failure. The scalpel is rarely the problem; the twelve minutes before it was picked up usually are.
  • False passage into pretracheal tissue, with ventilation producing surgical emphysema and no gas exchange
  • Posterior wall injury — through the trachea into the esophagus, from an over-deep stab or a blade angled posteriorly
  • Barotrauma and pneumothorax from needle ventilation without an exhalation route
  • Bleeding — expected and survivable acutely; anterior jugular veins and, rarely, an aberrant high thyroid vessel
  • Tube dislodgement, especially during transfer — the most common way a successful airway is subsequently lost
  • Subglottic stenosis as a late consequence, which is why conversion to a definitive airway is planned rather than indefinite
  • Choosing the slow technique — reaching for a Seldinger kit because it feels familiar, when the situation demanded a scalpel

• Secure it as though someone is going to pull on it, then check it again after every move.
  • Now get hemostasis — the bleeding you correctly ignored still needs dealing with.
  • Sedate and analgese. A patient who arrives at this point conscious has just had their neck cut open.
  • Chest radiograph for tube position and to look for the pneumothorax you may have caused, particularly after needle ventilation.
  • Plan the definitive airway early. A cricothyrotomy is a bridge; conversion to a formal tracheostomy or an oral tube is an elective, controlled decision made in daylight — not a 3 a.m. improvisation. See the Tracheostomy entry.
  • Debrief the team. These events are rare, fast, and frightening, and the learning evaporates within hours if nobody captures it.

If you are doing this, you have already failed two other airway plans. Commit fully. Mid-procedure second-guessing is what turns a survivable CICO into a death.

The hand on the larynx never leaves. If you remember one motor habit from this page, make it that one.

When you cannot feel the landmarks, cut vertically and use your finger. The midline is relatively avascular and the incision is how you find the anatomy — not something you do after finding it.

Tracheal clicks and hold-up are your confirmation, and they arrive before you commit the tube. Soft, endless bougie passage is the cheapest warning you will get; heed it.

Use a 6.0. The tube that will not fit is a predictable, preventable delay.

Needle technique needs somewhere for the gas to go. In complete obstruction it is not a rescue — it is a barotrauma generator.

Practice on a model, regularly. This is the definitive low-frequency, high-stakes psychomotor skill, and under adrenaline you will do what you have rehearsed, not what you have read.

procedures.title: Retrograde Intubation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: A backup technique for the difficult airway when fiberoptic and video laryngoscopy aren't available or aren't working — a wire from below guiding the tube from above.
procedures.description: Wire-guided backup when fiberoptic/video fails.

blocks.html:
• Difficult airway where laryngoscopy and video-assisted techniques have failed or are unavailable
  • Blood or secretions obscuring the view — the one situation where this technique has a genuine edge, because it does not depend on seeing anything
  • Limited mouth opening that prevents a rigid scope, where the cricothyroid membrane is still accessible
  • Resource-limited settings without fiberoptic or video laryngoscopy
  • A patient who is maintaining oxygenation while you work — this is a difficult-airway technique, not a rescue one

Know where this sits on the ladder. Slower than video laryngoscopy, slower than fiberoptic, and far slower than a scalpel. It belongs to the difficult-but-not-yet-critical airway in a patient who is still oxygenating. If the patient is desaturating and you cannot oxygenate, this is the wrong page — go to Cricothyrotomy.

• True CICO. Absolutely. This technique takes minutes you do not have; go directly to a front-of-neck airway.
  • Distorted or unidentifiable anterior neck anatomy preventing safe membrane puncture
  • Coagulopathy, or infection/tumor overlying the puncture site (relative)
  • Any faster appropriate option is available — retrograde intubation is a backup, and choosing it over something quicker is itself the error

• Introducer needle (18 ga or the needle from a percutaneous cricothyrotomy/central line kit), with a saline-filled syringe so tracheal air shows as bubbles
  • A long wire — this is the critical spec. You need enough length to span from the neck, up through the larynx, out of the mouth, and still have the tube railroaded over it. A standard 45–50 cm central line wire is marginal; a long (≥110 cm) J-wire or an epidural catheter is what you actually want.
  • Magill forceps and a laryngoscope for retrieving the wire from the pharynx
  • An airway exchange catheter or the Aintree-type catheter — strongly preferred over railroading the ETT directly (see the technique note below)
  • ETT, a size smaller than you would normally pick
  • Local anesthetic if the patient is awake, plus topicalization as for any awake technique
  • A clamp or hemostat to grip the wire at the neck — losing the wire into the trachea is a real and avoidable complication
A wire from below, guiding a tube from above

steps.title: Identify and stabilize the cricothyroid membrane
steps.html: Laryngeal handshake, as for cricothyrotomy. Topicalize the skin and, if the patient is awake, the airway itself — a transtracheal injection of lidocaine at this point conveniently anesthetizes the very structures the wire is about to irritate.

steps.title: Puncture the membrane aiming CEPHALAD
steps.html: This is the one direction that is opposite to every other neck procedure. Cricothyrotomy, percutaneous tracheostomy, and transtracheal blocks all angle caudally, toward the carina. Here you angle cephalad, toward the head, because the wire has to travel up through the cords and out of the mouth. Confirm tracheal entry with free air bubbles into the saline-filled syringe before threading anything.

steps.title: Thread the wire up and out
steps.html: Advance the wire cephalad through the needle; it passes through the larynx and coils in the pharynx. Feed generously — you want plenty of length in the mouth. Then remove the needle over the wire, and immediately clamp the wire at the skin so it cannot migrate inward.

steps.title: Retrieve the wire from the mouth
steps.html: Laryngoscope in, Magill forceps to grab the wire and bring the end out through the mouth. If you cannot see it, a finger sweep will often hook it. Maintain tension at both ends from here on — one hand at the neck, one at the mouth. Slack is how wires get lost.

steps.title: Pass a catheter over the wire — not the tube directly
steps.html: Thread an airway exchange catheter over the oral end and advance it down to the larynx. This is the step that makes the technique work reliably: the catheter is stiff, small-calibre, and follows the wire faithfully, whereas an ETT bevel catches at the cords and the step-off between wire and tube is enormous. Advance the catheter until it meets the neck puncture site.

steps.title: Release the wire from below and advance the catheter deeper
steps.html: Unclamp and withdraw the wire out through the mouth while holding the catheter still. The catheter now sits in the trachea, but only as far as the cricothyroid membrane — so advance it further toward the carina before railroading. A catheter that stops at the membrane gives the tube almost nothing to track over.

steps.title: Railroad the ETT, rotating counterclockwise if it hangs up
steps.html: Advance the tube over the catheter with a gentle 90° counterclockwise rotation if it catches — the right arytenoid is the usual obstacle, exactly as in fiberoptic technique. Keep the catheter absolutely still.

steps.title: Remove the catheter, confirm, secure, and dress the neck
steps.html: Withdraw the catheter, inflate the cuff, confirm with capnography and auscultation, secure the tube. Then apply a dressing and light pressure to the puncture site and document that a transtracheal puncture was made — someone will otherwise be puzzled by subcutaneous air on a later film.

blocks.alt: Retrograde intubation wire direction, shown as a vertical schematic of the airway. The needle punctures the cricothyroid membrane and is angled cephalad, upward, so the wire travels up past the cricoid and thyroid cartilage, through the vocal cords, up the pharynx and out of the mouth where it is retrieved. A contrasting downward arrow marks the direction used by cricothyrotomy and percutaneous tracheostomy, which both angle caudally toward the carina.
blocks.caption: The needle angles cephalad — the most commonly inverted detail in this procedure, precisely because cricothyrotomy, percutaneous tracheostomy and transtracheal blocks all angle the other way.

blocks.title: Cephalad here; caudad everywhere else
blocks.html: The needle direction is the most commonly inverted detail in this procedure, precisely because every other anterior-neck technique you know goes the other way. Angling caudally sends the wire toward the carina and the technique simply fails. Say the direction out loud before you puncture.

blocks.title: The wire is the procedure — never let both ends go
blocks.html: From the moment the wire is through the membrane until it is removed, one end is clamped or held at all times. A wire released at the neck can be pulled entirely into the trachea; a wire released at the mouth retracts and has to be retrieved again. Both are avoidable with a hemostat and a habit.

rows: No air aspirated on puncture
Not in the trachea — pretracheal or paratracheal
Withdraw, re-identify the membrane, re-angle. Do not thread a wire you haven't confirmed
Wire won't advance after the needle is in
Bevel against the posterior wall, or angled caudally
Withdraw slightly, re-angle cephalad, rotate the needle. Never force a wire
Wire can't be found in the pharynx
Coiled in the vallecula or behind the tongue
Laryngoscope + Magill. Finger sweep. Feed more wire from below to give yourself something to grab
Tube catches at the cords
Right arytenoid, and a big wire-to-tube step-off
Rotate 90° counterclockwise. Downsize the tube. This is precisely why an exchange catheter is used as an intermediate
Tube advances but sits too shallow
Tube tip stopped at the membrane puncture level
Advance further once the catheter/wire is out — the guide only ever leads you as deep as the puncture site
Wire disappears into the trachea
Both ends released
Bronchoscopic or forceps retrieval; this may become a surgical problem. Prevent it with a clamp
Bleeding at the puncture site
Anterior neck vessels
Usually minor; pressure after the airway is secured. It rarely obscures this technique the way it does an open one
Subcutaneous emphysema afterwards
Air tracking from the puncture
Usually self-limiting; document it so it isn't misread later. Watch for pneumothorax if it's extensive
Patient desaturating during the procedure
You have run out of the time this technique needs
Abandon and go to a front-of-neck airway. The membrane is already identified and topicalized — you are unusually well positioned to cut

blocks.html:
• Time cost — the defining drawback, and the reason it is the wrong choice in a deteriorating patient
  • Wire loss into the trachea, or loss of position during tube advancement
  • Failure at the glottic inlet, from railroading an ETT directly over a thin wire
  • Bleeding, subcutaneous emphysema, and rarely pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum
  • Esophageal or posterior tracheal wall puncture from an over-deep needle
  • Infection at the puncture site, particularly if the field was rushed
  • False reassurance — persisting with a technique that is not progressing, and thereby delaying the surgical airway the patient actually needed

Cephalad. Say it out loud before you puncture. Every neighbouring procedure goes the other way.

Use an exchange catheter as an intermediate. Railroading a tube straight over a wire is where this technique earns its reputation for failing at the cords.

One end of the wire is always held. A hemostat at the neck costs nothing and prevents the worst complication.

Advance the catheter deeper before railroading — the guide otherwise only reaches the membrane, which is not deep enough to steer a tube.

Its niche is blood. When the view is obliterated and fiberoptics are useless but the patient is still oxygenating, this technique does something nothing else does.

Set a time limit before you start, and when you hit it, convert. You are already standing over an identified, anesthetized cricothyroid membrane — the fastest surgical airway of your career is one decision away.

procedures.title: Awake Fiberoptic Intubation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The controlled, spontaneously-breathing approach to the anticipated difficult airway — topicalize, sedate lightly, scope while the patient protects their own airway.
procedures.description: Controlled airway access preserving spontaneous ventilation.

blocks.html:
• Anticipated difficult airway — limited mouth opening, cervical immobility, airway mass or distortion, radiotherapy-scarred neck, prior documented difficult intubation
  • Upper airway pathology (tumor, abscess, angioedema, supraglottic swelling) where induction could convert a partial obstruction into a complete one
  • Unstable cervical spine where laryngoscopy positioning is contraindicated
  • Any situation where you want the patient's own respiratory effort preserved as the safety net through the intubation

The whole point is that nothing irreversible happens. Every other airway technique begins by removing the patient's ability to breathe for themselves and then betting you can replace it. This one doesn't place that bet. That is the reason to choose it, and also the reason oversedation is the cardinal sin — it quietly converts this procedure into the one you were trying to avoid.

• A rapidly deteriorating airway. This technique costs 15–30 minutes done properly. A patient who does not have that is a patient for a surgical airway or an awake look with a plan to cut.
  • Uncooperative patient — delirium, intoxication, learning disability, young children (relative; may force an alternative plan rather than heavier sedation, which defeats the purpose)
  • Active vomiting or frank blood in the airway — you cannot see through either, and topicalization of a wet airway is unreliable
  • Severe local anesthetic allergy (relative — alternative agents exist)
  • Critical stenosis where the scope itself may obstruct what little lumen remains — think carefully before passing a 5 mm scope through a 6 mm airway

sections.title: Equipment — Laid Out Before You Touch the Patient

blocks.html:
• Flexible scope, light source and screen, checked and focused before the patient is in the room. Anti-fog applied, or the tip warmed.
  • ETT preloaded on the shaft, pushed up to the handle and secured there. A reinforced or flexible-tip tube, or an Aintree/intubating catheter arrangement, snags far less than a standard PVC bevel.
  • One size smaller than you'd normally choose — a 6.0–7.0 in most adults. The narrower the tube, the smaller the step-off between scope and tube tip, and the step-off is what catches.
  • Lidocaine, and a plan for the total dose. Atomiser (MAD-type), nebuliser, and a syringe for spray-as-you-go down the working channel.
  • Antisialagogue — glycopyrrolate, given early enough to work (see below).
  • Vasoconstrictor for the nasal route — oxymetazoline or phenylephrine.
  • Sedation you can titrate in small increments — dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, or low-dose midazolam/fentanyl. Draw it up dilute.
  • Oxygen throughout — nasal cannula under the mask, or high-flow nasal oxygen, running the entire time.
  • The difficult airway trolley open in the room, and a named person ready to do a front-of-neck airway if this goes wrong.

blocks.title: Give the antisialagogue early or don't bother
blocks.html: Glycopyrrolate needs roughly 15–20 minutes to meaningfully dry secretions. Given as you walk into the room it contributes nothing except tachycardia. Secretions are the most common reason the view is unusable, and this is the cheapest intervention against them — but only if someone thought about it a quarter of an hour ago.
A well-topicalized patient needs almost no sedation; a poorly topicalized one cannot be rescued by any amount of it

Work through the territories in order, each with its own nerve supply:

  • Nasal cavity (if nasal route) — vasoconstrictor plus lidocaine; anterior ethmoidal and sphenopalatine supply.
  • Oropharynx and tongue base — glossopharyngeal. This is the gag reflex. Atomized lidocaine, and ask the patient to hold it at the back of the throat rather than swallowing immediately.
  • Supraglottis, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds — superior laryngeal nerve (internal branch).
  • Vocal cords and trachea below them — recurrent laryngeal. This territory is the one people under-treat, and it is where coughing comes from.

Spray-as-you-go through the working channel is the workhorse: advance a little, spray, wait ten or fifteen seconds, advance again. It topicalizes exactly what you are about to touch, in the right order, without a separate procedure.

Keep a running total of the lidocaine. Topical airway lidocaine is absorbed rapidly across mucosa — nebulized, atomized, and sprayed doses all add up, and it is easy to lose count across three different delivery devices. Know your institution's ceiling for topical airway use, say the running total out loud, and have intralipid available in the department. Early LAST is agitation, perioral tingling, and metallic taste — symptoms you may misread as inadequate sedation and treat by giving more of the wrong thing.

steps.title: Consent and coach the patient
steps.html: Explain it in plain terms — that they will stay awake and breathing, that their throat will feel numb and strange, that they may feel pressure but not pain, and that coughing is normal. A patient who knows what is coming tolerates it dramatically better. This conversation is part of the technique, not a courtesy before it.

steps.title: Position sitting up, and stand where you'll actually scope from
steps.html: Sitting or semi-recumbent is more comfortable, improves their respiratory mechanics, and drains secretions away. Decide early whether you scope from in front (facing them) or from behind at the head, and set the screen where you can see it without turning away from the patient.

steps.title: Oxygen on, monitoring on, sedation titrated to conversation
steps.html: The endpoint for sedation is a calm patient who still answers you. If they stop responding to voice, you have gone too far. Dexmedetomidine preserves respiratory drive well but takes time to load; remifentanil blunts cough well but will cause apnoea if you rush it. Small increments, and wait for the peak effect before giving more — stacking doses while waiting is the classic route to an apnoeic patient.

steps.title: Advance in the midline, and keep the scope straight
steps.html: Keep the shaft straight between your hand and the patient — a looped or coiled shaft means your tip movements stop corresponding to your wrist movements, which is the single most common reason a novice gets lost. Advance under continuous vision. If you cannot identify a structure, withdraw until you can rather than pushing on in hope. The one rule that recovers every lost scope: pull back to something you recognize.

steps.title: Identify the glottis, spray, and pass the cords
steps.html: Landmarks in order: uvula and soft palate, epiglottis, then the cords. Spray through the channel before passing them — this is where cough is generated. Advance the tip through the glottis and confirm you are tracheal by seeing cartilaginous rings and the carina. Rings and a bifurcation are proof; a dark hole is not.

steps.title: Railroad the tube — rotate, don't shove
steps.html: Hold the scope absolutely still, as a rail, and advance the tube with a 90° counterclockwise rotation if it hangs up. The tube catches on the right arytenoid in the great majority of cases, and that rotation turns the bevel away from it. Escalating force does not work and causes trauma; rotation almost always does.

steps.title: Confirm depth from inside before you withdraw
steps.html: Before removing the scope, look: you should see the carina a few centimeters beyond the tube tip. This is a better depth check than any external marking. Then withdraw the scope slowly, watching that the tube does not come with it.

steps.title: Confirm, secure, and only then induce
steps.html: Capnography, chest rise, bilateral air entry. Secure the tube. Only now give the induction agent. Inducing before confirmation discards the entire safety rationale of the technique — and it happens, under time pressure, when everyone in the room can see the tube is “obviously” in.

blocks.title: Sedation depth is the whole safety margin
blocks.html: Every milligram you give trades away the thing that makes this technique safe. The patient who stops breathing during an awake fiberoptic has not had a complication of the procedure — they have had a complication of the sedation, and they are now an unanticipated CICO with a scope in their mouth. If you are reaching for more sedation, the problem is almost always inadequate topicalization, and more local is the correct answer.

rows: View is a pink/red blur
Tip against mucosa — you're touching the wall
Withdraw a few centimeters until the lumen reappears. Do not suction blindly or push forward
View fogs or smears
Secretions or condensation
Touch the tip to mucosa to wipe, suction, or flush the channel. Anti-fog and a warmed tip prevent most of it
Completely lost, no recognizable structure
Off midline, or shaft looped
Withdraw to the nasopharynx/oropharynx and start again. Straighten the shaft. This recovers almost every lost scope
Patient coughing repeatedly
Under-topicalized cords/trachea — not under-sedated
More local through the channel, wait. Resist the reflex to deepen sedation
Patient gagging on the oral route
Tongue base not topicalized
More atomized lidocaine to the posterior tongue; consider switching to nasal
Tube hangs up at the glottis
Catching on the right arytenoid (the usual culprit)
Rotate 90° counterclockwise and advance gently. Downsize the tube if it still won't pass
Tube advances but the scope view is lost
Scope displaced by the tube, or tube went esophageal
Do not extubate on suspicion — confirm with capnography first. If esophageal, leave it as a marker and re-scope alongside
Brisk bleeding, nasal route
Turbinate trauma — inadequate vasoconstriction or too large a tube
Switch to the other nostril or go oral. Blood in the airway usually ends the fiberoptic plan
Respiratory rate falling, patient not answering
Oversedation
Stop sedation, stimulate, support ventilation, consider reversal. Be ready to abandon to plan B
Agitation, perioral tingling, metallic taste
Local anesthetic toxicity — not inadequate sedation
Stop dosing local, total up what's been given, intralipid available. Do not "treat" this with more sedation
Fifteen minutes gone, no progress
The technique is failing
Call it. Move to the pre-agreed plan B before the patient's reserve is gone

blocks.html:
• Oversedation converting an awake technique into an unplanned loss of airway — the central risk of the procedure
  • Local anesthetic systemic toxicity from cumulative topical dosing across multiple devices
  • Epistaxis obscuring the view and, occasionally, soiling the airway outright
  • Laryngospasm from instrumenting an inadequately topicalized larynx
  • Complete obstruction in a critical stenosis — the scope or the resulting edema taking the last of a marginal lumen
  • Esophageal intubation if orientation was lost and rings were never positively identified
  • Taking too long in a patient whose airway was deteriorating faster than the operator appreciated

Topicalization buys you everything; sedation buys you very little and costs a great deal. When tempted to deepen sedation, give more local instead.

Keep the shaft straight. Loops are why the tip stops obeying your hand.

When lost, withdraw. Pulling back to a recognized structure recovers nearly every disoriented scope; pushing forward in hope recovers none.

Rings and carina, or you are not in the trachea. A dark hole is not a diagnosis.

Rotate the tube, don't force it. The right arytenoid is the obstacle, and 90° counterclockwise is the answer.

Confirm before you induce. This is the entire safety argument for the technique; do not spend it at the last step.

Decide your abort criterion out loud beforehand — a time or a number of attempts — because in the moment there is always a reason to try once more.

Glycopyrrolate at least fifteen minutes ahead. Secretions ruin more of these than any technical problem.

procedures.title: Percutaneous / Surgical Tracheostomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Airway
procedures.subtitle: The definitive-airway conversation, not the crisis-moment tool. Adapted from the author's original “Introduction to Surgical Airways” teaching deck, used with permission.
procedures.description: Definitive long-term airway, not a rescue technique.

blocks.html:
• Anticipated prolonged mechanical ventilation — the commonest reason by far
  • Failure to wean, or a protracted weaning course where a trachy improves comfort, sedation requirements, and secretion clearance
  • Inability to protect the airway with an expected prolonged course (bulbar weakness, severe brain injury)
  • Upper airway obstruction requiring a durable bypass
  • Definitive conversion following an emergency cricothyrotomy, once the patient is stable

blocks.title: This is not a rescue airway
blocks.html: If the question is “can this patient breathe in the next four minutes,” the answer is a cricothyrotomy, not a tracheostomy. The cricothyroid membrane is superficial, avascular, and immediately below the skin; the trachea at the 2nd–3rd ring sits deeper, behind the strap muscles and often behind the thyroid isthmus, in a more vascular field. Attempting a tracheostomy in a true CICO costs time the patient does not have. See the Cricothyrotomy entry.

• Emergent CICO — absolute, for the reason above
  • Uncorrected coagulopathy (relative; correct first for an elective procedure)
  • Age under ~12–16 — pediatric tracheostomy is an open, specialist procedure; percutaneous technique is not appropriate

Palpable landmarks, normal neck
Obesity, short neck, impalpable cricoid, goitre, fixed neck
Prior surgery/radiotherapy
None
Previous neck surgery or radiotherapy — distorted planes, scarred tissue
Coagulation
Normal or corrected
Coagulopathy, or high aberrant vessels on ultrasound
Spine

Logistics
Avoids transfer of an unstable ICU patient
Difficult anatomy worth doing under direct vision

blocks.html:
Percutaneous dilational (bedside ICU)

  • Commercial PDT kit — introducer needle, guidewire, single graduated dilator (or sequential dilators), loading dilators, tracheostomy tube
  • Bronchoscope with a dedicated operator — a second clinician whose only job is the scope and the view
  • Ultrasound to map midline, tracheal rings, thyroid isthmus and, critically, aberrant anterior vessels before puncture
  • Capnography, suction, full monitoring, emergency reintubation equipment immediately to hand
  • A named airway operator at the head managing the existing ETT — this role is as important as the operator at the neck

Open surgical (theatre)

  • Scalpel, retractors (including a Cricoid/Langenbeck), dissecting scissors, diathermy, suction, ties/sutures
  • Tracheostomy tubes: your intended size, plus one smaller, plus a cuffed ETT for rescue
  • Tracheal dilator (Trousseau) and tracheal hook — the instruments that save a lost tract
  • Shoulder roll for neck extension

blocks.title: Have a smaller tube and a reintubation plan open in the room
blocks.html: The two moments this procedure goes wrong are losing the airway at the head during the exchange, and failing to place the tracheostomy tube after the trachea is already open. Both are survivable if a cuffed ETT and a smaller trachy tube are physically present and someone is assigned to the oral airway. Both are disasters if they must be fetched.
Two operators, two airways, one shared moment of vulnerability

steps.title: Position, pre-oxygenate, and map with ultrasound
steps.html: Shoulder roll, neck extended (if the spine allows), FiO2 1.0. Scan before you prep: identify midline, count the rings, find the cricoid, locate the thyroid isthmus, and look specifically for an aberrant anterior jugular or high innominate vessel crossing your intended puncture site. Mark the skin.

steps.title: Withdraw the ETT under bronchoscopic vision — do not extubate
steps.html: The head operator withdraws the existing tube until the cuff sits just below the cords, with the bronchoscope confirming. This is the single most dangerous step of the procedure: pulled too far you have extubated a critically ill patient; left too deep and your introducer needle will puncture the ETT cuff or the tube itself. The scope stays in the ETT throughout.

steps.title: Puncture between the 1st–2nd or 2nd–3rd rings, transilluminating and watching from inside
steps.html: Small horizontal skin incision, blunt-dissect down to pretracheal tissue, then introduce the needle in the midline, angled caudally, aspirating air. The bronchoscopist confirms the needle enters in the midline, at the correct interspace, and not through the posterior wall. Too high (through the cricoid or the 1st ring) causes subglottic stenosis; too low risks the innominate artery.

steps.title: Wire in, confirm it heads toward the carina
steps.html: Thread the J-wire caudally and have the bronchoscopist confirm it is running down toward the carina, not up toward the cords. Remove the needle. The wire is now the only thing preserving your tract — it does not get released.

steps.title: Dilate over the wire, countering with the other hand
steps.html: Pass the loading dilator, then the graduated dilator over the wire with a firm, steady, rotating advance. Support the anterior neck with your other hand to counter the force — unopposed pushing indents the trachea and risks posterior wall injury. Keep the wire moving freely; if it kinks, stop, straighten and start the dilation again rather than forcing over a bent wire.

steps.title: Railroad the tracheostomy tube, then remove obturator and wire together
steps.html: Load the tube on its dilator, advance over the wire into the trachea, then remove the inner dilator and the wire as one. Inflate the cuff, connect the circuit, and confirm with capnography and the bronchoscope passed down the new tube — you want to see rings and carina through the trachy, not just hear breath sounds.

steps.title: Only now remove the ETT
steps.html: The oral tube stays in place, cuff down, until the tracheostomy is confirmed working. It is your rescue airway, and withdrawing it early is how a recoverable problem becomes an emergency. Once confirmed, remove it, secure the trachy with ties and/or sutures, and document tube size, depth, and the number of dilations.

steps.title: Position and mark
steps.html: Supine, shoulder roll, neck extended if permitted. Palpate and mark the thyroid notch, cricoid, and sternal notch. Your target is the 2nd–3rd tracheal ring — roughly midway between cricoid and sternal notch, closer to the notch than the cricothyroid membrane.

steps.title: Incise and stay midline
steps.html: Transverse incision about two fingerbreadths above the sternal notch (better cosmesis) or vertical midline (faster, extensible). Then dissect strictly in the midline raphe between the strap muscles and retract them laterally — the midline is the avascular plane, and wandering off it is what produces bleeding.

steps.title: Deal with the thyroid isthmus deliberately
steps.html: Retract it superiorly if it will move; if not, divide it between clamps and suture-ligate both ends. A partially divided, inadequately ligated isthmus is a classic source of troublesome postoperative bleeding into the airway. Do not simply diathermy across it and hope.

steps.title: Expose the rings, place a tracheal hook, and confirm your level
steps.html: Clear the pretracheal fascia, identify the cricoid and count down. A tracheal hook under the cricoid steadies and lifts the larynx. Recount before you cut — this is the last moment the level is free to change.

steps.title: Open the trachea as a window, not a resected ring
steps.html: Create the opening at the bottom of the 2nd/top of the 3rd ring — a small window or a hinged flap per your institution's practice. Do not resect a full ring circumferentially; over-resection is a technical error that predisposes to tracheomalacia and stenosis. Warn the anesthetist before entering: FiO2 should be reduced and diathermy kept away from the open airway, because an airway fire is a real hazard at this moment.

steps.title: Withdraw the ETT, insert the tube, confirm before committing
steps.html: Ask for the ETT to be withdrawn to just above the stoma — not removed. Insert the tracheostomy tube, inflate the cuff, connect and confirm with capnography and chest rise. Only then is the oral tube removed. Secure with ties and stay sutures.

blocks.title: Stay sutures and a documented tract are the gift you leave the night team
blocks.html: In the first week the tract is immature and will not reliably reopen if the tube falls out. Place stay sutures (traction sutures on either side of the tracheal opening, taped to the chest and clearly labelled), record the tube size and type at the bedside, and ensure the same-size and one-size-smaller tubes stay with the patient. An accidental decannulation on day two with no stay sutures is a genuine emergency.

rows: Needle punctures the ETT or its cuff
Tube not withdrawn far enough
Withdraw the ETT further under vision and re-puncture. Have a replacement ETT ready — a punctured cuff may need exchanging
Accidental extubation during withdrawal
ETT pulled past the cords
Reintubate immediately — this is why the scope and a reintubation plan are mandatory. Abandon and restart once stable
Wire kinks during dilation
Force applied off-axis
Stop. Withdraw the dilator, straighten or replace the wire. Never dilate over a kinked wire — that's how a false passage forms
Brisk bleeding during dissection
Off midline, or an undivided/unligated isthmus
Return to the midline plane. Formally ligate the isthmus. Pack and get proper exposure rather than blindly diathermying
Tracheostomy tube won't pass after dilation
Under-dilated tract, or false passage
Re-dilate over the retained wire. Confirm position bronchoscopically before another attempt. Drop a size
Tube in, but no capnography
Pretracheal false passage
Do not ventilate through it. Revert to the oral ETT (still in place — this is why), reassess, restart
Surgical emphysema after connection
Tube tip outside the lumen, or over-tight closure around the stoma
Stop ventilating via the trachy, reconfirm position, leave the stoma loosely closed
Sudden heavy bleeding days later
Tracheo-innominate fistula until proven otherwise — tube placed too low
Surgical emergency. Hyperinflate the cuff to tamponade, apply digital pressure via the stoma, call vascular/ENT immediately
Accidental decannulation in the first week
Immature tract, tube not secured
Do not blindly reinsert. Oxygenate from above, reintubate orally, then re-establish the stoma under controlled conditions. Stay sutures if present

blocks.html:
• Loss of the airway during the exchange — the defining intraoperative risk of both techniques
  • False passage and pretracheal placement, particularly with percutaneous dilation over a kinked wire
  • Bleeding — isthmus, anterior jugular veins, aberrant vessels; and late, catastrophic tracheo-innominate fistula from a tube placed too low
  • Posterior tracheal wall injury and tracheo-esophageal fistula — from unopposed dilation force or an over-deep needle
  • Subglottic stenosis from a stoma placed too high (through the cricoid or 1st ring)
  • Tracheomalacia and tracheal stenosis from over-resection of cartilage
  • Airway fire at the moment of tracheal entry with diathermy and a high FiO2
  • Accidental decannulation into an immature tract — the commonest serious ward-level emergency afterwards
  • Attempting it as a rescue in CICO — the error this whole entry exists to prevent

If the question is “can this patient breathe right now,” the answer is a cricothyrotomy. Tracheostomy is a planned conversation about the next fortnight.

The oral tube stays in until the tracheostomy is proven. It is the rescue airway, and removing it early converts every recoverable problem into an emergency.

Site selection is the long game. Too high buys subglottic stenosis; too low buys a tracheo-innominate fistula. Count the rings, and count them again before cutting.

Ultrasound before you puncture, specifically to find the vessel that is not supposed to be there.

Midline is the avascular plane. Nearly all troublesome bleeding comes from drifting off it.

A window, not a resected ring.

Stay sutures, a labelled bedside sign, and a spare tube one size down. The procedure's most dangerous day is often day two, on a ward, with a team who didn't place it.

procedures.title: Chest Tube Placement (Tube Thoracostomy)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: A full open technique for hemothorax and pneumothorax — from site selection through the post-placement film and removal timing.
procedures.description: Full open technique for hemo/pneumothorax.

blocks.html:
• Pneumothorax — traumatic, tension (after immediate decompression), or a simple pneumothorax large enough or symptomatic enough to need drainage
  • Hemothorax and traumatic hemopneumothorax
  • Any pneumothorax in a patient about to receive positive-pressure ventilation or go to the operating room — a small pneumothorax that was tolerable breathing spontaneously can tension under a ventilator
  • Empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion (a non-emergent variant of the same technique)
  • Definitive management after a finger thoracostomy or needle decompression — neither of those is an endpoint

• None absolute in a tension pneumothorax or hemothorax with hemodynamic compromise
  • Coagulopathy — relative; correct it if the patient is stable enough to wait, and prefer a smaller-bore tube
  • Suspected diaphragmatic hernia at the intended site — abdominal contents in the chest will be entered instead. If the mechanism suggests it and the patient can wait, image first.
  • Dense pleural adhesions — may need an alternative site or a surgical approach
  • Skin infection over the site — choose a different interspace

• Tube. Traditional teaching is 32–36 Fr for traumatic hemothorax. Note this is genuinely contested — multiple trials comparing 14 Fr pigtail catheters against large-bore tubes for traumatic hemothorax have found comparable drainage and failure rates with considerably less pain. Know which your institution and trauma service favour, and know that "bigger drains blood better" is no longer an unexamined truth.
  • #10 scalpel, large Kelly clamp, and a second clamp for the tube tip
  • 0 or 1-0 silk/nylon on a cutting needle for securing
  • Drainage system (three-chamber or digital), primed, with tubing long enough to reach
  • Local anesthetic — plenty of it. 20–30 mL of lidocaine is not excessive for an awake patient; the periosteum and parietal pleura are the painful bits and are frequently under-infiltrated.
  • Chlorhexidine, full drapes, petroleum gauze, dressings, tape
  • Systemic analgesia on board before you start, not requested afterwards

blocks.title: Do not use a trocar
blocks.html: Tubes supplied with a sharp internal trocar are still found on some trolleys. Passing a tube on a trocar converts a controlled blunt dissection into a blind stab and is the classic mechanism for lung, cardiac and intra-abdominal injury. Blunt dissection and a finger, every time. If the tube you have comes with a trocar, remove it and set it aside before you start.
Get the site right and most of the complications disappear

Boundaries:

  • Anterior: lateral border of pectoralis major
  • Posterior: anterior border of latissimus dorsi
  • Inferior: a horizontal line at the level of the nipple (roughly the 5th intercostal space)
  • Apex: the axilla

Why this triangle and not somewhere more convenient: the chest wall is thinnest here, so dissection is shorter and less traumatic. Going lower risks the diaphragm and, beneath it, the liver on the right and the spleen on the left — and the diaphragm rises much higher than people expect, especially supine and in expiration. Going too far posteriorly puts the tube under the patient where it kinks and is agonising to lie on. Going too far anteriorly and medially approaches the internal mammary vessels.

blocks.title: Count from a landmark you can actually feel
blocks.html: The nipple is an unreliable landmark in women, in the obese, and in anyone lying on their side. Count down from the sternal angle to the 2nd rib and work down, or use the inframammary fold with the breast tissue retracted superiorly. Placing a tube through breast tissue is painful, cosmetically poor, and easily avoided.

steps.title: Position and mark
steps.html: Supine or semi-recumbent, with the arm abducted and the hand behind the head to open the axilla. Identify and mark the triangle of safety before you prep — landmarks are much harder to find through drapes. Confirm the side against the imaging and, out loud, against the examination findings.

steps.title: Anesthetize generously, and reach the two structures that hurt
steps.html: Skin first, then infiltrate down onto the rib periosteum, then walk the needle over the superior edge of the rib and infiltrate the parietal pleura. Those two are the painful structures; a wheal in the skin alone leaves the patient feeling everything that matters. Aspirating air or blood as you enter the pleura also confirms your depth and your diagnosis before you cut.

steps.title: Incise parallel to the rib, over the rib below your target space
steps.html: A 2–3 cm incision through skin and subcutaneous fat, sited over the rib below the interspace you intend to enter. That offset is what creates the short oblique tunnel — it makes the tract self-sealing when the tube comes out.

steps.title: Blunt-dissect up and over the rib
steps.html: Open the Kelly clamp to spread tissue, withdraw, reinsert, and repeat — tunnelling superiorly over the top of the rib. Stay on the upper border. The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the groove beneath each rib, so hugging the inferior margin of the space above is how you find the artery. Expect this to take longer than you want; this is the part that protects everything underneath.

steps.title: Puncture the pleura deliberately
steps.html: With the closed clamp tip on the superior edge of the rib, push through the parietal pleura with controlled force, then open the clamp to widen the hole. There is usually a distinct give, often a rush of air or blood. Control the depth with your hand — choke up on the instrument so it cannot plunge.

steps.title: Put a finger in. Every time.
steps.html: Sweep a gloved finger through the tract into the pleural space. You are confirming you are inside the chest and not in a false tract, feeling for lung sliding under your fingertip, and sweeping for adhesions or — the reason this step exists — abdominal contents from an unrecognised diaphragmatic injury. This is the single step most often skipped to save seconds and most likely to cause a serious injury when it is.

steps.title: Railroad the tube on the clamp
steps.html: Clamp the tube tip and guide it along your finger through the tract. Posteriorly and apically is a reasonable default that drains both air and fluid in a supine trauma patient; strictly apical for air, basal for fluid, if you have the luxury of choosing. Advance until every side hole is inside the pleural space — the last hole sits on the tube's radiopaque line interruption, and leaving it outside gives a persistent air leak and subcutaneous emphysema. Typically 10–14 cm at the skin in an adult; more in a large chest.

steps.title: Secure it so it cannot move
steps.html: A single heavy interrupted stitch closing the incision snugly around the tube, then wrap the free ends around the tube several times and tie. Add a second anchoring stitch. Do not place a purse-string — it is obsolete, it necroses the skin edge, and it leaves a puckered scar without improving the seal. Then tape the tubing to the chest wall in a loop so that a tug pulls on the tape rather than the tube.

steps.title: Connect, look for swing and bubble, then film
steps.html: Connect to the drainage system below the level of the chest. Look immediately for respiratory swing in the fluid column — that is your confirmation the tube communicates with the pleural space. Suction at around −20 cm H2O if indicated. Then get a chest radiograph for position and re-expansion.

blocks.html: The bottle tells you what is happening inside the chest

rows: Swinging (fluid column rises and falls with respiration)
The tube is patent and communicating with the pleural space. This is the reassuring sign you want.
Bubbling on coughing only
A small air leak, resolving. Expected early after a pneumothorax.
Continuous bubbling
Ongoing air leak — from the lung, or from the system. Check the system first: a side hole outside the chest, a loose connection, or a cracked bottle are all commoner than a bronchopleural fistula.
No swing, no bubbling
Either the lung is fully re-expanded and the tube is redundant, or the tube is blocked, kinked, or clamped. Do not assume the happy explanation — check the tube and the film.
Sudden stop in a previously draining hemothorax
Clot occluding the tube. The blood is still accumulating; the drain has simply stopped telling you about it.
Brisk ongoing blood loss

Institutional thresholds vary, but figures around 1–1.5 L immediately, or >200 mL/hr for 2–4 hours, are widely used triggers for surgical consultation. Trend and physiology matter more than any single number.

blocks.title: Drain a large chronic effusion slowly
blocks.html: Removing a very large, long-standing effusion rapidly risks re-expansion pulmonary edema — uncommon but occasionally severe. A widely taught ceiling is around 1–1.5 L in one sitting, then clamp and continue later, stopping earlier if the patient develops chest tightness or cough. This does not apply to acutely draining a hemothorax or tension pneumothorax, where you drain what needs draining.

rows: Cannot get through the pleura
Not enough controlled force, or dissecting into the rib
Reconfirm you are on the superior rib edge; commit with controlled pressure. Hesitation causes more trauma than a decisive pass
Subcutaneous emphysema after placement
A side hole left outside the pleura, or tube dislodged
Check the film and the insertion depth. Advance or replace — do not simply add dressings
Persistent large air leak
System fault far more often than bronchopleural fistula
Work from patient to bottle: insertion site, connections, tubing, bottle. Then consider a genuine lung injury
Tube drains nothing, film shows it in a fissure
Malposition
Common and often functionally adequate. Replace if it isn't draining what it needs to
Tube appears intraparenchymal on CT
Passed into lung, usually through adhesions
Surgical/thoracic input before manipulating it
Patient in severe pain despite the tube working
Under-treated, very common
The parietal pleura is exquisitely sensitive. Systemic analgesia, and consider regional blockade. Pain is not a sign of malfunction
Retained hemothorax on follow-up imaging
Clotted blood the tube never evacuated
Early surgical referral. Retained clot is a route to empyema and trapped lung; a second tube rarely fixes it
Tube falls out
Inadequate securing
Occlusive dressing immediately, reassess clinically, replace through a fresh site — never reinsert the old tube through the old hole

blocks.html:
• Intercostal neurovascular injury from dissecting along the inferior margin of the space
  • Organ injury — lung, liver, spleen, diaphragm, and rarely heart or great vessels. Nearly always a consequence of a trocar, a site that was too low, or a skipped finger sweep
  • Placement into the abdomen through an unrecognised diaphragmatic rupture
  • Malposition — fissural, subcutaneous, intraparenchymal, or simply not in far enough
  • Re-expansion pulmonary edema after rapid drainage of a large chronic effusion
  • Empyema and retained hemothorax as later consequences of incomplete drainage
  • Inadequate analgesia — consistently under-recognized, and one of the procedures patients recall most unpleasantly

• Criteria: the original indication is resolved — no air leak, drainage volume acceptably low, lung re-expanded on film, and the patient off positive pressure or stable on it per your unit's practice.
  • Analgesia first. Removal hurts.
  • Have the occlusive dressing prepared and in your hand before the tube moves.
  • Timing with the respiratory cycle: remove at end-inspiration or during a Valsalva, when intrapleural pressure is least likely to draw air in. Practice varies; what matters is that the patient is not inhaling as the tube exits and the dressing goes on immediately.
  • One smooth, brisk pull, then seal.
  • Follow-up film a few hours after removal to exclude a recurrent pneumothorax.

The finger sweep is not optional. It is what stands between a routine procedure and putting a tube through a diaphragm into a liver.

Superior edge of the rib, always. The bundle lives under the rib above.

Anesthetize the periosteum and the pleura, not just the skin. Those are the structures that hurt.

Swing confirms position better than the film does — and you get it instantly, at the bedside.

Continuous bubbling is a system fault until proven otherwise. Work from the patient outward before diagnosing a lung injury.

No trocar. No purse-string. Both are legacy practice that cause harm.

A tube that stops draining a hemothorax has not cured it. Suspect clot, and re-image rather than relaxing.
