procedures.title: Finger Thoracostomy / Needle Decompression
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: Immediate decompression of tension pneumothorax — the bridge to a formal chest tube, not a replacement for one.
procedures.description: Immediate tension pneumothorax decompression.

blocks.html:
• Tension pneumothorax — hypotension with unilateral absent or reduced breath sounds, respiratory distress, distended neck veins, and rising airway pressures in a ventilated patient
  • Traumatic cardiac arrest — bilateral finger thoracostomies are a standard component of the algorithm, performed for every traumatic arrest regardless of examination findings
  • Any decompensating patient where tension physiology is a credible explanation and you cannot afford to wait for imaging

blocks.title: Tracheal deviation is a late and unreliable sign
blocks.html: Waiting for the textbook triad means waiting too long. Distended neck veins are frequently absent in a hypovolemic trauma patient — there is no volume to distend them. In a ventilated patient the earliest reliable signal is often a sudden rise in peak airway pressure with falling blood pressure. Treat the physiology you have, not the sign you were taught to look for.

• None in a genuine tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise. The risk of inaction dominates.
  • The real hazard is not a contraindication but a misdiagnosis — decompressing a chest that was never under tension, when the hypotension was hemorrhage, tamponade or a right mainstem intubation.

Needle decompression

  • Large-bore cannula, and length is the whole problem. A standard 5 cm catheter fails to reach the pleural space in a substantial proportion of adults — chest wall thickness at the 2nd intercostal space commonly exceeds it. An 8 cm cannula is what most current trauma guidance recommends. Check what is actually on your trolley.
  • A syringe, so you can aspirate rather than rely on hearing a hiss in a noisy resuscitation room

Finger thoracostomy

  • Scalpel and a large blunt clamp — that is genuinely all you need
  • Gloves, and whatever prep the situation permits; in an arrest, do not trade time for sterility you cannot achieve anyway
  • A chest tube and drainage system ready to follow, because this is not the endpoint
The classic teaching site is the one most likely to fail

2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line — the traditional landmark. Problems: the chest wall is thickest here, so a short cannula frequently does not reach the pleura; and going too medial approaches the internal mammary vessels and the subclavian.

4th–5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line — increasingly preferred, and the same site as a chest tube. The chest wall is thinner, the success rate is better, it is where you will be putting the tube anyway, and it is the natural site for a finger thoracostomy.

Practical answer: if you are going lateral, you may as well cut. Finger thoracostomy at the lateral site is more reliable than a needle at either site, and it does not depend on a cannula being long enough.
Needle decompression — fastest, least reliable

steps.title: Insert over the top of the rib, syringe attached
steps.html: Perpendicular to the chest wall, immediately superior to the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. Advance while aspirating — a sudden free draw of air is more dependable confirmation than trying to hear a hiss in a working resuscitation bay.

steps.title: Advance the cannula, withdraw the needle, secure
steps.html: Slide the plastic cannula fully in and remove the needle. Secure it, and accept that it will kink, clot or dislodge — a soft cannula in a moving chest wall has a short working life.

steps.title: Treat success as temporary and move on
steps.html: Improvement buys minutes. Arrange the definitive tube immediately — and if there was no improvement, do not conclude the diagnosis was wrong until you have decompressed properly with a finger.

blocks.html: Finger thoracostomy — slower by seconds, far more reliable

steps.title: Incise in the triangle of safety
steps.html: Same site as a chest tube: 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line, arm abducted. A 3 cm incision over the rib below your target space, parallel to the rib.

steps.title: Blunt-dissect up and over the rib, then through the pleura
steps.html: Spread with the clamp, tunnelling superiorly over the top of the rib, and push through the parietal pleura with deliberate, controlled force. Expect a rush of air under tension — though absence of a dramatic hiss does not mean you are in the wrong place.

steps.title: Put your finger in and sweep
steps.html: Confirm you are in the pleural space, feel for lung, and sweep for adhesions and for abdominal contents from an unrecognised diaphragmatic injury. In a traumatic arrest this sweep is also diagnostic — you may find a massive hemothorax that changes the entire resuscitation.

steps.title: Leave it open, and follow with a tube
steps.html: In a ventilated patient the open thoracostomy continues to decompress, and many services deliberately leave it open with a simple dressing during transfer rather than tubing immediately. In a spontaneously breathing patient an open hole can entrain air — place the tube promptly.

blocks.title: In traumatic arrest, do both sides
blocks.html: Bilateral finger thoracostomies are performed in traumatic cardiac arrest without waiting for examination findings, alongside hemorrhage control and volume. Auscultation is unreliable during CPR, and a unilateral decision based on breath sounds in that setting is a guess.

• Hemodynamic improvement — blood pressure rising within a minute or two is the most meaningful endpoint
  • Falling peak airway pressures in a ventilated patient
  • Free rush of air on entry — supportive, but its absence proves nothing
  • Return of lung sliding on POCUS over the decompressed side
  • Your finger feeling lung — the most direct confirmation available

blocks.title: No improvement does not mean no tension pneumothorax
blocks.html: It commonly means the needle was too short, kinked, blocked, or in the wrong place. Before you discard the diagnosis, decompress properly with a finger. And if a correctly performed bilateral finger thoracostomy genuinely changes nothing, the diagnosis was something else — go back to hemorrhage, tamponade, and the rest of the arrest algorithm.

rows: No air, no improvement after needle
Cannula too short for the chest wall — the commonest failure
Go lateral and use a finger. Do not repeat the same short needle at the same site
Initial improvement, then deterioration
Cannula kinked, clotted or dislodged
Expected behavior for a needle. Convert to finger thoracostomy and a tube
Rush of air but no hemodynamic change
Pneumothorax present but not the cause of shock
Look elsewhere — hemorrhage, tamponade, or a second pneumothorax on the other side
Finger finds bowel or liver
Diaphragmatic injury; you are in the abdomen
Stop. Do not place a tube. Immediate surgical involvement
Finger finds a large volume of blood
Massive hemothorax
This is now a hemorrhage problem. Tube, activate transfusion, surgical referral against thoracotomy thresholds
Bleeding from the incision
Intercostal vessel — dissected too close to the inferior rib margin
Pressure, then a tube through the tract; may need surgical control
Spontaneously breathing patient worsens after an open thoracostomy
Air entrained through the open wound
Occlusive dressing and place the definitive tube now
Nothing found on either side in traumatic arrest
Tension pneumothorax was not the cause
Correct — you have excluded a reversible cause in seconds. Continue the algorithm

blocks.html:
• Failed decompression from an inadequate needle — the dominant failure mode, and entirely a matter of equipment and site selection
  • Lung laceration from a needle inserted into a chest that was not under tension
  • Vascular injury — internal mammary or subclavian if too medial at the 2nd space; intercostal vessels if dissecting along the wrong rib margin
  • Entry into the abdomen through an unrecognised diaphragmatic injury
  • Creating a pneumothorax in a patient who did not have one
  • Treating decompression as definitive — it never is
  • Infection in the survivor, from a necessarily unsterile field

If you are going lateral, cut. A finger is more reliable than any cannula, and you are already at the site the tube needs.

Length is the whole argument for needles. A 5 cm cannula frequently does not reach the pleura in an adult chest; carry 8 cm.

Aspirate rather than listen. A syringe gives you an answer in a room too noisy for a hiss.

Tracheal deviation and distended neck veins are late and often absent — especially in the hypovolemic. Rising airway pressure with falling pressure is the earlier tell.

Bilateral, in traumatic arrest, without debate.

The finger sweep is diagnostic as well as therapeutic. Blood, bowel or adhesions all change what happens next.

Nothing here is definitive. The tube always follows.

procedures.title: Pericardiocentesis
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: Needle decompression of cardiac tamponade — subxiphoid approach, ultrasound-guided when time allows.
procedures.description: Subxiphoid needle decompression of tamponade.

blocks.html:
• Cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise — hypotension, raised venous pressure, and echocardiographic tamponade physiology
  • Peri-arrest or arrest where tamponade is a credible reversible cause
  • Symptomatic effusion needing drainage in a controlled setting (a different, far less urgent version of the same procedure)

Tamponade is an echocardiographic diagnosis, not a volume one. A small effusion that accumulated fast can tamponade; a liter that collected over months may not. Look for right atrial systolic collapse (sensitive), right ventricular diastolic collapse (specific), a plethoric non-collapsing IVC, and exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow velocities. Beck's triad is present in a minority of cases and its absence excludes nothing.

sections.title: Contraindications — and When to Do Something Else

blocks.html:
• None absolute in an unstable patient with confirmed tamponade.
  • Traumatic hemopericardium with surgical capability available — this is the important one. Blood in the pericardium after penetrating trauma clots, so a needle frequently drains little or nothing and the negative tap is falsely reassuring. If you have a surgeon and an operating room, the answer is thoracotomy or sternotomy; the needle is at best a bridge while that is mobilized.
  • Aortic dissection with hemopericardium — relative, and genuinely dangerous. Decompressing can raise the blood pressure, re-establish flow through the false lumen, and precipitate catastrophic rupture. Drain only what restores a perfusing rhythm, and get to theatre.
  • Uncorrected severe coagulopathy — relative; correct alongside, not instead.

• Ultrasound with a phased-array cardiac probe — this is the single item that changes the procedure's safety profile, and it should be considered standard rather than optional
  • Long needle: 18 ga spinal needle (~9–15 cm), or a dedicated pericardiocentesis kit
  • Guidewire, dilator and pigtail catheter — reaccumulation is the norm, not the exception
  • Three-way stopcock and a large syringe, plus a collection system
  • Agitated saline — 10 mL saline with a small air bubble, briskly exchanged between two syringes. This is how you confirm needle position (see below), and it costs nothing to prepare in advance.
  • Full monitoring, defibrillator to hand, and sterile prep/drapes
With ultrasound, the subxiphoid route is often the wrong answer

The rule with ultrasound is simple: scan all the windows and puncture wherever the fluid is largest, closest to the skin, and free of lung or liver in the path. The needle follows the fluid, not a memorised landmark.

  • Apical — frequently the best target. Needle enters just lateral to the apex beat, directed toward the right shoulder, running roughly parallel to the long axis of the heart. Risks the lingula and the left internal mammary if too medial.
  • Parasternal — a short, direct route to an anterior effusion. Enter immediately lateral to the sternal edge to avoid the internal mammary artery, which runs about 3–5 cm from the sternal border; a perpendicular puncture through the 5th intercostal space is short and often the safest of all when the fluid is anterior.
  • Subxiphoid — the traditional blind landmark, and the right choice when there is no ultrasound or the chest is inaccessible. Enter just left and inferior to the xiphoid at about 45° to the skin, aiming toward the left shoulder. It has the longest needle path of the three and traverses the liver — which is why it is no longer the automatic first choice when imaging is available.

steps.title: Position and scan before you prep
steps.html: Sit the patient up 30–45° if tolerated — it pools the effusion dependently and brings it toward the anterior chest wall. Then scan subxiphoid, parasternal and apical and choose your window deliberately, noting depth to fluid and what lies in the path.

steps.title: Prep, drape, and anesthetize the whole track
steps.html: Full sterile technique if there is any time at all. Infiltrate generously down to and including the parietal pericardium in an awake patient.

steps.title: Advance under vision, aspirating continuously
steps.html: Keep the needle tip in view — in-plane if your skill allows, otherwise watch for tissue movement and the tenting of the pericardium as you press against it. Aspirate the whole way in. Entry into the pericardial space is usually a distinct give followed by free return of fluid.

steps.title: Confirm with agitated saline before you dilate
steps.html: This is the step that prevents the disaster. Inject a few millilitres of agitated saline down the needle while watching on ultrasound. Bubbles appearing in the pericardial space, surrounding the heart confirm correct position. Bubbles appearing inside a cardiac chamber mean you are in the heart — withdraw, do not dilate, and reassess. Never railroad a dilator over a wire whose position you have not confirmed.

steps.title: Aspirate to effect, not to dryness
steps.html: Remove enough to restore perfusion — often only 30–100 mL transforms the hemodynamics, because tamponade physiology sits on the steep part of the pericardial pressure-volume curve. Chasing complete drainage through a needle adds risk without adding benefit.

steps.title: Leave a pigtail over a wire
steps.html: Seldinger the catheter in and secure it. Reaccumulation is expected; a drain converts a procedure you would otherwise repeat under worse conditions into a monitored one. Send fluid for the studies the clinical context demands.

steps.title: Re-scan, and keep the definitive plan moving
steps.html: Confirm the effusion has reduced and the chambers are filling. Then continue arranging whatever actually fixes the cause — a surgical window, thoracotomy, or treatment of the underlying disease. Pericardiocentesis buys time; it rarely cures.

blocks.title: Is this blood from the pericardium or from a ventricle?
blocks.html: Two checks, neither perfect. Pericardial blood is usually defibrinated and does not clot in the syringe, whereas fresh intracardiac blood clots — useful, but unreliable with very recent bleeding. Comparing the aspirate's hematocrit with a venous sample is slower but more objective. Agitated saline under ultrasound is better than either and gives an answer in seconds, which is why it belongs in the routine rather than the troubleshooting list.

rows: Dry tap in suspected traumatic tamponade
Clotted hemopericardium — the needle cannot drain clot
A negative tap does not exclude tamponade after trauma. Escalate to surgical decompression
Agitated saline appears inside a chamber
Needle is in the heart
Withdraw slowly, re-scan, re-site. Do not dilate. Watch for a new or enlarging effusion
Ectopy or ST elevation as you advance
Needle contacting myocardium
Withdraw a few millimeters; the ectopy should settle. Redirect using the image rather than by feel
Blood aspirated that clots in the syringe
Probably intracardiac
Confirm with agitated saline before proceeding either way
Hemodynamics worsen after drainage
RV puncture with ongoing bleeding, or pericardial decompression syndrome
Re-scan immediately for a re-accumulating effusion. Support, and get surgical help — this can be catastrophic
Desaturation after the procedure
Pneumothorax from the needle path
POCUS for lung sliding; treat as needed
Effusion reaccumulates quickly
Ongoing bleeding or ongoing production
Expected. This is why a pigtail goes in. Escalate to definitive management
Cannot find a safe window at all
Loculated or posterior effusion, or a hyperinflated chest
Do not improvise a blind route. This is a surgical drainage problem

blocks.html:
• Cardiac chamber puncture or laceration — classically the right ventricle, which sits immediately anterior
  • Coronary artery laceration, with the hemopericardium it causes
  • Pneumothorax, and rarely hepatic injury via the subxiphoid route
  • Arrhythmia from myocardial irritation
  • Pericardial decompression syndrome — uncommon but well described: paradoxical ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary edema after rapid drainage. An argument for draining to effect rather than to dryness
  • The falsely reassuring dry tap in traumatic tamponade — arguably the most dangerous outcome of the whole procedure, because it ends the search
  • Delay to definitive management while attention stays on the needle

Puncture where the fluid is, not where the textbook says. With ultrasound the apical or parasternal window is frequently shorter and safer than subxiphoid.

Agitated saline before dilating. Seconds to perform, and it is the difference between a drain in the pericardium and a dilator in a ventricle.

Drain to effect. Thirty to a hundred millilitres often restores the blood pressure; chasing dryness adds only risk.

A dry tap after penetrating trauma means clot, not absence of tamponade. Escalate rather than relax.

Leave a pigtail. Reaccumulation is the rule.

Sit them up. Thirty to forty-five degrees brings the effusion to the needle.

If there is a surgeon and an operating room, a traumatic hemopericardium belongs to them — you are buying minutes, not providing treatment.

procedures.title: Resuscitative Thoracotomy (Clamshell)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Thoracic
procedures.subtitle: The last-resort maneuver for the peri-arrest or arrested trauma patient — direct access to the heart, the hilum, and the descending aorta.
procedures.description: Last-resort direct cardiac and hilar access.

blocks.html: Candidacy is decided in seconds, and it decides the outcome more than technique does

rows: Penetrating thoracic trauma, arrest witnessed, signs of life within ~15 min
Strongest indication. Best reported survival, particularly for a stab wound to the cardiac box with tamponade
Penetrating thoracic trauma, no signs of life, <15 min CPR
Reasonable — still a candidate group
Penetrating extra-thoracic trauma, signs of life
Weaker, but defensible for aortic cross-clamping in exsanguination
Blunt trauma, signs of life present
Low survival, but performed at many centres. Know your institution's stance
Blunt trauma, no signs of life
Survival approaches zero. Most guidance advises against
Prolonged CPR (>15 min penetrating, >10 min blunt) with no signs of life
Against

blocks.html: “Signs of life” has a specific meaning — pupillary response, spontaneous ventilation, a palpable pulse, measurable blood pressure, spontaneous movement, or organized electrical activity. It is not the same as “arrived with CPR in progress.” Establish what the prehospital team actually witnessed, and when, in the first fifteen seconds of handover.

blocks.title: The physiological targets, not just the diagnosis
blocks.html: This procedure exists to do four things: release tamponade, control intrathoracic hemorrhage, cross-clamp the aorta to redistribute what blood remains to heart and brain, and deliver internal cardiac massage or defibrillation. If none of those four is plausibly the problem, opening the chest will not help.

• Blunt arrest with prolonged downtime and no signs of life
  • Penetrating trauma with >15 minutes of CPR and no signs of life
  • Injuries obviously incompatible with survival
  • No surgical capability to follow. This is a bridge. Opening a chest in a facility that cannot then repair what you find, and cannot transfer, commits the patient and exposes the team for nothing — a decision to make before the patient arrives, not over the body.

• #10 scalpel, heavy Mayo scissors, and toothed forceps
  • Finochietto rib spreader
  • Heavy scissors, Gigli saw or a Lebsche knife for the sternum if converting to clamshell
  • Vascular clamps — a DeBakey or aortic clamp for the descending aorta, and a second for the hilum
  • Internal defibrillator paddles, and a defibrillator that will accept them
  • Foley catheter — an improvised but genuinely effective tamponade for a ventricular hole
  • Skin stapler, 2-0/3-0 pledgeted sutures, suction, packs
  • Full barrier PPE for everyone at the table — face shield, gown, double gloves. This is among the highest body-fluid-exposure procedures in medicine, performed fast, around cut bone and sharps.
  • Massive transfusion running before the chest is open, and a named person running it
Incision to pericardium is the interval that matters — aim for well under a minute

steps.title: Declare it, assign roles, arms up
steps.html: Say out loud that you are performing a resuscitative thoracotomy. Assign: airway, the transfusion, and one person on instruments. Abduct the left arm above the head. Continue chest compressions and ventilation until the moment you cut.

steps.title: Left anterolateral incision, 4th–5th interspace, one confident pass
steps.html: From the sternal edge to the table — go further posteriorly than instinct suggests, because inadequate length is the commonest reason exposure fails. Follow the curve of the rib, in the inframammary crease, retracting breast tissue superiorly rather than cutting through it. Cut deeply through skin, fat and muscle in a single deliberate stroke; timid repeated passes waste the seconds this procedure is spending.

steps.title: Open the intercostal muscle and pleura with scissors
steps.html: Puncture the intercostal muscle just above the rib, then run heavy scissors along the superior border of the rib for the length of the incision, pushing the lung away. Ask for ventilation to be held briefly if the lung is in the way.

steps.title: Insert the spreader with the handle toward the axilla
steps.html: A small practical point that matters enormously: orient the Finochietto's ratchet and handle inferiorly/laterally, toward the axilla. Placed the other way, the handle sits over the sternum and physically blocks the clamshell extension you may be about to need. Open it wide.

steps.title: Extend to clamshell if you need the other side
steps.html: If the injury is right-sided, bilateral, or exposure is inadequate, mirror the incision on the right and divide the sternum transversely with heavy scissors or a Gigli saw. The internal mammary arteries will be cut and they must be found and ligated. They often do not bleed while the patient is exsanguinated and pressureless — and then bleed briskly the moment you restore a blood pressure. Ligate them before that happens.

steps.title: Open the pericardium longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve
steps.html: Identify the phrenic nerve running vertically on the lateral pericardium — stay anterior to it. Tent the pericardium with forceps and incise longitudinally with scissors, then extend the opening widely. Under tamponade the pericardium is tense and bluish. Evacuate clot with your hand; clot is exactly what the needle could not remove.

steps.title: Control cardiac bleeding — finger first
steps.html: Deliver the heart into the wound. Put a finger over the hole; that alone controls most wounds and buys thinking time. Then: a Foley through the defect with the balloon inflated and gentle traction for a larger ventricular wound, skin staples for a rapid closure, or pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures placed underneath the coronary artery so you do not ligate it. Atrial wounds can often be clamped with a side-biting vascular clamp and repaired.

steps.title: Internal massage, correctly
steps.html: Two hands, flat, hinged at the wrists — one posterior and one anterior, compressing the heart between the flat palmar surfaces at around 100/min. Do not squeeze with fingertips: point pressure perforates a flaccid ventricle. Compress from apex toward base.

steps.title: Cross-clamp the descending aorta if you need it
steps.html: Sweep the left lung anteriorly and medially. The aorta lies posteriorly, against the vertebral bodies — and the structure immediately anterior to it is the esophagus, which is easy to clamp by mistake. A nasogastric tube makes the esophagus palpable and is worth the seconds. Open the mediastinal pleura, bluntly dissect the aorta circumferentially, and apply the clamp. Note the time: aim to release within roughly 30 minutes, and anticipate a reperfusion insult when you do.

steps.title: Internal defibrillation — start low
steps.html: Internal paddles applied directly to the heart, one anterior and one posterior. Start at 10–20 J, not external energies. External doses applied directly to myocardium cause injury and are unnecessary — you have removed the chest wall from the circuit.

steps.title: If you get a perfusing rhythm, go to theatre now
steps.html: The chest stays open, packed, with the clamp noted. Everything from here is damage control in an operating room. If there is no response after adequate exposure, tamponade release and massage, stop and say so out loud — a clear termination is part of the procedure, and the team needs to hear it.

blocks.title: Protect the team while you work
blocks.html: Sharp bone edges, a scalpel and scissors moving fast, and blood everywhere. Announce every sharp, hand instruments rather than reaching, and keep the number of hands in the chest to the minimum that works. A needlestick or a splash here is a genuine occupational exposure, and the adrenaline that makes this procedure possible is exactly what makes people careless.

rows: Cannot see anything once open
Incision too short, or too anterior
Extend posteriorly to the table. Convert to clamshell — poor exposure is the commonest reason this fails
Spreader blocks sternal division
Handle oriented toward the sternum
Reposition with the ratchet toward the axilla. Easier to get right first time than to fix mid-procedure
Brisk bleeding from the sternal edges after ROSC
Unligated internal mammary arteries
Find and ligate both. Anticipate this the moment a pressure returns
Pericardium looks normal, no tamponade
Diagnosis was something else
Look for hilar injury, aortic injury, or a source below the diaphragm. Cross-clamp if exsanguinating
Clamp applied but no improvement
Esophagus clamped instead of aorta
Re-identify against the vertebral bodies; use the NG tube to distinguish. Aorta is posterior
Heart fills poorly despite massage
Hypovolemia — there is nothing to pump
Massage moves only what volume exists. Transfusion is the treatment; consider a source below the diaphragm
Air in the coronaries / sudden arrest on ventilation
Systemic air embolism from a bronchovenous fistula
Clamp or twist the hilum of the injured lung, place head down, aspirate air from the LV apex and aortic root
Repair sutures cause ST changes or regional akinesis
A coronary artery has been ligated
Remove and replace, passing the suture beneath the vessel
ROSC then deterioration after clamp release
Reperfusion — acidosis, hyperkalemia, vasoplegia
Release gradually, anticipate it, treat metabolically. Note total clamp time

blocks.html:
• Very high mortality even when everything is done correctly — the team should hear this framed before it begins
  • Phrenic nerve injury from opening the pericardium in the wrong plane
  • Coronary artery ligation during a hurried cardiac repair
  • Esophageal injury from a misplaced aortic clamp
  • Myocardial perforation from fingertip massage
  • Reperfusion injury after cross-clamp release
  • Occupational exposure — a real and under-discussed outcome for the team
  • Performing it outside criteria, consuming blood, people and exposure risk without realistic prospect of survival

Candidacy decides outcome more than technique does. Have the criteria conversation before the patient arrives.

Cut long, cut deep, cut once. Inadequate exposure is the commonest technical failure, and timid incisions cost more time than they save.

Spreader handle toward the axilla — so it never blocks the clamshell.

Anterior to the phrenic nerve, longitudinally.

Ligate the internal mammaries before the blood pressure comes back and reminds you.

Flat hands, not fingertips.

The aorta is posterior; the esophagus is in front of it. Feel for the NG tube.

Internal defibrillation is 10–20 J.

Say the ending out loud. Terminating clearly is part of running the procedure well.

procedures.title: Synchronized Cardioversion vs. Defibrillation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Knowing which button to press, and why the timing of the shock relative to the QRS is the entire distinction between the two.
procedures.description: Timing the shock relative to the QRS — and why it matters.

blocks.html:
Synchronized cardioversion — an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse and a discernible, organized QRS:

  • Unstable SVT refractory to vagal maneuvers/adenosine
  • Unstable atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response
  • Unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse

Defibrillation (unsynchronized) — no pulse, or no synchronizable QRS:

  • Pulseless VF or pulseless VT
  • Polymorphic VT, including torsades — the QRS varies beat to beat, so the machine cannot reliably find an R wave. Unsynchronized, even if a pulse is present.

“Unstable” means the rhythm is causing the problem: hypotension, altered mentation, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure attributable to the rate. A heart rate alone is not an indication — and a rate below about 150 rarely explains shock by itself in an adult, so look hard for another cause before shocking.

• Stable tachyarrhythmia — treat pharmacologically; you have time
  • Do not attempt to synchronize a rhythm without a consistent QRS. The machine will either refuse to discharge or sync to the wrong deflection. Polymorphic VT goes unsynchronized.
  • Digoxin toxicity — cardioversion can precipitate refractory ventricular arrhythmias. If unavoidable, use the lowest effective energy and have magnesium and antidote available.
  • Atrial fibrillation of >48 hours or unknown duration in a stable patient — elective cardioversion carries thromboembolic risk and needs anticoagulation or TOE first. In the genuinely unstable patient this consideration does not override shocking.
  • Implanted device — not a contraindication; place pads at least 8 cm from the generator, ideally anteroposterior, and have the device interrogated afterwards.
Device-specific — these are starting points, not a substitute for your machine's guidance

rows: SVT / atrial flutter
Sync
50–100 J — these terminate at the lowest energies
Atrial fibrillation
Sync
Monomorphic VT with a pulse
Sync
VF / pulseless VT
Unsync
120–200 J per manufacturer; if unknown, use the maximum
Polymorphic VT / torsades
Unsync
Defibrillation doses
Pediatric defibrillation
Unsync
2 J/kg first, then 4 J/kg, subsequent ≥4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose)
Pediatric cardioversion
Sync
0.5–1 J/kg first, escalating to 2 J/kg
Internal paddles (open chest)
Unsync
10–20 J — an order of magnitude lower; external doses injure myocardium

blocks.title: Escalate if the first shock fails
blocks.html: If a synchronized shock does not convert the rhythm, step the energy up for the next attempt rather than repeating the same dose. Repeating an identical failed shock is the same error as repeating an identical failed laryngoscopy.
Synchronized cardioversion

steps.title: Confirm instability and a synchronizable rhythm
steps.html: Pulse present, organized QRS, and symptoms attributable to the rate. Print or freeze a strip — you want to be certain this is monomorphic before choosing sync.

steps.title: Prepare the skin and place pads
steps.html: Dry the chest, clip dense hair, remove transdermal patches. Anteroposterior placement is generally preferred for atrial fibrillation and for patients with implanted devices; anterolateral is acceptable and faster. Keep pads ≥8 cm from any device generator.

steps.title: Sedate — this is a conscious patient about to be shocked
steps.html: If there is any time at all, provide procedural sedation and analgesia. Titrate carefully: the blood pressure you are worried about is already low. Small doses, pre-oxygenation, airway equipment and a vasopressor within reach.

steps.title: Press SYNC, then look at the screen
steps.html: Activate synchronization and visually confirm a marker sitting on every R wave — and only on R waves. If markers are landing on T waves or appearing intermittently, increase the ECG gain or switch to a lead with a taller R. Do not shock until the markers are right. This look at the screen is the entire safety mechanism of the procedure.

steps.title: Charge, clear, and hold the button
steps.html: Announce and confirm everyone is clear. Hold the shock button down — in sync mode the machine waits for the next R wave, so there is a perceptible delay between pressing and discharge. Releasing early is a common reason “the shock didn't work.”

steps.title: Reassess — and re-arm SYNC before the next shock
steps.html: Check rhythm and pulse. If still unstable and unconverted, escalate energy and shock again — but first re-confirm sync is active. Most defibrillators revert to unsynchronized after every delivery, by design, so that a patient who arrests can be defibrillated immediately.

blocks.html: Defibrillation

steps.title: Confirm pulselessness, charge during compressions
steps.html: Keep compressions going while the machine charges — this is the single biggest modifiable factor in minimizing the peri-shock pause. Ensure sync is off.

steps.title: Clear, shock, and resume compressions immediately
steps.html: Brief clear, deliver, and go straight back to compressions without a pulse or rhythm check. Reassess at the next scheduled rhythm check. A perfusing rhythm rarely appears instantly after a shock, and pausing to look costs coronary perfusion pressure that took a minute to build.

blocks.title: Check SYNC every single time
blocks.html: Two failures, opposite directions, both common. Sync left off when cardioverting a patient with a pulse: the shock can land on the T wave and induce VF — the R-on-T phenomenon that synchronization exists to prevent. Sync left on when the patient has arrested into VF: the machine hunts for an R wave it will never find and refuses to discharge, and precious seconds are lost to a defibrillator that appears broken. Look at the mode indicator before every shock.

rows: Machine will not discharge
Sync is on and it cannot find an R wave
If the patient is pulseless, turn sync OFF and defibrillate. This is the classic time-waster in a peri-arrest
Sync markers on T waves, or missing beats
Low-amplitude R waves in the selected lead
Increase gain, switch lead, or reposition pads. Never shock with markers you don't trust
Pressed shock, nothing happened
Button released before the next R wave
Hold it down until discharge
Second shock delivered unsynchronized by accident
Device reverted to unsync after the first
Re-arm sync every time. Build it into the verbal sequence
Rhythm converts, then immediately recurs
Untreated underlying driver
More shocks won't fix it. Correct electrolytes, ischemia, sepsis, hypoxia, drug effect
Shock fails to convert AF
Impedance, energy too low, or pad position
Escalate energy, switch to anteroposterior, press pads firmly, ensure skin is dry
VF induced after cardioversion
R-on-T, or underlying ischemia/digoxin toxicity
Immediately defibrillate unsynchronized. Then ask why
Patient recalls the shock
Inadequate sedation
A genuine harm, not a minor one. Sedate properly if any time exists
Skin burns after repeated shocks
Poor pad contact, dry gel, hair
Replace pads, clip hair, ensure full contact

blocks.html:
• R-on-T induction of VF from an unsynchronized shock in a patient with a pulse
  • Failure to discharge because sync was left on in a pulseless patient
  • Thromboembolic stroke after cardioverting AF of >48 hours without anticoagulation
  • Ventricular arrhythmia in digoxin toxicity
  • Sedation-related hypotension or apnoea in an already marginal patient
  • Skin burns, and myocardial injury from unnecessarily high repeated energies
  • Implanted device malfunction from pads placed too close to the generator
  • Shocking a stable patient who needed a drug and a conversation instead

Sync protects a pulse. That is the whole distinction — if there is an organized QRS and a pulse to preserve, time the shock away from the T wave; if there is neither, there is nothing to protect.

Look at the markers, not just the mode light. Sync engaged but marking T waves is more dangerous than no sync at all.

Hold the button. The delay is the machine doing its job.

Re-arm sync after every shock. The revert-to-unsync default is deliberate, and it will catch you.

Polymorphic means unsynchronized, pulse or no pulse.

Charge during compressions and resume them immediately after — the peri-shock pause is the thing you control.

Internal paddles are 10–20 J. Two orders of magnitude of error are possible here.

If it converts and immediately recurs, the problem is not the shock.

procedures.title: Targeted Temperature Management Initiation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Post-ROSC neuroprotection — starting the cooling/normothermia protocol in the critical early window after return of spontaneous circulation.
procedures.description: Post-ROSC neuroprotection protocol.

blocks.html:
• Comatose after ROSC from cardiac arrest — not following commands, no purposeful response to voice. Out-of-hospital or in-hospital, shockable or non-shockable initial rhythm.
  • The practical test is the motor response: a patient who localizes to voice or follows a command does not need this. Everyone else does.
  • Start as soon as ROSC is established and the patient is stabilized — airway, hemodynamics, and a 12-lead first, then temperature.

blocks.title: What the trials actually changed
blocks.html: The field has moved, and the entry point has moved with it. TTM (2013) found 33 °C no better than 36 °C. TTM2 (2021) found 33 °C no better than normothermia with active fever prevention. HYPERION (2019) suggested possible benefit at 33 °C specifically in non-shockable rhythms. The result is that current guidance has shifted from “cool everyone to 33” to “actively prevent fever in everyone, and 33 remains a permitted option.”

• Following commands after ROSC. Not indicated — though fever avoidance still applies.
  • Goals of care that do not support ongoing intensive treatment.
  • Major uncontrolled hemorrhage — a reason to choose strict normothermia rather than 33 °C, since hypothermia impairs platelet function and enzyme kinetics. Rarely a reason to permit fever.
  • Sepsis, recent major surgery, or established coagulopathy — the same reasoning: target higher, not warmer than normal.
  • Already hypothermic on arrival — do not actively rewarm to a target. Hypothermic arrest is a different pathway entirely and drowning or environmental exposure changes the prognosis.

• A device with closed-loop feedback — surface pads or an intravascular catheter. Both work. Feedback control is what keeps you at target instead of oscillating, and manual ice packs cannot do it.
  • Continuous core temperature probe. Esophageal is the most accurate and most responsive; bladder is acceptable but lags badly when urine output is low; rectal lags. Tympanic and axillary are not adequate for this. Two sites is better than one, because a single failed probe is otherwise invisible.
  • Sedation and analgesia, titratable and short-acting where possible.
  • Neuromuscular blockade available — but as the last anti-shivering step, not the first.
  • Continuous EEG, or at least access to it. Essential if the patient is paralyzed.
  • Arterial line, and frequent electrolytes and glucose.
  • What not to use: cold intravenous fluid boluses in the prehospital setting. Trials of prehospital cold saline showed increased pulmonary edema and re-arrest without benefit. Cool in hospital, with a device.

sections.title: Shivering — the Thing That Defeats This

blocks.html: Shivering raises metabolic rate and oxygen consumption sharply, defeats the target, and is treated in the wrong order almost everywhere.

Assess it formally and repeatedly using a structured scale — the Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale grades it 0 (none) to 3 (generalized). Shivering is often missed because it starts in the masseter and neck and can be felt on the jaw or chest before it is visible.

Escalate in this order:

  • 1. Counterwarm the skin. Warm the face, hands and feet with a forced-air blanket while cooling the core. This is the most underused intervention in temperature management: shivering thresholds are driven substantially by skin temperature, so warming the periphery raises the threshold and lets you cool the core with far less sedation.
  • 2. Acetaminophen, plus buspirone — both lower the shivering threshold and are non-sedating.
  • 3. Magnesium infusion to a level around 3–4 mg/dL — lowers the threshold and is generally well tolerated.
  • 4. Opioids — fentanyl, or meperidine, which lowers the shivering threshold more than any other opioid but accumulates a proconvulsant metabolite.
  • 5. Sedation — propofol or dexmedetomidine.
  • 6. Neuromuscular blockade — last. It abolishes shivering without treating it, and it does something worse: it masks seizures. A paralyzed post-arrest patient needs continuous EEG, and if you cannot provide that, think hard before paralyzing.

sections.title: What Cooling Does to the Rest of the Patient

rows: Potassium
Shifts into cells → hypokalemia. Do not chase it aggressively; a level of 3.0–3.5 is acceptable at target.
Shifts back out → rebound hyperkalemia. Stop replacement several hours before rewarming begins. This is the classic and avoidable harm.
Glucose
Insulin resistance → hyperglycemia, often needing an infusion
Insulin sensitivity returns → hypoglycemia. Reduce insulin as you rewarm.
Heart rate
Bradycardia is expected and, if perfusion is adequate, is not treated. Prolonged QT; Osborn J waves.
Rate recovers.
Volume
Cold diuresis → hypovolemia, often substantial
Vasodilation → hypotension. Anticipate needing volume or pressors.
Coagulation
Platelet dysfunction and slowed enzyme kinetics → bleeding risk
Normalizes.
Drugs
Hepatic and renal clearance fall; sedatives and opioids accumulate
Accumulated drug is why neuroprognostication is confounded for days — see §07.
Magnesium, phosphate, calcium
All fall
All rebound. Recheck through the transition.
Immunity
Suppressed — pneumonia is common and fever may be blunted
Watch for infection unmasked by rewarming.
Cerebral metabolism
CMRO<sub>2</sub> falls roughly 6–8% per °C

steps.title: Stabilize first, then cool
steps.html: Airway secured, hemodynamics supported, 12-lead done and the decision made about urgent coronary angiography. Temperature control is important and it is not the first thing.

steps.title: Core probe in before the device goes on
steps.html: Esophageal where possible. Record the starting temperature — many post-arrest patients arrive spontaneously hypothermic, and knowing that changes what the device needs to do.

steps.title: Set the target your institution uses, and reach it
steps.html: Somewhere in the 32–37.5 °C band depending on local protocol — commonly strict normothermia at 36–37.5 °C, or 33 °C where that is the chosen strategy. Choosing a number is less important than holding it: the failure that matters is drifting into fever.

steps.title: Get ahead of shivering
steps.html: Counterwarm the skin from the start. Assess formally every hour. Escalate up the ladder in §04 rather than reaching for paralysis.

steps.title: Maintain for 24 hours, and watch the chemistry
steps.html: Electrolytes and glucose every 4–6 hours. Potassium at the lower end of normal, deliberately. Continuous EEG if paralyzed, and a low threshold for it otherwise — non-convulsive seizures after arrest are common and invisible.

steps.title: Rewarm slowly — no faster than 0.25–0.5 °C per hour
steps.html: Use the device to control the rate; do not simply switch it off. This is the most dangerous phase. Expect hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and vasodilatory hypotension arriving together. Stop potassium replacement before you start, reduce insulin as you go, and have volume and a pressor available.

steps.title: Then keep them out of fever for at least 72 hours
steps.html: Leave the device on in normothermia mode. Rebound hyperthermia after rewarming is extremely common and is the part everyone stops watching for, because the protocol feels finished. It is not.

blocks.html:
Temperature is one element of a bundle, and the others are what the patient is most likely to be harmed by in the first hours.

  • Oxygen: avoid hypoxia and hyperoxia. Titrate to SpO2 92–98%. Leaving the FiO2 at 1.0 after ROSC is a real and common harm.
  • Ventilation: normocapnia, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg. Hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction; hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure.
  • Blood pressure: MAP ≥65 mmHg, and many units target 80–100 in the hope of better cerebral perfusion through impaired autoregulation. Avoid hypotension above all.
  • Coronary angiography: immediately for ST elevation. For patients without ST elevation and no shock, early routine angiography has not shown benefit, so it becomes a case-by-case decision.
  • Glucose: roughly 140–180 mg/dL. Avoid hypoglycemia more than you chase tight control.
  • Seizures: treat electrographic seizures. Distinguish myoclonic status from post-hypoxic myoclonus — they are not prognostically equivalent and the distinction needs EEG.
  • Neuroprognostication: not before 72 hours after return to normothermia, and not while sedation is on board. Hypothermia and accumulated drug both suppress the examination. Use multiple modalities — clinical examination, bilaterally absent N20 on SSEP, EEG pattern, neuron-specific enolase, and imaging — and never a single test. Early pessimistic prognostication is a self-fulfilling prophecy, and it remains one of the commonest serious errors in post-arrest care.

rows: Cannot reach target
Shivering — usually subclinical
Feel the jaw and chest wall. Counterwarm the skin, then escalate the ladder. Do not simply turn the device colder.
Temperature oscillating
Manual cooling, or a probe reading a lagging compartment
Use closed-loop feedback. Switch to an esophageal probe.
Two probes disagree
One is lagging or displaced
Trust the esophageal reading. Check the bladder probe against urine output — it is unreliable when oliguric.
Potassium falling during cooling
Intracellular shift — expected
Replace sparingly to 3.0–3.5. Stop replacing before rewarming.
Hyperkalemia during rewarming
Potassium returning from cells, usually on top of replacement given at target
Treat it, and learn the sequencing lesson. This is why replacement stops early.
Hypotension as you rewarm
Vasodilation on a volume-depleted patient
Anticipate it. Slow the rewarming, give volume, add a pressor.
Bradycardia at 33 °C
Expected physiology
Do not treat if perfusion and lactate are adequate. It is not a complication.
Fever on day 2 or 3
Rebound hyperthermia, or infection
Keep the device on in normothermia mode for 72 h. Look for pneumonia — cooled patients aspirate and their fever response is blunted.
Paralyzed and “settled”
Possible unrecognized seizures
Continuous EEG. Paralysis hides status epilepticus completely.
Team discussing withdrawal at 24 h
Premature prognostication
Stop. Not before 72 h after normothermia and off sedation, and never on one modality.

blocks.html:
Prevent fever. If only one thing survives from this page, it is that — it is the element every trial still supports, and it lasts 72 hours.

Holding the target matters more than which target. Drift into fever is the failure; the exact number is institutional.

Warm the skin while you cool the core. The single most underused anti-shivering measure, and it saves sedation.

Paralysis is last, and it hides seizures. If you paralyze, you need EEG.

Stop replacing potassium before you rewarm. It comes back out of the cells.

Rewarming is the dangerous phase. Hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and hypotension arrive together, and switching the machine off is not rewarming.

Do not leave the FiO2 at 1.0. Hyperoxia after arrest is a harm, not a safety margin.

Bradycardia at target is physiology. Leave it alone if the patient is perfusing.

Esophageal probe. Bladder lags when it matters most.

No prognosis before 72 hours off sedation and at normothermia — and never from a single test.

procedures.title: Transcutaneous & Transvenous Pacing
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: From pads on the chest to a wire in the right ventricle — bridging unstable bradycardia to a definitive rhythm.
procedures.description: Bridging unstable bradycardia to a definitive rhythm.

blocks.html:
• Symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine and/or refractory to initial pharmacologic management
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, third-degree) with hemodynamic instability
  • Bradycardic peri-arrest rhythms where pacing is part of the resuscitation algorithm
  • Bradycardia-dependent ventricular arrhythmias (pause-dependent torsades) — overdrive pacing suppresses the pauses that trigger it
  • Transvenous pacing specifically when transcutaneous pacing fails to capture, is not tolerated despite sedation, or the bradycardia will clearly outlast what pads can reasonably bridge

Pick the modality by time course, not by severity. Transcutaneous is fast, non-invasive, and buys minutes to an hour or two. Transvenous is slower to place but is what you want the moment you believe the problem will still be there in several hours — complete heart block that isn't reversing, a beta-blocker/CCB overdose that hasn't peaked yet, an infiltrative or ischemic conduction system. Start pads while someone opens the transvenous kit; these are sequential, not alternative.

• Severe hypothermia with bradycardia — the cold myocardium is often refractory to pacing, and instrumentation of an irritable hypothermic ventricle can precipitate VF that is itself refractory until rewarming. Bradycardia is an appropriate physiologic response at low core temperatures; treat the temperature.
  • Transvenous: coagulopathy, or inability to obtain safe central venous access (relative — weighed against the urgency of the indication; a subclavian stick in a coagulopathic patient is a non-compressible site, so favor IJ or femoral if you must proceed)
  • Transcutaneous: no absolute contraindication in an unstable patient. Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted device generator (keep ≥8 cm away) or over a transdermal medication patch — remove the patch and wipe the skin first.

blocks.title: Don't pace a bradycardia the patient needs
blocks.html: Sinus bradycardia with a normal blood pressure and mentation in a fit patient, an athlete at rest, or a patient on a rate-controlling drug at steady state does not need pacing. The indication is symptomatic or peri-arrest bradycardia — hypotension, altered mentation, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure attributable to the rate. Rate alone is not the indication.

sections.title: Equipment — What's Actually in the Room

blocks.html:
Transcutaneous pacing

  • Monitor/defibrillator with pacing capability — know which button on your device enters pacing mode; this differs between Zoll, Philips, and LIFEPAK units and is not the time to learn it
  • Multifunction pacing/defibrillation pads (the same pads defibrillate — you do not need to change them if the patient deteriorates)
  • Razor and a towel — hair and diaphoresis are the two most common reasons pads won't capture
  • Sedation/analgesia drawn up before you start pacing, not after

Transvenous pacing — the full inventory

  • Introducer sheath with hemostatic valve and side port — sized to accept the wire (a 5 Fr wire needs at minimum a 6 Fr sheath). A standard triple-lumen central line will not accept a pacing wire.
  • Balloon-tipped bipolar pacing wire — typically 5 Fr, ~100 cm, marked in 10 cm increments. Two electrodes: the distal tip and a proximal ring a short distance behind it.
  • The sterile protective sleeve — the concertina-style plastic sheath that lets you advance or withdraw the wire later without contaminating it. See the alert below.
  • External pulse generator + a battery you have personally verified. Most units take a 9V; a dead generator discovered at the bedside is a recurring and entirely preventable disaster.
  • Connector cable with clearly marked positive and negative terminals
  • Alligator clip / V-lead adapter for ECG-guided placement
  • Small syringe (usually 1.5–3 mL) for balloon inflation — inflate with air, never fluid, and never beyond the volume printed on the wire
  • Full sterile barrier, ultrasound with sterile sheath, sterile saline
  • 12-lead ECG machine or a monitor that can display and print a V lead
  • Transcutaneous pads already on the patient — your backup runs the entire time you are floating the wire

blocks.title: Load the sterile sleeve onto the wire before it ever enters the patient
blocks.html: The protective sleeve only slides on from the proximal end. Once the wire is in the vein, it is too late — you now have a wire you cannot reposition without breaking sterility, and lead dislodgement is the single most common late failure of transvenous pacing. This is the classic, universally-taught error, and it is made by experienced operators in a hurry. Sleeve first.
Pad placement determines whether this works at all

steps.title: Prepare the skin
steps.html: Clip (don't shave raw) dense chest hair, wipe the skin dry, and remove any transdermal patches. Diaphoresis and hair are the two most common causes of a pad that will not capture, and both are trivially fixable in ten seconds — before you conclude the myocardium is refractory.

steps.title: Place pads anterior-posterior
steps.html: Anterior pad over the left precordium (roughly V2–V3 position, just left of the sternum); posterior pad on the left infrascapular back, lateral to the spine. This sandwiches the ventricle in the current path. Avoid bone — sternum and spine both shunt current. Anterolateral placement also works and is acceptable if the patient cannot be turned, but A-P generally captures at lower output.

steps.title: Set mode and rate
steps.html: Demand (synchronous) mode for any patient with an intrinsic rhythm — it paces only when the patient doesn't. Use fixed/asynchronous mode only for asystole or when artifact is causing the pacer to oversense and inhibit itself. Set rate 60–80/min for most adults; higher (90–100) if you are overdrive-pacing pause-dependent torsades.

steps.title: Find capture — choose your direction deliberately
steps.html: Two accepted approaches. Ramp up from the lowest output and climb until capture appears: better tolerated in a conscious, marginally stable patient. Start at maximum and dial down until you lose capture, then set above that: faster, and the right choice in a peri-arrest patient where you cannot afford to spend thirty seconds hunting. Typical capture thresholds are wide — commonly around 40–90 mA — and depend heavily on body habitus, pad contact, and effusion.

steps.title: Set a safety margin
steps.html: Once you identify the capture threshold, run the output roughly 10 mA above it. Thresholds drift with position, sweat, and pad gel drying out; running at exactly threshold means intermittent loss of capture you may not notice immediately.

steps.title: Sedate — and understand what hurts
steps.html: The pain is skeletal muscle contraction of the chest wall, not the heart. It is genuinely severe and patients describe it as the worst part of their resuscitation. Analgesia plus anxiolysis, titrated carefully — you are sedating a patient whose blood pressure depends on the thing causing the pain, so small doses, frequent reassessment, and a vasopressor within reach.

sections.title: Confirming Capture — And Why False Capture Fools People

blocks.html: This is the highest-yield teaching point in the whole procedure

Electrical capture means each pacing spike is followed by a genuine, wide paced QRS with a discordant T wave — the T deflects opposite to the main QRS vector, the same repolarization pattern you expect in LBBB. That discordance is a feature, not a problem: it is evidence the complex is a genuinely paced depolarization rather than artifact. (Concordant ST/T changes in a paced rhythm are the abnormal finding — one of the Sgarbossa criteria for ischemia.) Mechanical capture means that complex generated an actual contraction.

False capture is the trap: every pacing spike is followed by a wide squiggle on the monitor that looks exactly like a paced complex but is chest-wall muscle artifact, and the pacer is doing nothing to the heart. Operators declare success, stop escalating, and the patient stays in a perfusionless bradycardia with a monitor that looks reassuring. This is common enough that you should assume it until disproven.

How to actually prove capture, in order of reliability:

  • Femoral or right-sided pulse — palpate somewhere the pectoral muscle twitch isn't shaking the limb you're feeling. A left radial pulse during left-sided pacing is exactly where artifact fools you.
  • Bedside echo — look directly at the ventricle and watch it contract, one-for-one with the spikes. This is the definitive answer and takes seconds.
  • Arterial line waveform or a plethysmograph/SpO2 tracing — a mechanical pulse wave at exactly the paced rate is hard to fake.
  • End-tidal CO2 rising in an arrest context — indirect but real evidence you restored circulation.

blocks.caption: Both tracings have a spike before every wide deflection, and on a moving monitor they look alike. The difference is the discordant T wave and, decisively, whether there is a pulse wave beneath it — which is why you confirm with a femoral pulse, an arterial line, or bedside echo rather than the monitor alone.

blocks.title: Pacing spikes with no pulse is still PEA
blocks.html: If you have convincing electrical capture and no mechanical capture, the problem is no longer the conduction system — it is pump, volume, or obstruction. Pacing faster will not fix tamponade, a massive PE, profound hyperkalemia, or an empty ventricle. Go back to the arrest algorithm and the reversible causes.

sections.title: Transvenous Pacing — Assembly & Connections Before You Start

blocks.html: Everything here happens on the sterile field before the wire enters the patient

steps.title: Test the balloon, then fully deflate it
steps.html: Inflate to the labeled volume with air and look for symmetric inflation and no leak — some operators submerge it in sterile saline to check for bubbles. Then deflate completely and leave the syringe attached. A balloon you discover is ruptured after the wire is in the SVC costs you the entire insertion.

steps.title: Load the sterile sleeve onto the wire
steps.html: Slide it on from the proximal end and push it back out of your way toward the connector end. It gets extended and locked onto the sheath hub at the end of the procedure. This step cannot be done later.

steps.title: Know your polarity: distal tip = negative
steps.html: The distal tip electrode is the cathode (negative); the proximal ring is the anode (positive). Every connection downstream depends on this — the ECG clip, and later the generator cable. Identify which pin on your wire's connector corresponds to the distal tip now, on the field, with the packaging still in front of you.

steps.title: Clip the V lead to the distal electrode
steps.html: Attach an alligator clip from the distal/negative pin to the V1 lead of the ECG machine. The wire's tip now functions as a roving intracardiac electrode, and V1 on your ECG becomes a live readout of where the tip is. Only the distal tip completes this circuit usefully — clip the proximal ring by mistake and you will not get a clean injury pattern, and you will float the wire blind while believing you have guidance.

steps.title: Power up and pre-set the generator — but don't connect it yet
steps.html: Confirm the battery, set rate 70–80/min, output toward maximum (commonly ~10–20 mA to start), sensitivity to asynchronous/fixed for the float. Leave it off or disconnected. You connect the generator after you have your target position — ECG guidance and pacing output on the same wire at the same time interfere with each other.

blocks.html: Alternative: float it paced. If you have no usable ECG guidance, you can connect the generator up front at high output and asynchronous mode, and advance until paced capture suddenly appears on the monitor — capture is your position confirmation. It is a legitimate and sometimes faster approach in a crashing patient. It costs you the granular feedback of the injury pattern, so you learn position only at the moment you succeed.
Right IJ and left subclavian give the gentlest curve into the RV

steps.title: Place the introducer sheath
steps.html: Right internal jugular is the most direct, straightest path to the right ventricle and is the preferred site when you have a choice; left subclavian is the next most forgiving curve. Femoral works but usually requires fluoroscopy. Ultrasound-guided, full barrier, and confirm venous placement before dilating.

steps.title: Insert the wire to roughly 15–20 cm, balloon down
steps.html: Advance the deflated wire through the hemostatic valve until the tip is safely past the sheath tip and sitting in the vein — about 15–20 cm from a neck site. Use the wire's depth markings.

steps.title: Now inflate the balloon
steps.html: Never inflate inside the sheath — you will rupture the balloon against the introducer, and you will not know until the wire refuses to float. Once past the sheath tip, inflate to the labeled volume and lock the stopcock if your wire has one. The inflated balloon is what lets venous flow carry the tip in the right direction.

steps.title: Advance and read the V1 waveform as a map
steps.html: Advance in smooth, unhurried increments and watch V1. SVC: large negative P wave, small QRS. Right atrium: P wave becomes very large, often biphasic — the P is bigger than the QRS. Crossing the tricuspid into the RV: the P wave abruptly shrinks and the QRS becomes large. Tip against RV endocardium: ST-segment elevation — the current of injury. That is your endpoint. It means the electrode is in contact with ventricular wall, which is exactly what you need for capture.

steps.title: Recognize the depth you should be at
steps.html: From a right IJ, the RV is typically reached around 30–35 cm; from a left subclavian, a few centimeters more. Treat these as a sanity check, not a target — the waveform and capture tell you where you are; the centimeter markings only tell you when something is wrong. If you are at 45–50 cm with no ventricular signal, you are coiling in the atrium or have gone down the IVC. Withdraw and start again rather than pushing.

steps.title: Deflate the balloon, then connect the generator
steps.html: Deflate once you have the injury pattern. Connect the cable with distal/tip to negative, proximal ring to positive. Turn the generator on and confirm capture.

steps.title: Find the true capture threshold
steps.html: With capture established, reduce output until capture is lost — that value is the threshold. A well-positioned wire captures at a low threshold, commonly under 1 mA; a threshold above ~2 mA suggests the tip is not well apposed and you should consider repositioning now rather than at 3 a.m. Then set the running output at roughly 2–3× threshold.

steps.title: Set sensitivity and switch to demand
steps.html: Move off asynchronous to demand mode for any patient with an underlying rhythm. Remember the counterintuitive direction: on most generators a lower mV number means more sensitive. Undersensing (spikes landing on intrinsic beats, with R-on-T risk) means you should lower the number; oversensing (inappropriate inhibition and pauses) means raise it.

steps.title: Lock the sleeve, secure, and confirm with imaging
steps.html: Extend the sterile sleeve and lock it to the sheath hub, suture/secure the sheath, and tape the generator to the patient — not to the bed, where a transfer will avulse the wire. Obtain a chest radiograph to confirm the tip sits at the RV apex and to look for a pneumothorax from the access itself.

blocks.title: Balloon up going in, balloon down coming out — always
blocks.html: Advance only with the balloon inflated; withdraw only with it deflated. Dragging an inflated balloon backward across the tricuspid apparatus can entangle or damage chordae and valve leaflets. If you need to pull back even a centimeter, deflate first, every single time.

rows: Spikes, no capture (transcutaneous)
Pad contact, hair, sweat, or output below threshold
Dry and clip the skin, re-seat pads in true A-P, escalate output to maximum before concluding failure
Spikes, no capture (transvenous)
Loose connection far more often than true dislodgement
Check the cable and terminals first, then increase output, then reposition. Verify polarity wasn't reversed
Capture lost after being stable
Lead dislodgement, or perforation
Re-check connections, increase output, reposition. New hypotension + loss of capture = suspect perforation/tamponade and get an echo
Wide complexes after every spike but no pulse
False capture (artifact) or genuine PEA
Confirm with echo or femoral pulse. If truly electrical-only, treat as PEA and work reversible causes
Ventricular ectopy, VT, or VF while floating
The wire is mechanically irritating the RV — expected, usually transient
Stop advancing. Deflate and withdraw slightly; ectopy typically resolves. Defibrillator must already be attached before you start
SVT during the float
Atrial irritation from the catheter
Withdraw slightly; usually self-terminates. Treat per rhythm if sustained and unstable
Asystole / loss of underlying rhythm mid-procedure
The escape rhythm you were relying on has failed
Go straight to transcutaneous pacing and CPR. Do not keep manipulating the wire in an arrested patient — that's why the pads stayed on
Hiccups or rhythmic abdominal/chest wall twitching
Diaphragmatic or phrenic pacing — tip may be at a thin RV wall or through it
Reduce output and reposition. Consider perforation, especially with any hemodynamic change
Pauses / intermittent failure to pace
Oversensing — generator inhibiting on artifact or T waves
Make it less sensitive (raise the mV), or go asynchronous if the patient is dependent
Spikes landing on intrinsic beats
Undersensing
Make it more sensitive (lower the mV). Real R-on-T risk — fix promptly
Wire won't advance past ~20 cm / coils
Balloon not inflated, or going down the IVC / into a tributary
Confirm balloon is up and past the sheath. Withdraw to the SVC and re-float rather than forcing

blocks.html:
• RV perforation and tamponade — the most feared complication. Presents as loss of capture with new hypotension, sometimes with diaphragmatic pacing beforehand. Echo immediately; be prepared for pericardiocentesis.
  • Induced ventricular arrhythmia during floating — common, usually transient, occasionally VF. Non-negotiable reason to have pads and a defibrillator on before starting.
  • Lead dislodgement — the most common late failure, and the reason the sterile sleeve and proper securing matter more than they feel like they do at the time.
  • Access complications — pneumothorax, arterial puncture, and in a coagulopathic patient a non-compressible subclavian hematoma.
  • Infection — rises sharply with dwell time; these are a bridge to a permanent device or to recovery, not a destination.
  • Knotting or entanglement in the tricuspid apparatus — almost always from withdrawing with the balloon inflated, or from repeatedly forcing a wire that won't float.
  • Inadequate sedation during transcutaneous pacing — a genuine harm, not a comfort nicety; patients who have had it describe it as the defining trauma of the resuscitation.
  • Declaring success on false capture — the failure mode most likely to kill the patient quietly while the monitor looks fine.

• Document the threshold you measured, the output you set, the mode, the rate, and the insertion depth at the hub. The next clinician troubleshooting a loss of capture needs to know whether 22 cm at the hub is where it started.
  • Recheck the threshold periodically — thresholds rise over the first days as local inflammation develops around the tip. A wire that captured at 0.8 mA on day one may need more by day two.
  • Keep the transcutaneous pads on the patient while the patient is pacer-dependent, particularly through any transfer, turn, or imaging trip — those are exactly when wires dislodge.
  • Every transport is a dislodgement risk. Secure the generator to the patient, and have someone whose specific job is the wire during any move.
  • Arrange the definitive plan early — cardiology/EP for a permanent device, or treatment of the reversible cause (hyperkalemia, drug toxicity, ischemia). A temporary wire is a bridge with a short safe lifespan.

Electrical capture is not mechanical capture. Prove circulation with an echo or a pulse that muscle twitch cannot fake, every single time, before you relax.

Check connections before you believe in dislodgement. A loose terminal at the generator is dramatically more common than a wire that has moved, and it is fixed in two seconds rather than by re-floating a wire.

The injury pattern is the endpoint, not a waypoint. ST elevation on the V1 tracing means tip-to-endocardium contact. If it appears and then vanishes, you have lost contact — don't interpret its disappearance as progress.

Only the distal tip completes the sensing circuit. Clipping V1 to the proximal ring gives you a tracing that looks plausible and tells you almost nothing.

Sleeve first, balloon up going in, balloon down coming out. Three habits that prevent most of the procedure's avoidable disasters.

Transcutaneous pacing is a bridge measured in minutes to an hour or two, both because of capture reliability and because it is agonizing. If the underlying problem won't resolve on that timescale, start arranging the wire immediately rather than waiting for the pads to fail.

Pace the patient, not the monitor. A patient whose mentation and blood pressure improve is captured; a monitor that looks tidy is not evidence of anything by itself.
