procedures.title: Manual Uterine Massage & Bimanual Compression
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: First-line mechanical management of uterine atony — the hands-on step that often works before any medication does.
procedures.description: First-line mechanical management of uterine atony.

blocks.html:
• Postpartum hemorrhage with a soft, boggy, poorly contracted uterus — uterine atony, which causes 70–80% of postpartum hemorrhage
  • Prophylactically, in the third stage, as part of active management alongside a uterotonic
  • Any postpartum bleeding that looks more than ordinary, before you have worked out the cause — massage costs nothing and buys time

The current definition of postpartum hemorrhage is cumulative blood loss of ≥1000 mL, or blood loss accompanied by signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth — regardless of route of delivery. The older 500 mL vaginal threshold is retained by many units as a trigger for heightened attention, which is reasonable.

blocks.title: You are underestimating the blood loss — everyone does
blocks.html: Visual estimation of obstetric blood loss under-reads by 30–50%, and the error grows as the volume grows. Quantify it: weigh pads, drapes and sponges (1 g = 1 mL, minus dry weight) and use a graduated under-buttocks drape. And remember that a healthy pregnant woman's blood volume is up 40–50%, so she compensates beautifully and then collapses: vital signs can stay near-normal until 1500 mL is gone. Watch the shock index (HR ÷ SBP) — above 0.9 to 1.0 is an early and validated trigger, well before hypotension appears.

sections.title: When Massage Is the Wrong Answer

blocks.html:
• A firm uterus with ongoing bleeding is not atony. Stop massaging and go looking. Inspect the cervix, vagina and perineum for lacerations, consider retained placental tissue, consider uterine rupture, and consider coagulopathy — including amniotic fluid embolism, which presents as coagulopathic bleeding with cardiorespiratory collapse.
  • Uterine inversion. If the fundus is not palpable abdominally and there is a mass at or through the cervix, with shock out of proportion to the visible loss, this is inversion, and massaging or giving uterotonics makes it irreversible. See §06 — the treatment is the opposite of everything else on this page.
  • Retained placenta. A uterus cannot contract around retained tissue. It has to come out first.
  • Continuing massage as a substitute for escalation. A uterus that firms under your hand and softens the moment you stop is telling you atony is ongoing and unresponsive. That is a signal to escalate, not to keep rubbing.

The four T's, in order of frequency: Tone (atony, ~70–80%) · Trauma (lacerations, rupture, hematoma, ~20%) · Tissue (retained products) · Thrombin (coagulopathy). Inversion sits outside the list and is the one that punishes the reflexive response.

• Gloved hands — long gloves if you have them, because bimanual compression puts your forearm in the vagina.
  • A urinary catheter. Frequently skipped and genuinely effective: a full bladder mechanically prevents the uterus from contracting. Empty it early.
  • Uterotonics, drawn and ready — see §05 for doses and the two contraindications that matter.
  • Large-bore IV access ×2, crystalloid, and the massive transfusion pathway on standby.
  • Tranexamic acid.
  • Analgesia or sedation. Sustained bimanual compression is extremely painful in a woman who is usually awake and alert.
  • Escalation equipment within reach: intrauterine balloon (Bakri, or a condom catheter improvised over a Foley), vacuum-induced tamponade device, and the number for whoever performs compression sutures, embolization, or a hysterectomy.
  • A scale for quantitative blood loss, and a whiteboard.
Fundal massage — two hands, not one

steps.title: Empty the bladder first
steps.html: Catheterize. A distended bladder displaces the uterus and physically prevents contraction, and this single step sometimes resolves the problem. It also gives you urine output as a perfusion marker for everything that follows.

steps.title: Support the lower segment with the second hand
steps.html: Cup the fundus with one hand and place the other just above the symphysis, pressing back and supporting the lower uterine segment. Vigorous one-handed massage of an atonic uterus can invert it. The lower hand is a guard, not an afterthought.

steps.title: Massage firmly — and know what you are feeling for
steps.html: A deep, firm, kneading circular motion, not a light rub. The endpoint is a uterus that feels like a clenched fist, globular and hard, at or below the umbilicus. Boggy, wide, and doughy means atony continues. Express retained clot from the lower segment as tone returns — clot in the cavity perpetuates atony.

blocks.html: Bimanual compression

steps.title: Vaginal hand into the anterior fornix, as a fist
steps.html: Insert the whole hand, make a fist in the anterior fornix, and press upward and forward against the anterior wall of the uterus. Say what you are about to do — she is awake, and this is frightening as well as painful.

steps.title: Abdominal hand behind the fundus, pulling it forward
steps.html: Reach behind the uterus abdominally, cup the posterior wall, and draw the fundus down and forward onto the vaginal fist. You are not pressing straight down — you are bringing the two hands together.

steps.title: Compress and hold
steps.html: Squeeze the whole uterus between your hands, hard, and sustain it. This works two ways: it compresses the myometrium directly, and it kinks the uterine arteries in the broad ligament. It is exhausting within minutes — plan to rotate operators before anyone weakens. Do not release intermittently to check; hold, while the drugs and the team catch up.

steps.title: Everything else happens around you
steps.html: Compression is a holding action. While it is held: uterotonics given, TXA given, two lines in, blood ordered, bladder emptied, the genital tract inspected, and the next step being prepared. Bimanual compression that continues for twenty minutes with nothing else happening is not a plan.

steps.title: Aortic compression, if it is catastrophic
steps.html: In torrential hemorrhage, a closed fist pressed hard just above the umbilicus, directed posteriorly onto the vertebral column, compresses the abdominal aorta. Confirm by loss of femoral pulses. A crude, tiring, temporary measure — and it buys minutes when nothing else is working.

sections.title: Uterotonics — Doses and the Two That Can Harm

blocks.html: Massage and drugs go together. Neither is the second step.

rows:
Oxytocin
first line
10 units IM, or 10–40 units in 500–1000 mL crystalloid as an IV infusion, titrated
Never undiluted as a rapid IV push — causes hypotension, tachycardia and arrhythmia. Dilute it.
Methylergonovine
0.2 mg IM, may repeat every 2–4 h
Hypertension, preeclampsia, or Raynaud phenomenon. It is a vasoconstrictor and can precipitate stroke or severe hypertension. Never IV.

Carboprost
15-methyl PGF2α
250 mcg IM or intramyometrial, repeat every 15–90 min, max 8 doses (2 mg)
Asthma — it causes bronchospasm. Expect diarrhea, vomiting and fever as routine effects.
Misoprostol
600–1000 mcg sublingual, oral or rectal
No absolute contraindication. Causes fever and shivering, which is easily mistaken for sepsis.
Tranexamic acid
1 g IV over 10 min; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24 h
Within 3 hours of onset of bleeding — give it early. Pushed fast, it causes hypotension.
Calcium
CaCl 1 g, or Ca gluconate 3 g IV
Ionized calcium is required for myometrial contraction and falls with citrate from transfused product. Replete it.

blocks.html:
The two that catch people: methylergonovine in a preeclamptic woman, and carboprost in an asthmatic. Both are given in a rush by someone reaching for the next ampoule, and both patient groups are common on a labor ward. Say the contraindication out loud as you draw it up.

Uterine artery blood flow at term is roughly 500–700 mL/min. Hemostasis after delivery is mechanical — contracted myometrium strangling the spiral arteries, the “living ligatures” — not clot formation. That is why a woman with normal coagulation can exsanguinate from an atonic uterus in minutes, and why a profoundly coagulopathic woman stops bleeding once the uterus contracts.

blocks.title: If the fundus is missing, stop and think before you massage
blocks.html: Recognize it: the fundus cannot be palpated abdominally, or there is a dimple where it should be; a soft mass is felt at the cervix or seen at the introitus; and there is shock out of proportion to the visible blood loss, from the vagal response to traction on the peritoneum. Often follows cord traction on a fundally implanted placenta.

• Stop all uterotonics.
  • Replace it immediately — every minute makes it harder. Johnson maneuver: grasp the fundus in the palm, direct the fingertips toward the posterior fornix, and push steadily upward along the axis of the vagina toward the umbilicus. Steady pressure, not jabbing.
  • If the ring has already tightened, relax the uterus — nitroglycerin 50–100 mcg IV, terbutaline, magnesium, or a volatile anesthetic — then replace.
  • Leave the placenta attached until after reduction if it is still adherent; removing it first increases blood loss.
  • Only once the uterus is back: give uterotonics, and keep a hand inside until it contracts around it.
  • Resuscitate throughout, and call for surgical help early — failed reduction needs an operating room.

Massage and compression are the first rung. Bleeding that persists despite a well-contracted uterus, or atony that will not hold, moves up the ladder — and the movement should be by the clock, not by feel.

  • Intrauterine balloon tamponade — a Bakri balloon filled with 300–500 mL of saline, or a condom tied over a catheter where no device exists. The “tamponade test”: if bleeding stops with the balloon up, laparotomy is usually avoidable; if it does not, the patient needs an operation and you have learned that in minutes.
  • Vacuum-induced tamponade — a suction device that collapses the cavity rather than distending it. Fast where stocked.
  • Examination under anesthesia — for lacerations, retained tissue, and rupture. Do not persist with medical management on an undiagnosed cause.
  • Compression sutures (B-Lynch and variants) at laparotomy.
  • Uterine artery embolization, where interventional radiology is available and the patient is stable enough to travel.
  • Uterine or internal iliac artery ligation.
  • Hysterectomy — definitive, and the decision that is most often made too late. In refractory hemorrhage, deciding early saves lives.
  • Aortic compression, REBOA Zone 3, or a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment as bridges, particularly during transfer.
  • Massive transfusion throughout, with attention to fibrinogen — obstetric hemorrhage depletes it early, and the target in obstetric bleeding is higher: above 200 mg/dL.

rows: Uterus firms, then softens the moment you stop
Ongoing unresponsive atony
Escalate the uterotonic ladder and prepare a balloon. Do not simply keep massaging.
Uterus firm, still bleeding
Not atony — trauma, retained tissue, or coagulopathy
Inspect the genital tract properly, with light and retraction. Send coagulation studies and fibrinogen. Consider rupture.
Uterus will not contract at all
Full bladder, retained clot or placental tissue, or inversion
Catheterize, express clot, explore the cavity. Confirm the fundus is where it should be.
Fundus not palpable, profound shock, modest visible loss
Uterine inversion
Stop uterotonics. Replace immediately (§06). Relax the uterus if the ring has closed.
Vital signs normal, losses mounting
Pregnancy physiology masking hypovolemia
Do not be reassured. Quantify losses and watch the shock index. Decompensation is abrupt.
Steady trickle nobody escalates for
Slow accumulation — the pattern that kills quietly
Quantify. A persistent trickle reaches 1500 mL without a single dramatic moment.
Sudden hypertension after a uterotonic
Methylergonovine, probably in a preeclamptic patient
Treat the hypertension. Do not repeat the dose. Check what else was given.
Bronchospasm after a uterotonic
Carboprost in an asthmatic
Treat the bronchospasm. Switch agents.
Hypotension right after oxytocin
Given undiluted as a rapid push
Support pressure; give it as a dilute infusion from now on.
Oozing everywhere, contracted uterus
Coagulopathy — consider amniotic fluid embolism
Massive transfusion, fibrinogen replacement, TXA, calcium. AFE is a separate pathway — look for the cardiorespiratory collapse that precedes it.
Operator tiring, compression slackening
Entirely predictable
Rotate before it happens, not after. Assign the relief in advance.

blocks.html:
• Uterine inversion from vigorous unsupported fundal massage or cord traction — the reason the second hand exists.
  • Delayed escalation — the dominant harm. Compression is comfortable to keep doing and feels like treatment, and hours are lost inside it.
  • Delayed recognition of a non-atonic cause, because the reflex response was applied to the wrong problem.
  • Pain and distress in an awake patient — treatable, and frequently untreated.
  • Uterotonic adverse effects — hypertensive crisis, bronchospasm, hypotension, fever, vomiting.
  • Consequences of massive hemorrhage: dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy, transfusion reactions, acute kidney injury, Sheehan syndrome, ARDS, and hysterectomy with its own permanent consequences.
  • Psychological sequelae for the patient — postpartum hemorrhage is a recognized cause of birth trauma and post-traumatic stress. Debrief her, afterwards, properly.

Empty the bladder. Simple, frequently skipped, and sometimes the whole answer.

Two hands on the fundus. The lower hand supports the segment and prevents the inversion your massage could cause.

Firm uterus plus bleeding means look elsewhere. Cervix, vagina, retained tissue, rupture, coagulopathy.

Missing fundus plus disproportionate shock means inversion — and every instinct on this page is then backwards. Stop the uterotonics and replace it.

You are underestimating the loss. Weigh it. Watch the shock index, not the blood pressure.

She looks fine until she does not. Forty to fifty percent extra blood volume buys compensation that ends abruptly.

Methylergonovine and hypertension; carboprost and asthma. Say it aloud as you draw it up.

Oxytocin goes in dilute.

Hemostasis here is muscle, not clot. A contracted uterus stops bleeding even in a coagulopathic woman.

Compression is a holding action. If nothing else is being organized while you hold it, the plan has stopped.

Rotate before you tire.

procedures.title: Perimortem Cesarean Section / Resuscitative Hysterotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: The 4-minute rule: a maternal resuscitation maneuver first, a delivery second. Speed and aortocaval decompression over sterility and anatomic precision.
procedures.description: The 4-minute rule — maternal resuscitation first.

blocks.html: The modern name is resuscitative hysterotomy, and the change is not cosmetic — it names what the procedure is for.

• Maternal cardiac arrest with a uterus palpable at or above the umbilicus — roughly 20 weeks — without ROSC in the first few minutes of high-quality resuscitation
  • Peri-arrest with profound, refractory shock in late pregnancy, where aortocaval compression is plausibly the limiting factor
  • Fundal height is the trigger, not a documented gestational age. Nobody has dates in an arrest, and a stated LMP is not a reason to wait. Put a hand on the abdomen.

This is a maternal resuscitation maneuver. The gravid uterus at term can sequester a substantial fraction of cardiac output and compresses both the inferior vena cava and the aorta against the spine. Chest compressions already generate only a fraction of normal output; against aortocaval obstruction they may generate almost nothing. Emptying the uterus restores venous return, and it is frequently the intervention that makes the rest of the resuscitation work.

It is indicated even when the fetus is already dead, and even below the threshold of fetal viability, if the uterus is large enough to obstruct. Between about 20 and 24 weeks the procedure is performed for the mother alone. Framing this out loud to the team — “we are decompressing the aorta and vena cava” rather than “we are delivering a baby” — measurably reduces hesitation, and hesitation is the main failure mode.

blocks.title: The four-minute rule is a prompt, not a deadline
blocks.html: Katz's 1986 recommendation — incision at 4 minutes, delivery by 5 — was derived from case reports, and it remains the right thing to aim for. But its modern misuse is the opposite of its intent: teams look at a clock reading eleven minutes and conclude they have missed the window. They have not. Maternal ROSC and intact neonatal survival are both documented well beyond 5 minutes, including past 15. If the mother is still in arrest and the uterus is still obstructing, the procedure is still indicated. Aim for four minutes; never use having passed it as a reason not to act.

• A uterus that does not reach the umbilicus. Below roughly 20 weeks there is no meaningful aortocaval compression and nothing to be gained.
  • ROSC already achieved. If she has a pulse, this becomes an obstetric decision made with obstetrics, not a resuscitation maneuver.
  • Obvious, unequivocal signs of irreversible death predating the arrest.

Things that are not contraindications, and which are used as reasons to delay:

  • Absent fetal heart tones. Do not look for them. The procedure is for the mother, the ultrasound takes time you do not have, and a normal fetal heart does not change the decision either.
  • No obstetrician present. Whoever is there does it. Waiting for the right specialist is the commonest way the window is lost.
  • Not being in an operating room. It happens where the arrest happened. Moving the patient means stopping compressions, and transport time is the one thing that cannot be recovered.
  • No consent. Emergency doctrine. This is standard of care.
  • No sterile field, no anesthesia, no formal instrument tray. A patient in cardiac arrest does not need anesthesia, and infection is a problem for survivors.
  • Uncertain dates. See above — palpate.

• A scalpel. A No. 10 blade. That is the whole essential list, and saying so out loud helps people start.
  • Two cord clamps and scissors — or any two clamps and anything that cuts.
  • Bandage or Mayo scissors for extending the uterine incision, if reaching for them costs nothing.
  • Abdominal packs and towels for after ROSC.
  • Suction, if it is already in the room.
  • Neonatal resuscitation equipment and a separate team — warmer, bag-mask with a neonatal mask, towels, cord clamp. This is a second resuscitation and it needs its own people. Where there is any warning at all, stage them before incision.
  • Oxytocin, drawn and ready for the moment ROSC is achieved — see §07.

A pre-assembled pack helps, but only if it is where the patient is. Many units keep a resuscitative hysterotomy tray on the maternal arrest trolley. If yours does, know where it lives. If it does not, the scalpel on the intubation trolley is sufficient, and the procedure has been done with less.
Several things people “know” about this are out of date.

• Manual left uterine displacement, not lateral tilt. Stand at the patient's left and pull the uterus up and to the left with both hands, or push it leftward from her right side. Keep her supine. Tilting the whole body degrades compression quality substantially, and the evidence now favors displacement on a flat back. Continue displacement until the uterus is opened.
  • Standard hand position for compressions. The old teaching to move the hands higher on the sternum in pregnancy has not held up. Compress where you always compress.
  • Defibrillate at standard energies. Pads in the usual positions; move a lateral pad slightly if breast tissue is in the way. Fetal monitors come off before the shock.
  • Standard drugs at standard doses. No modification for pregnancy, and none withheld out of fetal concern — the fetus does not survive a mother who does not.
  • Airway early, and expect it to be hard. Mucosal edema, a fuller airway, larger breasts against the laryngoscope, and a reduced functional residual capacity with raised oxygen consumption mean desaturation is fast and the view is worse than you expect. Have a smaller tube ready — 6.0 to 7.0 — and go to a supraglottic device early rather than repeating attempts. Aspiration risk is high.
  • Access above the diaphragm. A femoral line delivers drugs through a vena cava the uterus is compressing. Use an upper-limb IV, a humeral IO, or an upper-body central line.
  • Think about the obstetric causes while you work. Hemorrhage (including concealed abruption and rupture), amniotic fluid embolism, pulmonary embolism, eclampsia and intracranial hemorrhage, peripartum cardiomyopathy, sepsis, anesthetic complications including high spinal and local anesthetic toxicity, and magnesium toxicity — for which the treatment is calcium, and which is easy to miss in a patient receiving an infusion nobody mentioned.

steps.title: Announce the arrest time, and have someone call the clock
steps.html: “Arrest at 14:06. I want the time called every minute. If there is no ROSC at 14:10 we are doing a hysterotomy.” Naming the decision in advance is what converts a four-minute target into something that actually happens, because in the moment nobody wants to be the person who says it.

steps.title: Compressions and displacement continue throughout
steps.html: Nothing stops for this. Not for the incision, not for the delivery. Someone maintains left uterine displacement until the uterus is open.

steps.title: Vertical midline, umbilicus to symphysis, through everything
steps.html: A single firm stroke from just above the umbilicus down to the pubic symphysis, through skin, fat, and fascia. There is very little bleeding in arrest — no perfusion pressure — and this surprises people the first time. Do not creep through the layers. Vertical is chosen because it is fast and forgiving of anatomy you cannot see.

steps.title: Open the peritoneum, sweep the bladder down
steps.html: Enter bluntly with fingers where you can, to avoid bowel and bladder. The bladder sits over the lower uterine segment and is often distended — push it inferiorly out of the way rather than cutting through it.

steps.title: Vertical uterine incision — start small, extend with fingers
steps.html: Make a short vertical incision in the lower uterine segment and continue until you are through the myometrium and into the cavity. Then put the scalpel down. Extend the opening upward with your fingers, or with bandage scissors advanced between two fingers held inside the uterus as a shield. Scalpel extension is how fetuses get lacerated, and it is entirely avoidable.

steps.title: Deliver, clamp, cut, hand off
steps.html: Deliver the fetus by whatever presentation you find — a hand under the head, or by the feet if breech. Double-clamp and cut the cord and hand the neonate to a different person with a different job. The mother remains your patient. If no neonatal team exists yet, that is a hard reality to state out loud and then work within.

steps.title: Remove the placenta, then keep resuscitating
steps.html: Deliver the placenta manually if it comes easily; do not spend time on it if it does not. The decompression has already happened. Reassess rhythm and continue the algorithm — venous return may now be dramatically better, and this is the point at which arrests sometimes convert.

steps.title: Record every time
steps.html: Arrest, decision, incision, delivery. Someone writes these down as they happen. They will be needed for the neonatal team, for the debrief, and for the review that follows.

rows: Minutes passing, nobody starting
Hesitation — the dominant failure mode of this procedure
Name it: the arrest time, the decision point, and who holds the scalpel. Frame it as decompression, not delivery.
Team wants to move to an OR
Reasonable instinct, wrong answer
It happens here. Transport costs CPR quality and minutes that cannot be recovered.
Someone is reaching for the ultrasound
Looking for fetal heart tones
Stop them. It does not change the decision in either direction, and it costs the window.
Far more bleeding than expected
She has ROSC — or never fully lost output
Good news. Now it is an operation: pack, control, get to an OR, get obstetrics and anesthesia.
Cannot find the uterus in the wound
Incision too short, or still above the peritoneum
Extend the incision fully to the symphysis. The gravid uterus is unmissable once you are actually inside.
Fetus lacerated on delivery
Uterine incision extended with the blade
Preventable: extend with fingers or shielded scissors. Hand the injury to the neonatal team explicitly.
No improvement after delivery
Aortocaval compression was not the limiting problem
Return to the differential — hemorrhage, AFE, PE, magnesium toxicity, local anesthetic toxicity, tamponade. Consider ECPR if available.
ROSC, then torrential bleeding
Uterine atony in an open uterus
Oxytocin immediately, bimanual compression, pack the uterus and abdomen. See the postpartum hemorrhage entry — this is now that problem.
Neonate delivered, nobody free to take it
Single-team resuscitation
Anticipate it. Assign a person before incision if there is any warning at all. Dry, warm, stimulate, and ventilate — most need no more.
Magnesium infusion running
Magnesium toxicity as the arrest cause
Stop it and give calcium. Easily missed because the infusion is routine and nobody mentions it.

blocks.html:
The moment perfusion returns, an open atonic uterus becomes a hemorrhage of a scale few clinicians have seen. Be ready for it before it happens.

  • Oxytocin immediately — a dilute infusion, not an undiluted rapid push, which causes hypotension and arrhythmia in an already unstable patient. Add further uterotonics per the postpartum hemorrhage pathway, observing their contraindications.
  • Bimanual compression and uterine massage, and pack the uterus and abdomen with laparotomy sponges. Count them.
  • Activate massive transfusion and give TXA if within the window.
  • Move to an operating room for formal closure. The abdomen can travel packed and open; it must not stay that way.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics — the field was not sterile and now she is a survivor for whom infection matters.
  • Targeted temperature management and post-arrest care as for any other arrest. Pregnancy and recent delivery are not contraindications.
  • Treat the cause. The hysterotomy relieved an obstruction; it did not treat an embolism, an eclamptic bleed, or a cardiomyopathy.

• Debrief, and mean it. This is among the most distressing events in clinical medicine, and it is frequently performed by people who have never done it and will never do it again. Debrief on the day and follow up afterwards, with a specific offer rather than a general one.
  • Expect the review, and welcome it. Maternal deaths are formally reviewed everywhere. Contemporaneous times and a clear account of the decision are what make that review useful rather than adversarial.
  • Rehearse it. Every unit that cares for pregnant patients — including emergency departments and non-obstetric hospitals — should have run this in simulation. The failure is almost never technical; it is the four minutes spent deciding. The single strongest predictor of doing it in time is having said out loud, beforehand, that you would.

Call it a resuscitative hysterotomy. The name is the intervention: it tells the room this is for the mother, and that is what gets it started.

Fundus at or above the umbilicus is the trigger. Not dates, not an ultrasound, not an obstetrician's opinion.

Past four minutes is not too late. The rule is a prompt. Survivors exist well beyond it.

Do not go looking for fetal heart tones. They do not change the decision and they cost the window.

Do it where she is. Moving means stopping compressions.

Manual left uterine displacement, supine. Not tilt — tilt ruins the compressions.

Access above the diaphragm. Drugs given below a compressed vena cava may never arrive.

Put the scalpel down once you are in the uterus. Fingers from there.

Almost no bleeding in arrest — and torrential bleeding at ROSC. Have oxytocin drawn before you need it.

One scalpel is enough. Saying so is part of the technique.

procedures.title: Symphysiotomy & Procedural Shoulder Dystocia Maneuvers
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Obstetric
procedures.subtitle: The escalation ladder for shoulder dystocia, ending in a rarely-needed but field-relevant last resort.
procedures.description: The escalation ladder, ending in a rare last resort.

blocks.html:
• The head delivers and the shoulders do not follow with gentle downward traction and the next contraction
  • Turtle sign — the head delivers, then retracts tightly back against the perineum as the anterior shoulder catches on the symphysis
  • The head fails to restitute, sitting stuck facing directly down or up rather than rotating to one side
  • A head-to-body interval beyond about 60 seconds, or any delivery requiring maneuvers beyond gentle axial traction — this is the working definition, and it is deliberately broad

You cannot predict it. Most shoulder dystocias occur in normal-weight infants of women with no risk factors, and the recognized associations — macrosomia, diabetes, prior dystocia, instrumental delivery, prolonged second stage — have poor predictive value individually. Every delivery is a delivery where this can happen, which is why the response has to be drilled rather than reasoned out on the spot.

blocks.title: The clock is the whole problem
blocks.html: Once the head is out, the chest cannot expand and the cord is compressed against the pelvis. Fetal pH falls by roughly 0.04 units per minute from that moment. Beyond about 5 minutes, the risk of hypoxic-ischemic injury rises steeply. Announce the time the head delivered and have someone call it out every 30 seconds. Under pressure, teams consistently believe far less time has elapsed than actually has — a called clock is the only reliable correction for that.

sections.title: The Three Things That Cause the Injuries

blocks.html:
Most permanent harm from shoulder dystocia comes not from the impaction but from the response to it.

  • Never apply fundal pressure. It drives the anterior shoulder harder onto the symphysis, worsening the impaction it is meant to relieve, and it causes uterine rupture. Suprapubic pressure is the correct external maneuver, and the two get confused under stress precisely because both involve a hand on the abdomen. Say which one you want, and watch where the hand goes.
  • Never apply excessive or lateral traction to the head. Brachial plexus injury is caused by stretching the neck away from the shoulder. Traction is gentle, axial — in the line of the fetal spine, not downward-and-sideways — and it is applied only in coordination with a maneuver that is actually creating space.
  • Never twist or rotate the head. Rotation is done internally, on the shoulders, with a hand in the vagina. Turning the head turns nothing but the cervical spine.

Shoulder dystocia is among the most litigated events in obstetrics, and the record of what was and was not done matters. That is a secondary reason to get it right; the primary one is that these three errors are the ones that leave a child with a permanent deficit.

• People. The single most useful resource. Call for obstetric, anesthetic and neonatal help the moment you recognize it. You will need at least two for the legs, one for suprapubic pressure, one scribe, and a neonatal team.
  • A scribe and a visible clock. Every maneuver, with its time. This is both a clinical aid and the record.
  • A bed that flattens, and the ability to drop the foot of it and remove the end.
  • A stool — suprapubic pressure is delivered with body weight from above, which needs height.
  • Neonatal resuscitation equipment, warm and ready.
  • Cord gas syringes. Paired arterial and venous samples after delivery.
  • Episiotomy scissors and local anesthetic — not routinely required, but available.
  • Postpartum hemorrhage supplies. Prolonged dystocia is followed by atony often enough to anticipate it.
  • For symphysiotomy only (see §06): scalpel, urinary catheter, local anesthetic, and two assistants.
Roughly 30 seconds per maneuver. Move on. Do not repeat what has already failed.

blocks.caption: The ladder is drawn against the clock because teams consistently believe far less time has passed than actually has — which is why a scribe calls it out every 30 seconds. Note where the sequence ends up: working it through once takes roughly four minutes, so there is no spare time for repeating a maneuver that has already failed.

steps.title: Call for help. Note the time. Stop pushing.
steps.html: Say the words “shoulder dystocia” out loud — it summons a specific response that “I need a hand” does not. Ask the mother to stop pushing for the moment; maternal effort against an impacted shoulder achieves nothing and makes the maneuvers harder. Flatten the bed and bring her buttocks to its edge.

steps.title: McRoberts — hyperflex the hips
steps.html: One person per leg, hips sharply flexed onto the abdomen and slightly abducted. This does not enlarge the pelvis. It rotates the symphysis cephalad and flattens the sacral promontory, which frees the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone. Simple, non-invasive, and it resolves a large share of cases on its own.

steps.title: Suprapubic pressure — downward and lateral, from the fetal back
steps.html: Stand on a stool. Heel of the hand just above the symphysis, over the anterior shoulder, pressing downward and toward the fetal chest — that is, from the side the baby's back is on. The aim is to adduct the shoulder, narrowing the bisacromial diameter, and nudge it into the oblique. Steady pressure first; a rocking CPR-like motion if steady fails. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the majority of dystocias.

steps.title: Consider an episiotomy — for access, not for space
steps.html: The obstruction is bone against bone, and cutting the perineum does not relieve it. What it can do is give your hand room for the internal maneuvers that follow. Not routine; a judgment call when you cannot get a hand in.

steps.title: Internal rotation — get a hand in posteriorly
steps.html: Enter alongside the posterior shoulder, where the sacral hollow gives you room. Then either: Rubin II — fingers behind the anterior shoulder, pushing it toward the fetal chest to adduct and rotate it; or Woods screw — fingers on the front of the posterior shoulder, rotating the opposite way. Combining Rubin II with Woods on opposite shoulders, turning them like a screw, is more effective than either alone. The aim is to move the shoulders out of the anteroposterior plane into the oblique. If one direction fails, try the reverse.

steps.title: Deliver the posterior arm — the highest-yield internal maneuver
steps.html: Reach into the sacral hollow, follow the posterior humerus to the elbow, and press the antecubital fossa to flex the forearm. Grasp the forearm or hand — never the upper arm, which fractures — and sweep it across the chest and out over the face. Removing one arm reduces the shoulder diameter by around 20% and usually frees the impaction immediately. A humeral or clavicular fracture during this maneuver is an accepted cost; it heals, and hypoxic brain injury does not.

steps.title: Gaskin — roll her onto all fours
steps.html: Onto hands and knees. The change in pelvic geometry and the effect of gravity frees a proportion of dystocias on its own, and the shoulder that was posterior becomes the accessible one. Underused, because it looks disruptive mid-emergency. It is quick, it needs no equipment, and the internal maneuvers can all be repeated in this position. Impractical with an epidural or in an exhausted woman — but worth attempting when it is not.

steps.title: Then the last resorts — and say so out loud
steps.html: If the sequence has been worked through twice without success, you are in genuinely rare territory: deliberate clavicular fracture, the Zavanelli maneuver, abdominal rescue, or symphysiotomy (§06). All carry major morbidity, all are rarely performed, and the choice depends entirely on whether an operating room is reachable. Get the most senior help available and state clearly what you are about to do.

rows:
Deliberate clavicular fracture
(cleidotomy)
Direct pressure on the anterior clavicle, outward against the ramus, to fracture it and collapse the shoulder girdle
Rarely achievable deliberately in a live fetus. Heals well. Risk of underlying vascular and lung injury.
Zavanelli
Rotate the head back to occiput-anterior, flex it, and push it back into the vagina; hold it there; deliver by immediate cesarean. Tocolysis (e.g. terbutaline or nitroglycerin) helps.
The preferred last resort wherever an operating room is available. Significant maternal morbidity, and it depends on being able to get to theater immediately.
Abdominal rescue
Laparotomy and hysterotomy, with the impacted shoulder rotated transabdominally while an assistant delivers vaginally
Where a cesarean is available but the head cannot be replaced.
Symphysiotomy
Division of the symphyseal fibrocartilage to widen the pelvic outlet
Only where cesarean is genuinely unavailable within the survivable interval. See §06.

blocks.html: A resource-limited last resort with a difficult history and real, permanent maternal cost.

Where it belongs. Symphysiotomy retains a narrow place in settings where cesarean delivery is not available in the time the fetus has. Where an operating room is reachable, Zavanelli and abdominal rescue are the correct last resorts and symphysiotomy is not. The procedure was historically performed on women without consent and without adequate analgesia, and it left many with lifelong disability — that history is a reason to hold the indication narrowly and to obtain consent wherever it is possible, not a reason to pretend the procedure does not exist.

steps.title: Confirm there is no surgical option in time
steps.html: State it aloud and record it. All standard maneuvers must have failed, and cesarean must be genuinely unreachable — not merely inconvenient or slow to organize.

steps.title: Catheterize, and displace the urethra
steps.html: Place an indwelling catheter — it both empties the bladder and lets you feel where the urethra is. An assistant's fingers in the vagina push the urethra laterally, away from the midline, and stay there throughout the cut. Urethral and bladder injury is the characteristic complication and this is what prevents it.

steps.title: Two assistants on the legs — and a hard limit on abduction
steps.html: One assistant per leg, supporting the thigh. Total abduction must not exceed about 80–90°. Once the symphysis is divided the pelvis is a hinge, and over-abduction tears the sacroiliac joints and the urethra. This limit is the difference between a recoverable injury and a permanently disabled woman, and it is the instruction most easily lost in the urgency.

steps.title: Infiltrate local anesthetic
steps.html: Over and into the joint. Seconds well spent, and she is awake.

steps.title: Divide the fibrocartilage in the midline
steps.html: A stab incision over the symphysis, then divide the joint from front to back with the blade under the guiding finger. The aim is partial division and roughly 2–2.5 cm of separation — measured, not maximal. Complete division does not help further and worsens the injury.

steps.title: Deliver, then close and support the pelvis
steps.html: Deliver immediately with the maneuvers that previously failed — they will now usually succeed. Then close the skin, keep the catheter in for several days, apply a firm pelvic binder or strapping, and arrange bed rest with gradual mobilization. She needs analgesia, follow-up, and an honest explanation of what was done and why.

rows: Nothing working, and it feels like seconds have passed
Time distortion — universal under stress
This is what the called clock is for. Believe the scribe, not your sense of it.
Someone pushing on the fundus
Confusion between fundal and suprapubic pressure
Stop them. Name the landmark: “just above the pubic bone.” Watch the hand.
Traction is increasing as frustration rises
The instinctive and most harmful response
Take your hands off the head. Traction does not resolve a bony impaction; it only injures the plexus.
Cannot get a hand in
Insufficient room posteriorly
Enter in the sacral hollow, not anteriorly. Consider episiotomy for access. Empty the bladder.
Rotation will not move the shoulders
Wrong direction, or pressure on the wrong aspect
Try the reverse direction. Combine anterior and posterior hands as a screw rather than pushing one shoulder alone.
Cannot reach the posterior arm
The arm is extended alongside the body
Follow the humerus to the elbow and press the antecubital fossa to flex it. Never pull on the upper arm.
Something snapped during a maneuver
Clavicle or humerus
Keep going. It heals; hypoxia does not. Tell the neonatal team and document it.
Whole sequence failed once
Not yet a failure
Repeat the sequence, with a different operator if one is available. Fresh hands and a different position frequently succeed where the first attempt did not.
Brisk bleeding after delivery
Atony after prolonged dystocia, or a significant tear
Anticipate it. Uterotonics, quantify the loss, inspect the genital tract.
Baby flat at delivery
Expected after a prolonged head-to-body interval
Full neonatal resuscitation. Paired cord gases. Early assessment for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and for cooling eligibility.

blocks.html:
Fetal / neonatal:

  • Brachial plexus injury — most commonly Erb palsy (C5–C6). The majority resolve within a year; a minority are permanent. Related to traction, but also occurs with none.
  • Clavicular and humeral fracture — heal well, and acceptable in exchange for delivery.
  • Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and death — the reason for the clock.

Maternal:

  • Postpartum hemorrhage from atony — common after a prolonged dystocia.
  • Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears, vaginal and cervical lacerations.
  • Symphyseal separation, with pain and difficulty walking, even without symphysiotomy.
  • Uterine rupture — from fundal pressure.
  • After symphysiotomy specifically: urethral and bladder injury, vesicovaginal fistula, stress incontinence, sacroiliac disruption, chronic pelvic pain, infection, and long-term gait disturbance.
  • Psychological trauma — a frightening, chaotic delivery with many hands and shouted instructions. Debrief her afterwards, with the sequence explained.

• Paired cord gases, arterial and venous, from a doubly clamped segment.
  • Neonatal examination for plexus injury and fractures, and assessment for therapeutic hypothermia if the interval was long or the baby was depressed.
  • Document, in this order and with times: time of head delivery, which shoulder was anterior, each maneuver performed with its time and who performed it, the time of body delivery, who was present, cord gases, the neonatal condition and examination, and the maternal assessment. Which shoulder was anterior is the detail most often omitted and most often asked for later.
  • Examine the genital tract and quantify blood loss.
  • Explain it to the parents on the day, in plain language, and again later. They saw an emergency and understood almost none of it.
  • Debrief the team.
  • Drill it. Simulation training for shoulder dystocia has been shown to improve outcomes — one of the few obstetric interventions where that is demonstrable. The sequence must be automatic, because there is no time to reason it out.

Say the words and start the clock. “Shoulder dystocia” summons a response; anything vaguer does not.

McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure solves most of them. Do both properly before moving on.

Suprapubic, never fundal. Name the landmark aloud and watch the hand.

Take your hands off the head. Increasing traction is the instinct that causes the permanent injury.

The posterior arm is the highest-yield internal maneuver. Flex at the elbow, grasp the forearm, sweep across the chest — never pull the upper arm.

All fours is quick and underused. No equipment, and every internal maneuver still works there.

A fracture is an acceptable price. Bone heals; brain does not.

Failing once through the sequence is not failure. Repeat it, ideally with fresh hands.

Expect the hemorrhage afterwards.

Record which shoulder was anterior. It is always asked for and rarely written.

Symphysiotomy only where there is no operating room. And then: catheter in, urethra held aside, and abduction capped at 90°.

procedures.title: Active Internal Rewarming (ECMO/CPB Crossover)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Core rewarming for severe hypothermia with cardiac instability — where extracorporeal circulation becomes both the rewarming method and the resuscitation.
procedures.description: Core rewarming for hypothermic cardiac instability.

blocks.html:
• Hypothermic cardiac arrest — extracorporeal rewarming is the definitive management, and outcomes here are unlike any other arrest population
  • Severe hypothermia (below about 28 °C) with cardiac instability — ventricular arrhythmia, profound bradycardia, or hypotension unresponsive to volume
  • Hypothermia with a core temperature that will not rise despite adequate external and minimally invasive rewarming
  • Hypothermia complicated by a condition requiring circulatory support in its own right

blocks.title: Why this population is different
blocks.html: Cooling that occurs before hypoxia is profoundly neuroprotective: cerebral oxygen consumption falls roughly 6–8% per degree, and intact neurologic survival has been documented after hours of CPR and core temperatures below 15 °C. Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead.

sections.title: Staging, and Measuring the Temperature Properly

rows: HT I
Conscious, shivering
HT II
Impaired consciousness, shivering has stopped
HT III
Unconscious, vital signs present but may be barely detectable
HT IV
No detectable vital signs — apparent death
Below ~24 °C

blocks.html:
Take the pulse for a full minute, with ECG and ideally ultrasound. A profoundly hypothermic patient may have a rate of 10 with a barely palpable pulse, and being wrongly declared pulseless leads to chest compressions on a perfusing, irritable myocardium.

Measure the core temperature correctly, because everything depends on it.

  • Esophageal probe in the lower third of the esophagus — the standard in an intubated patient. Accurate and responsive.
  • Epitympanic probe with the ear canal insulated — acceptable in a non-intubated patient, and only if there is no snow or water in the canal and a pulse is present.
  • Rectal and bladder lag substantially, and lag most during active rewarming — exactly when you need accuracy.
  • Infrared tympanic thermometers are not adequate, and most standard clinical thermometers do not read low enough to be useful at all.

Rescue collapse: arrest during or shortly after extrication. The cold myocardium is exquisitely irritable and will fibrillate with mechanical stimulation, and standing a patient up removes the hydrostatic support their vasoconstricted, volume-depleted circulation depends on.

  • Keep them horizontal throughout extrication and transport.
  • Move them as little and as gently as possible. No rough handling, no sitting up, no unnecessary transfers.
  • Remove wet clothing by cutting, and insulate with a vapor barrier plus insulation.

Afterdrop: the core temperature continues to fall after rescue, as cold peripheral blood returns centrally and heat continues to equilibrate inward. Do not massage or actively warm the limbs; direct external warming at the trunk — axillae, chest, groin, neck. Keep the periphery still.

Below roughly 30 °C the myocardium responds poorly to both electricity and drugs, and drugs given are not metabolized — they accumulate and then act all at once as the patient warms.

  • Defibrillation: attempt up to three shocks. If unsuccessful, defer further attempts until the core is above 30 °C. Below that, repeated shocks achieve nothing.
  • Drugs: European and mountain-medicine guidance is to withhold epinephrine and other ACLS drugs until above 30 °C, then double the dosing interval between 30 and 35 °C, returning to standard intervals above 35 °C. American guidance is more permissive, allowing that drugs may be reasonable to consider. The reason for caution is accumulation, not futility — know which protocol your service follows.
  • Compressions continue. The chest is stiff; a mechanical device is a substantial advantage over a long transport.
  • Where continuous CPR is genuinely impossible — a technical rescue, a long carry off a mountain — guidelines permit intermittent CPR: below 28 °C, alternating 5 minutes of CPR with pauses of no more than 5 minutes; below 20 °C, pauses of up to 10 minutes. This is an explicit concession to terrain, not a general license to interrupt.
  • Intubate if indicated. Fear of triggering fibrillation should not prevent airway management; careful technique is enough.
  • They are profoundly volume depleted from cold diuresis. Give warmed crystalloid generously.

sections.title: Who Goes on a Circuit — and Where

blocks.html:
• Serum potassium is the single most useful triage marker. A markedly elevated potassium indicates cell lysis that preceded the cooling — that is, death before hypothermia. Thresholds vary: above 12 mmol/L is widely used as indicating non-survivability, with a lower threshold around 8 mmol/L applied after avalanche burial. Confirm the figure your regional protocol uses.
  • The HOPE score is the modern validated tool estimating survival probability with extracorporeal rewarming, and it has largely replaced potassium alone as the decision instrument where it is available.
  • Asphyxia before cooling — airway obstruction in an avalanche burial beyond about 60 minutes without an air pocket, or submersion in non-icy water — carries a poor prognosis regardless of temperature.
  • Obvious lethal injury, a chest that will not compress, or ice within the airway are the findings that justify not resuscitating. Rigidity and fixed dilated pupils are not — both are expected in deep hypothermia.
  • Take them to a center with extracorporeal capability, bypassing closer hospitals. This is a declared bypass decision in the same category as trauma or STEMI, and it needs to be made prehospital, by protocol, rather than discovered after arrival at a hospital that cannot help.
  • Call ahead early. The receiving team needs to assemble a cannulation team and prime a circuit before the patient arrives.

rows: Passive external — dry clothing removed, insulation, vapor barrier, warm room
0.5–2 °C/h if still shivering
HT I. Shivering is the patient's own heat engine — protect it.
Active external — forced-air warming, radiant heat, heat packs to the trunk
HT I–II. Trunk only; never the limbs.
Warmed IV fluid (38–42 °C)
Prevents further cooling more than it warms
All stages — essential, but do not expect it to rewarm anyone on its own.
Warmed humidified oxygen
Small
Adjunct. Harmless, modest.
Body cavity lavage — bladder, gastric, colonic
Slow, low surface area
Largely superseded; low yield for the effort.
Thoracic lavage — warmed saline via two chest tubes, in one and out the other
The best option when no circuit is available. Substantially more effective than other lavage routes, and deliverable in any hospital with chest tubes.
VA-ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass
Definitive for arrest or refractory instability. See §07.

blocks.html:
Cannulation follows the standard peripheral VA pathway — see the ECMO cannulation entry for technique, sizing, wire confirmation, and the distal perfusion catheter. What differs here is the intent and the pacing.

  • VA-ECMO is generally preferred over cardiopulmonary bypass: it needs less anticoagulation, and crucially it can continue supporting the circulation after rewarming is complete — which matters, because a rewarmed myocardium is often stunned and not immediately able to sustain an output.
  • Rewarm gradually. Keep the blood-to-core gradient modest — commonly no more than about 10 °C — and many centers now deliberately rewarm slowly, on the order of 1–2 °C per hour after arrest, to limit reperfusion injury rather than racing to normothermia.
  • Re-attempt defibrillation and standard drugs as thresholds are crossed — a rhythm that was refractory at 26 °C often converts readily at 30.
  • Expect enormous volume requirements as the periphery vasodilates. Hypotension on rewarming is anticipated, not a surprise.
  • Consider deliberate normothermia rather than overshoot — these patients have had a cardiac arrest, and the post-arrest fever-avoidance principles apply once they are warm.

rows: Arrest during or just after extrication
Rescue collapse
Prevent it: horizontal, gentle, minimal movement. Once it happens, CPR and move toward a circuit.
Temperature still falling after rescue
Afterdrop — expected
Trunk warming only, keep the limbs still, warmed fluids. Do not massage the extremities.
Shocks not working
Myocardium too cold to respond
Stop after three. Rewarm, then try again. Repeated shocks below 30 °C achieve nothing.
Nothing improving despite drugs
Drugs not being metabolized — accumulating
Withhold further doses until above 30 °C, then lengthen intervals. Expect a delayed effect from what has already been given.
Rigid, fixed dilated pupils, no reflexes
Expected at this temperature — not death
Continue. These findings have no prognostic value while cold.
Rectal temperature not rising on the circuit
Probe lag, not treatment failure
Use an esophageal probe. Rectal readings lag most exactly during active rewarming.
Profound hypotension as they warm
Rewarming shock — vasodilation onto a depleted circulation
Anticipate it. Warmed volume, slow the rewarming rate, pressors.
Hyperkalemia, arrhythmia, dark urine during rewarming
Reperfusion and rhabdomyolysis
Treat the potassium, fluids for myoglobin, monitor renal function.
Bleeding from everywhere
Hypothermic coagulopathy plus DIC
It corrects with temperature. Product support meanwhile.
Taken to the nearest hospital, no circuit available
Bypass decision not made
Preventable only by protocol. Transfer urgently and start thoracic lavage in the meantime.

blocks.html:
• Rescue collapse and ventricular fibrillation from handling a cold, irritable myocardium.
  • Afterdrop and continued cooling after rescue.
  • Rewarming shock — vasodilation outpacing a profoundly volume-depleted circulation.
  • Hyperkalemia and arrhythmia during reperfusion.
  • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
  • Coagulopathy and DIC — hypothermia impairs both platelet function and enzyme kinetics, and laboratory clotting studies run at 37 °C look deceptively normal.
  • Pulmonary edema and ARDS.
  • Pancreatitis — classically described after severe hypothermia and easily missed.
  • Frostbite of the extremities, needing its own management once the core is safe.
  • All the complications of extracorporeal support — bleeding, limb ischemia, and the rest.

Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead — unless they were asphyxiated first. That sequence is the prognosis.

Feel for a pulse for a full minute. A rate of 10 is easy to miss and compressions on a perfusing cold heart cause fibrillation.

Esophageal probe. Rectal and bladder lag most during rewarming, which is when you are relying on them.

Horizontal and gentle. Rescue collapse is a handling complication.

Warm the trunk, never the limbs.

Three shocks, then stop until 30 °C. And be cautious with drugs that will not be cleared.

Fixed pupils and rigidity mean nothing while cold.

Potassium is your triage test, and the HOPE score where you have it.

Bypass to a center with a circuit, and call them before you leave the scene.

No circuit? Two chest tubes. Thoracic lavage is far better than the alternatives and available almost anywhere.

procedures.title: Escharotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Releasing the constricting, unyielding burn eschar before it compromises circulation or ventilation.
procedures.description: Releasing constricting burn eschar from limb or chest.

blocks.html: Full-thickness eschar is inelastic. Resuscitation edema underneath it turns the burn into a tourniquet.

• Circumferential or near-circumferential full-thickness limb burn with developing vascular compromise — rising compartment pressure beneath a skin envelope that cannot expand
  • Circumferential chest or torso burn restricting ventilation — falling chest wall compliance, rising peak airway pressures, falling tidal volumes on pressure-controlled ventilation, worsening hypercapnia
  • Circumferential neck burn with airway compromise or venous congestion of the face
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome from circumferential abdominal eschar, usually on a background of large-volume resuscitation

Timing is the thing most often misunderstood. The need for escharotomy usually develops 6 to 24 hours after the burn, as resuscitation fluid accumulates in the tissue under a rigid eschar. A limb that is warm and well perfused on arrival can be threatened by morning. This is a serially reassessed decision, not a one-time assessment at presentation — and the corollary is that a patient with circumferential burns needs an hourly perfusion check written down, not a single note on admission.

blocks.title: Absent pulses are a late sign — do not wait for them
blocks.html: By the time a radial pulse disappears, muscle has been ischemic for some time. The earlier and more useful signals are loss of the Doppler signal in the palmar arch or digital vessels (not just the named artery), a falling or lost pulse oximetry waveform on the affected digit, progressive pain, paresthesia, and tense, woody swelling distal to the burn. Compartment pressures above about 30 mmHg support the decision where the picture is unclear. Assess with a Doppler and a pulse oximeter, hourly, and act on the trend.

sections.title: Contraindications — and What This Is Not

blocks.html:
• None absolute where there is genuine vascular or ventilatory compromise from constricting eschar.
  • Partial-thickness burns without circumferential involvement. Superficial and superficial-partial burns retain elasticity and do not constrict. Cutting them creates a painful, bleeding, full-thickness wound in a patient who did not have one.
  • Distal ischemia with another explanation — arterial injury, a tight dressing, positioning, hypotension, or hypothermic vasoconstriction. Take the dressings off and look before you reach for a blade.

Escharotomy is not fasciotomy. Escharotomy divides constricting skin and stops at the subcutaneous fat. Fasciotomy opens muscle compartments. They address different pressures at different depths, and the mistake goes in both directions:

  • Cutting too deep in a simple thermal burn turns a clean release into a bleeding fasciotomy the patient did not need.
  • Stopping at escharotomy when the muscle itself is the problem leaves the limb ischemic. High-voltage electrical injury, crush, and deep thermal burns involving muscle need fasciotomy, and escharotomy alone will not save them.

If perfusion does not improve after an adequate escharotomy, measure compartment pressures. That is the branch point.

• Electrocautery, if available — strongly preferred over a scalpel. These incisions bleed from viable dermis and fat at the base, and the patient is frequently coagulopathic. Cautery cuts and controls in one pass.
  • Scalpel (a No. 10 or 20 blade) as the alternative, plus hemostats and ties.
  • Doppler probe — for assessing before, and for proving the release worked afterward. Have it before you start, not after.
  • Pulse oximeter to put on a distal digit.
  • Skin marker — mark the lines before cutting. See §04; the landmarks that matter are the ones you cannot see through eschar.
  • Analgesia and sedation. The eschar is insensate; the patient is not. See the warning in §05.
  • Hemostatic dressings, bulky dressings, and a way to elevate the limb.
  • A phone. Burn centers expect and welcome a call before an escharotomy, and most will talk you through the lines in real time. This is one of the few genuinely emergent burn procedures and also one where remote guidance is easy and routine.

sections.title: Where the Lines Go — and the Two Nerves

blocks.html: Mid-medial and mid-lateral, full length. Two places deviate, and both are permanent if you get them wrong.

blocks.alt: Escharotomy incision map, anterior view. Limb incisions run mid-medial and mid-lateral along both sides of each arm and leg, the full length of the burn and across every joint, ending one to two centimeters into unburned skin. The chest release is a rectangular shield: bilateral anterior axillary lines joined by transverse incisions along the clavicles and along the costal margin. Two nerves change the line. At the elbow the medial incision passes anterior to the medial epicondyle, because the ulnar nerve lies subcutaneously behind it. At the knee the lateral incision passes clear of the fibular neck, where the common peroneal nerve wraps around it and division causes a permanent foot drop. Hand incisions run dorsally between the metacarpals and digital incisions are mid-axial, off the pinch surface.
blocks.caption: Length is what fails, not placement: an incision that stops short of the joint or ends inside burned skin leaves the constriction where it is tightest. The two amber points are the only places the line deviates, and both are marked on the skin before cutting, because eschar hides the landmarks you would normally navigate by.

rows: Arm and forearm
Mid-medial and mid-lateral, from proximal to distal end of the burn
Ulnar nerve at the elbow. The medial line must pass anterior to the medial epicondyle — the nerve sits in the cubital tunnel just behind it, immediately subcutaneous.
Hand
Dorsal longitudinal incisions over the intermetacarpal spaces (typically 2nd and 4th)
Extensor tendons. Stay in the valleys between metacarpals, not over the tendons.
Digits
Mid-axial, on the side that is not the working pinch surface (ulnar side of the thumb, radial side of the little finger)
Digital neurovascular bundles. Value is debated — discuss with a burn center before cutting fingers.
Thigh and leg
Mid-medial and mid-lateral, full length of the burn

Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck. It wraps the neck just distal to the fibular head and is subcutaneous there. Route the lateral incision clear of it — conventionally passing posterior to the fibular head. Dividing it is a permanent foot drop.
Foot
Dorsal medial and lateral
Dorsalis pedis and the extensor tendons.
Chest and torso

Bilateral anterior axillary lines from clavicle to costal margin, joined by transverse incisions along the clavicles and along the costal margin — producing a rectangular “shield” of released chest wall
Nipple–areolar complex; in children, the breast bud. Stay lateral.
Abdomen
Extend the torso pattern inferiorly; a midline or transverse release as needed
Consider true abdominal compartment syndrome — escharotomy may not be enough.
Neck
Lateral incisions, kept posterior
Carotid, jugular, and the external jugular in particular. Rare and high-stakes — get help.

blocks.html:
Cross the joints. An incision that stops at the wrist or the ankle because the anatomy looks intimidating leaves the constriction exactly where it is tightest. The incision runs the entire length of the circumferential burn, through normal-appearing skin at each end by 1–2 cm. Incomplete length is the single commonest reason an escharotomy fails to restore perfusion.

Mark before you cut. Eschar obliterates the surface landmarks you would normally navigate by. Palpate the medial epicondyle and the fibular head through the burn, mark them, and draw the line around them.

steps.title: Document the deficit first
steps.html: Record Doppler signals at the palmar arch or digital vessels, the pulse oximetry waveform, capillary refill, and sensation — before you cut. Without a baseline you cannot tell afterwards whether the release worked, and “it looks better” is not a finding you can hand over.

steps.title: Give real analgesia and sedation
steps.html: Opioid plus ketamine, or formal procedural sedation. See the warning below — the widely repeated line that escharotomy needs no anesthesia is half-true and causes real suffering.

steps.title: Position and mark
steps.html: Limb in anatomic position, slightly extended. Palpate and mark the medial epicondyle or fibular head, then draw the full line including where it curves around them and where it extends into unburned skin at each end.

steps.title: Cut through the eschar into fat — and stop
steps.html: Full thickness of the burned skin, down to and just into the subcutaneous fat. Do not cut the fascia. The endpoint is visible and unmistakable: the wound edges spring apart by a centimeter or more and the fat bulges out of the incision. If the edges sit together, you are not through.

steps.title: Expect bleeding — and use it
steps.html: The base of a correct incision is viable tissue and will bleed. That bleeding is a useful confirmation of depth, not a sign you have gone too far. Control it as you go with cautery. A completely bloodless incision means either that you are still within dead tissue, or that the tissue beneath is dead too — both change what happens next.

steps.title: Reassess immediately, with the Doppler
steps.html: Signals should return or improve within minutes. Compliance should improve at once on a chest release, with a visible fall in peak airway pressure. If nothing changes, the commonest reason is that the incision is not long enough — extend it before you conclude the diagnosis was wrong.

steps.title: Second line if needed, then reassess again
steps.html: A single mid-medial incision is often sufficient. If perfusion is still inadequate, add the mid-lateral line. Only after both lines are complete and full-length should you move on to considering compartment pressures and fasciotomy.

steps.title: Dress, elevate, and set a reassessment interval
steps.html: Hemostatic or bulky absorbent dressing, limb elevated above heart level. Then hourly Doppler and perfusion checks, documented — edema continues to accumulate for another day and a released limb can constrict again.

blocks.title: “The eschar is insensate” is only half the story
blocks.html: Full-thickness burn is anesthetic, so the middle of the incision may be painless. But the incision must extend into viable skin at both ends, it passes through sensate deep dermis wherever the burn is not truly full thickness, and the patient beneath it is awake, frightened, and in pain from the burn already. Give analgesia and sedation as a default. The bedside myth that escharotomy needs none has produced a great deal of avoidable suffering.

rows: Incision made, no improvement in Doppler
Incision not long enough — by far the most common cause
Extend it proximally and distally into unburned skin, and across the joints. Check this before anything else.
Wound edges do not separate
Not through the full thickness of eschar
Deepen until the fat bulges. The edges springing apart is the endpoint; nothing else is.
Both lines complete, limb still ischemic
True muscle compartment syndrome, or arterial injury
Measure compartment pressures. Fasciotomy, and consider vascular imaging. Think about electrical injury and crush.
No bleeding at all from the incision
Deeper tissue is also non-viable — or you are not deep enough
Reassess depth. If the muscle beneath is dead, this is a different and much larger conversation, and it is a burn-center one.
Brisk, hard-to-control bleeding
Coagulopathy, or the incision has run into viable vascularized tissue
Cautery, packing, correct the coagulopathy. Large-surface burns become coagulopathic and hypothermic quickly.
Chest released, peak pressures unchanged
The problem is not the chest wall
Reconsider: pneumothorax, inhalation injury, bronchospasm, mucus plugging, ARDS, or abdominal compartment syndrome pushing the diaphragm up. Measure a bladder pressure.
Foot drop after a leg escharotomy
Common peroneal nerve divided at the fibular neck
Preventable only by marking the landmark beforehand. Document and involve plastics/burns.
Limb re-tightens overnight
Ongoing resuscitation edema — entirely expected
This is why the hourly check exists. Extend the incisions or add lines. It is not a failure of the first procedure.
Needing escharotomy after escharotomy, everywhere
Over-resuscitation — “fluid creep”
Recheck the fluid plan (see §08). Escalating escharotomy requirements are a signal about the resuscitation, not only about the burn.

blocks.html:
• Hemorrhage — from viable dermis and fat, and worse in the coagulopathic large-burn patient. The reason cautery is preferred.
  • Nerve injury — ulnar at the medial epicondyle, common peroneal at the fibular neck, digital nerves in the fingers. All permanent, all avoidable by marking.
  • Incomplete release with continuing ischemia — the commonest and most consequential technical failure.
  • Cutting too deep, converting an escharotomy into an unintended fasciotomy with its attendant morbidity.
  • Escharotomy performed on a partial-thickness burn — a full-thickness wound created where none existed, which now needs grafting.
  • Infection — the incision opens a deep plane in a burn wound that will colonize.
  • Conversion of burn depth from desiccation of the exposed wound bed.
  • Scarring and contracture, particularly across joints, later requiring reconstruction.
  • Missed abdominal compartment syndrome, treated as a chest wall problem.

sections.title: Afterwards — and the Resuscitation Behind It

blocks.html:
• Hourly documented perfusion checks — Doppler signal, oximetry waveform, capillary refill, sensation, and compartment softness. Edema peaks well after the procedure.
  • Elevate the limb above heart level and keep it there.
  • Transfer to a burn center. Escharotomy is a temporizing procedure; the patient needs burn surgical care. Call early — before the procedure if time allows.
  • Revisit the fluid plan. Resuscitation edema is what created the constriction. Standard resuscitation is roughly 2–4 mL/kg per %TBSA of crystalloid over the first 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, titrated to urine output — about 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults and 1 mL/kg/h in children. Formulas are a starting point, not a prescription. Over-resuscitation drives escharotomy, abdominal compartment syndrome, and conversion of burn depth, and it is a far more common error than under-resuscitation in modern practice.
  • Watch for rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia, especially after electrical injury or a prolonged ischemic interval.
  • Tetanus and burn-center-directed wound care. Prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not routine.
  • Document the incisions — where, how long, what improved, and the Doppler findings before and after. The next team needs to know whether this has already been done adequately.

Not long enough is the usual failure. Full length of the burn, across the joints, into normal skin at both ends.

The endpoint is the edges springing apart and fat bulging. If they sit together, you are not through the eschar.

Absent pulses are late. Use a Doppler on the palmar arch and a pulse oximeter on a digit, hourly, and act on the trend.

Mark the medial epicondyle and the fibular head first. Two nerves, two permanent deficits, both avoidable with a pen.

Bleeding is confirmation. A bloodless incision is telling you something, and it is not good news.

Escharotomy is not fasciotomy. Skin, into fat, stop. If perfusion does not return after adequate release, measure pressures — and think about electrical and crush injury.

Give analgesia. The eschar is insensate; the ends of the incision and the patient are not.

This need develops overnight. Circumferential burns get an hourly documented check, not a single admission assessment.

Call the burn center before you cut if there is any time at all. They do this often and will walk you through the lines.

Repeated escharotomies are a message about the fluids.

Orgill DP, Piccolo N. Escharotomy and decompressive therapies in burns. J Burn Care Res. 2009;30(5):759–768.
ISBI Practice Guidelines Committee. ISBI practice guidelines for burn care. Burns. 2016;42(5):953–1021.
Pruitt BA. Protection from excessive resuscitation: “pushing the pendulum back.” J Trauma. 2000;49(3):567–568.
Saffle JI. The phenomenon of “fluid creep” in acute burn resuscitation. J Burn Care Res. 2007;28(3):382–395.
Your regional burn center's referral line. Early telephone consultation is expected practice and is available before as well as after the procedure.
