procedures.title: Field Amputation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Mass Casualty
procedures.subtitle: An exceedingly rare, last-resort extrication technique — entrapment with an unsalvageable limb and a threat to life that transport delay would worsen.
procedures.description: Rare last-resort extrication technique.

blocks.html: This is an extrication procedure, not a surgical one. The goal is a released patient, not a good stump.

• Entrapment that cannot be relieved by any other means, where remaining trapped will kill the patient — progressing structural collapse, fire, rising water, an unstable scene, or physiological deterioration that will not survive the extrication timeline
  • Completion of a near-total traumatic amputation — a limb held by a bridge of skin, tendon, or a strip of muscle, where dividing that bridge frees the patient. This is by far the most common version of this procedure, and it is a fundamentally different and easier act than cutting through an intact limb.
  • An unsalvageable limb whose continued attachment is itself the threat — extensive crush with a non-viable segment, in a patient deteriorating from that segment
  • Immediate scene danger requiring evacuation now, where the entrapment is the only thing preventing it

What makes this indicated is almost never the limb. It is the clock, the scene, or the patient's physiology. A mangled limb in a stable patient at a safe scene, however dreadful it looks, is an operating-room problem.

• Any remaining technical rescue option. Cutting the environment beats cutting the patient, every time, even when it is slower. Hydraulic spreaders, cutting torches, airbags, cribbing, and concrete saws release far more patients than scalpels do. Exhaust this first and say out loud that you have.
  • A salvageable limb in a patient who can wait. If the delay is survivable, the limb goes to the operating room attached.
  • A scene too unsafe for the operator. A second casualty helps nobody. This is the incident commander's call, not the clinician's.
  • No means of hemorrhage control. Do not cut without a functioning tourniquet already applied and tightened. This is not a sequencing preference — it is the difference between an extrication and an exsanguination.
  • Death already declared. Amputation to recover a body is a medical examiner and rescue decision, made outside this framework.

sections.title: The Decision, and Who Makes It

blocks.html:
Field amputation is among the rarest procedures in this library, and most clinicians will never perform one. The single most useful preparation is knowing your system's activation pathway before the day it is needed — who carries the kit, who is credentialed, and what number summons them.

  • It is physician- or surgeon-led in almost every system — a HEMS physician, an urban search-and-rescue medical team member, or a surgeon dispatched to the scene. It is not a standard prehospital scope of practice.
  • It is a joint decision with technical rescue and the incident commander. The clinician owns the patient; the rescue team owns whether any other route out exists, and whether the scene will still be standing in twenty minutes.
  • Two clinicians if at all possible. One to perform, one to manage the airway, sedation, and resuscitation. Doing both alone is possible and is much worse.
  • Consent is usually impossible. Act under emergency doctrine. If the patient is awake and able, tell them what is happening and why — they are frequently conscious throughout, and that fact deserves acknowledging rather than avoiding.
  • Brief the team before you start — including the rescue crew who will see it. Say what is about to happen, who does what, and what the signal to stop is. Then debrief afterwards. This is one of the small number of procedures where the psychological burden on the team is a foreseeable, plannable consequence rather than an afterthought.

• Two tourniquets minimum, windlass-type, applied proximally and tightened before the incision. Two, because one can fail and there is no re-doing this.
  • Gigli saw with handles — a flexible wire saw. The workhorse of field amputation: it needs no power, works in confined and awkward spaces where a rigid blade cannot be swung, packs into nothing, and cuts bone quickly. If your kit holds one instrument for bone, this is it.
  • Amputation knife or a large scalpel (No. 22 blade), plus heavy trauma shears — which alone are often enough to complete a near-total amputation.
  • Bone cutters for small bones and for trimming spicules.
  • Arterial clamps and ties — large vessels should be secured rather than left to a tourniquet alone where the anatomy allows.
  • Hemostatic gauze and bulky dressings for the stump.
  • Ketamine (and a benzodiazepine), airway equipment, and a monitor. See §05.
  • IV/IO access, warmed crystalloid, and blood products if the system carries them. Also calcium and the means to treat hyperkalemia — see §06.
  • Headlamp, and eye protection for everyone within range.
  • A marker and a watch. Tourniquet time starts the moment it is tightened.

A trapped, hypothermic, hypovolemic patient in a confined space is among the worst environments imaginable for sedating someone. The plan has to fit that.

  • Ketamine is the agent of choice — it preserves airway reflexes and respiratory drive, and it supports blood pressure rather than dropping it. Typical dissociative dosing is around 1–2 mg/kg IV or 4–5 mg/kg IM where no line exists, reduced substantially in shock, with repeat increments titrated to effect. Confirm against your own service's formulary.
  • Add a benzodiazepine for amnesia and to blunt emergence, if the hemodynamics tolerate it.
  • Opioid as an adjunct, with the usual caution about stacking respiratory depression on a patient you cannot reposition.
  • Have an airway plan you can actually execute in that space. If the patient is head-down under a vehicle, ask honestly whether you could intubate them where they lie. If the answer is no, that constrains the sedation depth you can safely aim for.
  • Local anesthetic infiltration at the incision line is a reasonable adjunct and costs nothing.
  • They may remain aware. Talk to them. Have someone whose only job is to be at their head.

sections.title: Crush Physiology — Treat Before You Release

blocks.title: The danger is the moment of release, not the cut
blocks.html: A limb crushed for hours is an ischemic reservoir of potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, and acid. The instant circulation is restored or the compressing force is removed, that load reaches the heart — the phenomenon historically called “rescue death” or “smiling death,” in which a conscious, talking, apparently stable trapped patient arrests within minutes of being freed. The resuscitation for this happens before extrication, not after.

• Fluids before release. Start warmed crystalloid early and run it generously before the limb is freed — often 1–1.5 L/h in an adult, begun while still entrapped and continued through extrication. Confirm rates against your own crush-injury protocol.
  • Have calcium drawn up for hyperkalemic cardiac membrane stabilization, and have your hyperkalemia treatments ready rather than in a bag somewhere.
  • Monitor the ECG through the release. Peaked T waves and a widening QRS are the warning.
  • Consider sodium bicarbonate for the acid load and to alkalinize urine against myoglobin, per your protocol.
  • One genuine advantage of amputation over simple release: the limb comes off above a tightened tourniquet, so the ischemic contents of the crushed segment leave with it rather than washing into the circulation. Tourniquet-first is not only hemorrhage control — it is metabolic containment.
  • Watch for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury downstream: pigmented urine, rising CK, and the potassium trend.

steps.title: Confirm no other route out, out loud
steps.html: Ask the rescue lead directly: “Is there any way to get this patient out without amputating?” Get an explicit answer and note the time. This is the decision that will be examined afterwards, and the people who can answer it are standing next to you.

steps.title: Resuscitate and sedate before you cut
steps.html: Access, fluids running, calcium available, monitor on, ketamine given and working. Airway person at the head. Do not begin because the scene is loud and urgent — begin because the patient is as ready as they will be.

steps.title: Two tourniquets, as proximal as the space allows, tight
steps.html: Apply and tighten both — not staged, not loosely pre-positioned. Tighten to loss of distal arterial signal. Write the time on the patient's skin. Every downstream decision depends on that number and it is routinely lost at handover.

steps.title: Cut at the most distal point that achieves release
steps.html: Preserve every centimeter of length you can. This is not a definitive amputation and no flaps are being planned — length preserved now is prosthetic function and reconstructive options later. Choose the level by what frees the patient, not by textbook amputation levels. Through a joint is often faster and easier than through a shaft, and disarticulation is entirely acceptable here.

steps.title: Guillotine: skin, then muscle, then bone
steps.html: A single circumferential incision through skin and soft tissue at one level — no flaps, no shaping. Clamp or tie large vessels as you meet them if you can see them; the tourniquet covers what you cannot. Retract the soft tissue proximally and pass the Gigli saw around the bone, cutting with long, steady, full-length strokes rather than short fast ones. Divide any remaining attachments and the limb is free.

steps.title: If it is a near-total amputation, this is much simpler
steps.html: Most field amputations are the completion of an injury that has already happened. Tourniquet first as always, then divide the remaining skin, tendon, or muscle bridge with heavy shears or a scalpel. No saw, no bone work. Recognizing that you are in this situation rather than the other one is worth the ten seconds it takes to look.

steps.title: Extricate immediately and reassess the tourniquets
steps.html: Move the patient out. Then look at the stump again — tourniquets loosen during extrication, and bleeding that was controlled in situ can restart the moment the patient is moved. Add a third tourniquet or pack the stump if needed.

steps.title: Dress, warm, and resuscitate properly
steps.html: Hemostatic gauze and a bulky dressing over the stump. Aggressive rewarming — these patients are cold from prolonged exposure and the coagulopathy that follows is avoidable. Blood products, TXA within the window, calcium, and analgesia.

steps.title: Bring the amputated part with the patient
steps.html: Wrapped in saline-moistened gauze, in a sealed bag, on ice — never in direct contact with ice and never frozen. Replantation is unlikely after a crush entrapment, but the decision belongs to the surgeon, and the part may also matter for identification and for tissue coverage.

rows: Cannot reach a proximal site for the tourniquet
The entrapment itself is above your working space
Do not cut. Junctional device, or direct compression held by a person, or reconsider whether extrication of the structure is truly exhausted.
Bleeding heavily despite a tourniquet
Not tight enough, or a second bone is splinting the vessels open
Tighten to loss of signal. Add the second tourniquet immediately above the first. Forearm and lower leg frequently need two.
Saw binds and will not advance
Soft tissue caught in the wire, or the blade angle has changed
Retract soft tissue proximally and protect it. Long full strokes, steady rate. A binding Gigli saw will snap.
Gigli saw breaks
Short jerky strokes, or a kinked wire
Carry a spare — this is a foreseeable failure. Bone cutters as the fallback.
Patient arrests at the moment of release
Hyperkalemia from reperfusion
Calcium immediately, then the rest of the hyperkalemia protocol. This is why the drugs are drawn up beforehand.
Patient wakes and fights mid-procedure
Ketamine under-dosed, or redistributed
Re-dose. Have the next increment already drawn. An interrupted amputation is worse than a slower one.
Scene deteriorating during the procedure
Structural, fire, or water progression
The incident commander's call, and it overrides yours. Agree the abort signal before starting.
Limb free but patient still trapped
Something else is holding them, or the level was wrong
Reassess with the rescue team before cutting anything further. Confirm the amputation will actually achieve release before you make it.
Stump bleeding restarts in transit
Tourniquet loosened during movement
Reassess after every move. Retighten, add another, pack the stump.

blocks.html:
• Exsanguination — the immediate risk, and almost entirely a function of whether the tourniquet was on and tight before the incision.
  • Hyperkalemic arrest on reperfusion and crush syndrome — the most under-anticipated hazard of the whole procedure.
  • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
  • Hypothermia and trauma-induced coagulopathy — prolonged entrapment, exposure, and cold fluids all compound.
  • Infection — the field is filthy by definition. Broad antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis; the stump needs formal surgical revision and washout.
  • Insufficient residual limb length, restricting prosthetic options. The reason to cut as distally as release allows.
  • Nerve and vessel retraction making later revision harder.
  • Awareness and recall in an under-sedated patient, with lasting psychological consequences.
  • Psychological injury to the team and to the rescue crew. Foreseeable, and therefore something to plan for rather than absorb.

• Pre-alert the receiving trauma center with the specifics: the level, tourniquet times, the drugs given, the entrapment duration, and the potassium risk. They should have an operating room and blood ready.
  • Tourniquet times, written and spoken. The single number most often lost and most consequential.
  • Entrapment duration matters as much as tourniquet time for predicting the metabolic picture.
  • Serial potassium, CK, creatinine, lactate, and gas — and urine color.
  • The stump goes to the operating room for formal revision, washout, and a decision about closure. A field amputation is never definitive.
  • Debrief the whole team, including the rescue crew, and follow up afterwards rather than only on the day. Make the offer specific and repeat it.
  • Document the decision-making carefully: who was present, what extrication options were exhausted, who concurred, and the time each decision was made. This will be reviewed, and it should be.

Cut the environment, not the patient — until you genuinely cannot. Then say out loud that you cannot, and note who agreed.

Most field amputations are completions. A bridge of skin and tendon divided with heavy shears. Look before you assume you need a saw.

Tourniquets on and tight before the blade. Two of them, and write the time on the skin.

The danger is the release, not the cut. Fluids running and calcium drawn before the limb comes free.

Amputating above a tourniquet contains the crush load — the ischemic metabolites leave with the limb instead of reaching the heart.

Keep every centimeter of length. No flaps, no shaping, most distal level that frees them. Disarticulation is fine.

The Gigli saw is the right tool — no power, confined spaces, packs into nothing. Carry a spare wire.

Ketamine, and someone whose only job is the patient's head.

Take the limb with you, cool but never frozen.

Know your system's pathway before the day. The best preparation for a procedure you will probably never do is knowing exactly who to call.

Brief before, debrief after. Including the rescue crew.

procedures.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Coordination & Prep
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Environmental
procedures.subtitle: Decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism — 100% oxygen first, chamber logistics in parallel, altitude avoided at every step of transport.
procedures.description: DCS/AGE — 100% oxygen first, altitude avoided.

blocks.html:
• Decompression sickness, Type I (musculoskeletal, cutaneous, lymphatic) or Type II (neurologic, inner ear, cardiopulmonary)
  • Arterial gas embolism — from diving barotrauma, or iatrogenic: central line insertion or removal, cardiac and neurosurgery, hemodialysis, lung biopsy, contrast injection
  • Any diver with new symptoms after a dive, however vague — fatigue, a rash, an odd ache. Dive profiles that look safe do not exclude it.
  • Severe carbon monoxide poisoning — managed by the same chambers and teams, though the evidence is more contested than for DCS
  • Related chamber indications: clostridial myonecrosis, necrotizing soft tissue infection, crush injury with compartment syndrome, compromised flaps and grafts

Why pressure treats this — three separate mechanisms:

  • Boyle's law: bubble volume falls as pressure rises. At 2.8 ATA a bubble is roughly a third of its surface volume, which mechanically relieves vascular obstruction and tissue distortion.
  • Inert gas washout: breathing 100% oxygen removes nitrogen from the breathing mixture, creating a steep diffusion gradient that drives nitrogen out of the bubble and out of the tissue.
  • Dissolved oxygen delivery: by Henry's law, plasma-dissolved oxygen rises enough at treatment pressures to meet resting tissue metabolic demand without hemoglobin at all, oxygenating tissue downstream of an obstruction.

The first two of these begin the moment you put on a non-rebreather. That is why oxygen is not a holding measure — it is the same treatment at lower intensity.

sections.title: Recognizing It — and the Ten-Minute Rule

rows: Arterial gas embolism
Sudden stroke-like deficit, loss of consciousness, seizure, or arrest — typically within 10 minutes of surfacing, often immediately on surfacing
Symptoms within 10 minutes of surfacing are AGE until proven otherwise. Classically follows breath-holding during ascent. Can occur after a very shallow dive.
DCS Type II — spinal
Low back or girdle pain, band-like paresthesia, ascending weakness, urinary retention
The commonest serious neurologic DCS. Urinary retention is easy to miss and should be asked about directly.
DCS Type II — cerebral
Confusion, visual disturbance, ataxia, personality change
Often attributed to fatigue or alcohol.
DCS Type II — inner ear
Vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss
Distinguish from inner ear barotrauma — the treatments differ, and this needs specialist input.
DCS Type II — “chokes”
Chest pain, dyspnea, cough — massive venous gas load
Uncommon and serious.
DCS Type I — bends
Deep aching joint pain, typically shoulder or elbow, unrelieved by movement
Full neurologic examination anyway — Type I and Type II coexist often.
Cutis marmorata
Marbled, mottled violaceous rash, usually trunk
Not a trivial skin finding. It is now regarded as a marker of substantial bubble load and serious DCS.

blocks.html: The dive history to take, and to hand over verbatim: maximum depth and bottom time; number of dives and surface intervals; ascent rate and any missed decompression stops; gas mixture; any rapid or uncontrolled ascent or breath-hold; the exact time of surfacing and the exact time of symptom onset; and any flying or altitude exposure afterwards. The onset interval is what separates AGE from DCS, and it is the detail most often lost.

• Untreated pneumothorax — absolute. Gas trapped in the pleural space expands on decompression at the end of treatment and will tension. A chest tube goes in before the chamber door closes, and the drainage arrangement must be one the chamber team can manage under pressure. This is the hard gate on the whole pathway.
  • Relative — and rarely enough to withhold treatment for a serious injury: bleomycin and certain other chemotherapy agents (pulmonary toxicity), disulfiram, uncontrolled seizure disorder, severe COPD with bullae and CO2 retention, untreated middle ear or sinus pathology preventing equalization, and claustrophobia — which a multiplace chamber with an attendant usually accommodates.
  • Pregnancy is a relative consideration for elective indications; for DCS and AGE it is not a barrier.
  • None of these delays 100% oxygen, fluids, or the phone call.

• A tight-fitting non-rebreather with a reservoir, or a demand valve. The distinction matters — a loosely applied mask delivers perhaps 60–70% oxygen, and the treatment depends on the inspired fraction being as close to 100% as you can manage. Check the seal and the reservoir.
  • IV access and isotonic crystalloid. Divers are dehydrated by immersion diuresis and DCS causes capillary leak. Avoid glucose-containing fluid in suspected neurologic injury.
  • Continuous oximetry and cardiac monitoring.
  • A urinary catheter if there is any spinal involvement — retention is common and the bladder gets forgotten in a chamber.
  • Chest imaging or ultrasound to exclude pneumothorax before transfer.
  • The numbers, saved in advance: your nearest operational chamber, and the Divers Alert Network emergency line, +1 919-684-9111, which provides 24-hour diving medical consultation and knows which chambers are actually open.
  • A transport plan that does not gain altitude — see §06.

Not every chamber can take every patient. A monoplace chamber holds one patient and limits what can be done to them inside; a multiplace chamber is pressurized with an attendant inside and can manage a ventilated, unstable, or critically ill patient. An intubated patient needs a multiplace chamber, and many chambers are elective-hours only. Confirm capability on the phone before committing to a destination.

steps.title: 100% oxygen now — before anything is arranged
steps.html: The single highest-yield intervention available to you, free, immediate, and already in the room. It shrinks bubbles and washes out nitrogen by the same mechanisms the chamber uses. Start it while someone else makes the phone calls, and do not stop it because symptoms improve — improvement on oxygen confirms the diagnosis, it does not treat it.

steps.title: Lie them flat — supine, not head-down
steps.html: Trendelenburg is no longer recommended. The old rationale was to keep bubbles out of the cerebral circulation; the position worsens cerebral edema and raises intracranial pressure, and the bubbles have already arrived. Supine and flat. The left lateral decubitus position belongs to venous air embolism trapping gas in the right ventricle — a different entity from arterial gas embolism.

steps.title: Fluids
steps.html: Isotonic crystalloid, generously — orally if fully alert, intravenously otherwise. Hemoconcentration worsens bubble-related tissue injury, and these patients are dry before they are ever injured.

steps.title: Document a full neurologic examination, with the time
steps.html: Cranial nerves, power, sensation, coordination, gait if safe, and bladder function. Serial examinations are how response to treatment is judged, and without a recorded baseline the chamber team cannot tell whether the patient is improving. This is worth the five minutes.

steps.title: Exclude a pneumothorax — the hard gate
steps.html: Imaging or ultrasound. If present, it is drained before the chamber. Do not send an undrained pneumothorax to be pressurized.

steps.title: Call the chamber and DAN, in parallel with everything above
steps.html: Describe the presentation, the dive profile, the onset timing, and what you have given. Confirm the chamber is staffed, open, and able to take this specific patient — ventilated, or unstable, or not. This call also gets you expert advice on a condition most clinicians see rarely.

steps.title: Transport without gaining altitude
steps.html: Ground transport by preference. If air transport is unavoidable, the cabin must be pressurized to sea level, or the aircraft kept below about 1000 feet. Altitude reduces ambient pressure, and by Boyle's law every bubble in the patient expands. This is the error that turns a treatable injury into a catastrophic one.

steps.title: Hand over the profile, the times, and the examination
steps.html: The hyperbaric team chooses the treatment table — commonly a US Navy Table 6 at 2.8 ATA for serious DCS and AGE, with shorter tables for resolved pain-only presentations, and repeat sessions daily until improvement plateaus. That decision is theirs; the history and the serial examination are yours.

blocks.title: Late presentation is not a reason to withhold treatment
blocks.html: Recompression benefits patients who present hours or even days after the event, particularly with neurologic symptoms. A diver who flew home, or spent a day hoping the numbness would settle, is still a candidate. “It has been too long” is a misconception — make the call anyway and let the hyperbaric physician decide.

rows: Oxygen not started while transport is arranged
The commonest and most costly error
Oxygen first, logistics in parallel. One person starts oxygen, another makes calls.
Symptoms resolve on oxygen, everyone relaxes
Improvement does not mean cure — relapse is common
Continue oxygen, continue the referral. This confirms the diagnosis rather than removing the indication.
Saturation is 100% on the mask, but no better
Pulse oximetry says nothing about dissolved nitrogen or inspired fraction
Check the mask seal and reservoir. Oximetry cannot tell you whether the treatment is working.
Deteriorating during air transport
Altitude — bubble expansion
Descend. Pressurize to sea level. This is predictable and preventable.
Sudden deterioration in the chamber on ascent
Expanding gas — pneumothorax tensioning
Why the pre-chamber exclusion is absolute.
Severe ear pain on compression
Middle ear barotrauma — the commonest chamber complication
Slow the compression, teach equalization. An unconscious patient cannot equalize and may need myringotomy or tubes.
Seizure in the chamber
CNS oxygen toxicity — preceded by visual changes, tinnitus, nausea, facial twitching, irritability, dizziness
A chamber-team problem: reduce the inspired oxygen fraction with an air break. Self-limiting, and not a reason to abandon treatment.
Chamber declines the patient
Monoplace, or no critical care capability, or unstaffed
Ask about capability on the first call, before the ambulance leaves.
“The dive profile was within limits”
DCS occurs within tables and computers routinely
A safe-looking profile excludes nothing. Treat the patient.
Presenting days later
Delayed presentation
Still treat. Benefit persists well after the event.
Given nitrous oxide for analgesia
Nitrous diffuses into bubbles and expands them
Never use nitrous oxide in a patient with suspected gas bubbles. Use another analgesic.

blocks.html:
• Middle ear barotrauma — the most frequent, and a particular problem in the sedated or unconscious patient who cannot equalize.
  • Sinus squeeze and dental barotrauma.
  • CNS oxygen toxicity seizure — managed with an air break, self-limiting.
  • Pulmonary oxygen toxicity with repeated or prolonged exposures.
  • Pneumothorax converting to tension on decompression — the reason for the absolute contraindication.
  • Confinement anxiety, and reversible myopia with repeated treatment.
  • Hypoglycemia in diabetic patients during long tables.
  • Risk to the inside attendant in a multiplace chamber, who is also being exposed and has their own decompression obligation.
  • Fire. An oxygen-enriched pressurized environment is a serious fire risk, which is why chamber teams control absolutely everything that goes through the door.

Oxygen first, logistics in parallel. It is the same treatment the chamber gives, at lower intensity, and it is already in the room.

Supine and flat. Trendelenburg is obsolete and harmful.

Symptoms within ten minutes of surfacing means arterial gas embolism. Later onset means decompression sickness. Both get recompressed.

Ask about urinary retention. Spinal DCS is the common serious form and the bladder is the sign people forget to look for.

Cutis marmorata is not a rash to reassure about.

Exclude a pneumothorax before the chamber. The only absolute gate.

Never gain altitude. Ground transport, or sea-level cabin pressure.

No nitrous oxide.

Improvement on oxygen is not a reason to cancel the chamber.

Late is still treatable. Days later, make the call anyway.

Save the numbers now — your regional chamber and DAN. Searching for a chamber during the emergency is a predictable and avoidable delay.

procedures.title: Mass Casualty Triage — START / SALT Execution
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Mass Casualty
procedures.subtitle: The initial sort when casualties outstrip resources. Two frameworks, one discipline: sort fast, intervene minimally, keep moving, reassess constantly.
procedures.description: The initial sort when casualties outstrip resources.

blocks.html:
• Any incident where casualties exceed immediately available resources. That ratio, not a headcount, is what defines a mass casualty incident — four critical patients is an MCI for a two-ambulance service.
  • The initial sorting pass at the scene, before individualized care begins
  • Again, repeatedly, as resources arrive and patients change — triage is a process, not a single pass

START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) remains the most widely used initial sort in US prehospital systems. SALT (Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment/transport) is the national model recommended under the Model Uniform Core Criteria, adding a global voice sort and a short list of interventions performed during the sort. Both do the same job; use whichever your region has adopted.

The governing principle is uncomfortable and has to be stated plainly: the goal changes from doing everything possible for each patient to doing the most good for the greatest number. Resources go to the salvageable, which means some patients who would receive maximal effort on an ordinary day will not. Making that shift deliberately, and saying so out loud, is what separates triage from chaos.

blocks.title: Scene safety comes before any of this
blocks.html: Triage does not begin until the scene is safe. Secondary devices are deliberately timed for the arrival of responders; structural collapse continues; active threats move. Unstable structures, fire, traffic, hazardous materials and contamination all take precedence, and a contaminated scene requires decontamination before or alongside triage. A responder who becomes a casualty subtracts twice — one fewer rescuer and one more patient.

• Triage tags or tape — Red/Immediate, Yellow/Delayed, Green/Minor, Gray or Black for Expectant and Deceased. Tape is faster to apply than tags and easier to see; tags carry information. Know which your system uses.
  • Tourniquets — several, carried on the person doing the sort.
  • Basic airway adjuncts, occlusive dressings, and decompression needles.
  • Antidote auto-injectors where the incident involves nerve agents or cyanide.
  • Nothing else. No monitors, no IV starts, no detailed examination. Diagnostic equipment during the sort is a trap: it slows the pass and it does not change the category.

The roles, assigned explicitly and early: Incident command (owns the scene and the whole picture) · Triage officer (sorts and moves, and treats nobody) · Treatment officer (runs the casualty collection areas) · Transport officer (decides who goes where, and in what order) · Staging (holds and assigns incoming units).

The triage officer's job is to sort, not to treat. This is the hardest discipline in the whole framework and the one that fails most often — the pull to stop and fully manage the first critically injured person found is enormous, and giving in to it means the rest of the scene goes unsorted.
Under 60 seconds per patient. Respirations, perfusion, mental status — in that order, stopping at the first Red.

steps.title: Clear the walking wounded first
steps.html: Call out for anyone who can walk to move to a designated area. Tag them Green. This removes a large fraction of the scene from individual assessment in a single sentence — and it is why you say it before you touch anyone. Someone must go with them: Green patients are not unassessed forever, and occasionally one of them is deteriorating.

steps.title: Respirations
steps.html:
Not breathing → open the airway with a single positioning maneuver. Breathing now → Red. Still not breathing → Black.
Rate above 30/min → Red. Below 30 → go on to perfusion.

steps.title: Perfusion
steps.html: No radial pulse (or capillary refill beyond 2 seconds) → control major hemorrhage and tag Red. Radial pulse present → go on to mental status. The radial pulse is the more reliable of the two in cold, dark, or dirty conditions.

steps.title: Mental status
steps.html: Cannot follow a simple command → Red. Can follow commands → Yellow.

steps.title: Tag, say it out loud, and move on
steps.html: The only interventions permitted during START are opening an airway and stopping catastrophic hemorrhage — both take seconds and both save lives that would otherwise be lost before the treatment phase. Anything further waits.

blocks.html:
JumpSTART — for children, and the differences matter. A child's normal respiratory rate would be tagged Red by adult criteria, and children are far more likely to arrest from a primary respiratory cause and to respond to rescue breaths.

  • Respiratory rate: Red if below 15 or above 45 per minute — not the adult threshold of 30.
  • If apneic: check for a pulse. No pulse → Black. Pulse present → give 5 rescue breaths. If breathing resumes → Red. If not → Black. This rescue-breath step has no adult equivalent and is the heart of JumpSTART.
  • Mental status by AVPU: inappropriate response to pain, posturing, or unresponsive → Red.
  • Infants and children who cannot walk are carried to the Green area and assessed there — the walking sort does not work for them.

steps.title: Sort — the global voice sort
steps.html:
Two instructions, shouted, before anyone is touched: “If you can hear me and can walk, come to [place].” Then, to those remaining: “If you can hear me, wave or move a limb.”
That produces three groups and their assessment order, in reverse: still or obviously in extremis → assessed first; waving or purposefully moving → second; walking → last. Most of the categorization work is done before a single hand is laid on anyone.

steps.title: Assess, and perform lifesaving interventions as you go
steps.html: Working in that priority order, assess each patient individually — and unlike START, perform the interventions during the pass rather than deferring them. The permitted list is deliberately short: open the airway (and in a child, two rescue breaths), control major hemorrhage with a tourniquet or packing, decompress a tension pneumothorax, and give auto-injector antidotes. Each takes seconds. Anything beyond belongs to the treatment phase.

steps.title: Assign a category, after the intervention
steps.html:
Four questions, in order:
Breathing? No, after the airway is opened → Dead.
Obeys commands or makes purposeful movements? Has a peripheral pulse? Not in respiratory distress? Major hemorrhage controlled? — if any is a no → Immediate, provided survival is likely with the resources available; if survival is unlikely given those resources → Expectant.
All yes, with injuries → Delayed. All yes, minor injuries only → Minimal.

steps.title: Treatment and transport — then re-triage
steps.html: Move patients to collection areas by category, and reassess at every stage. Categories are a snapshot of the patient against the resources available at that moment, and both change.

blocks.html:
The category people avoid using, and misusing it in either direction causes harm.

  • Expectant is not a synonym for dead, and it is not abandonment. It means: injuries unlikely to be survivable given the resources presently available, so those resources go elsewhere first.
  • It is explicitly resource-relative. The same patient is Immediate in a fully staffed trauma center and Expectant at a rural scene with two crews. As resources arrive, Expectant patients are reassessed and can be re-categorized upward. Build that reassessment into the plan rather than leaving it to conscience.
  • Comfort care is still care. Analgesia, a blanket, a place out of the rain, and somebody with them if anyone can be spared. Assign it when the surge subsides.
  • Name the decision out loud and share it with incident command. Individual responders should not be silently carrying it alone, and it is the part of an MCI that responders carry longest afterwards.

rows: The triage officer starts treating
Every instinct and all prior training pulls that way
The single most important discipline. Tag and move. Say it aloud before starting: “I am triaging, not treating.”
Over-triage — too many tagged Red
Caution, and discomfort with the categories

It is not a safe default: over-triage dilutes resources and, in the bombing literature, correlates with higher mortality. Around 25–35% over-triage is tolerated; under-triage should stay under about 5%.
Under-triage — a quiet patient missed
Attention follows noise
The screaming patient has an airway and perfusion. The silent, still one is the one to reach first.
No reassessment
The first pass feels like the job finished
Yellow patients deteriorate. Re-triage at every stage and whenever resources change.
Nearest hospital overwhelmed
Most casualties self-transport, and they arrive before the ambulances
A predictable pattern, not a surprise. Distribute deliberately across the region, and expect the closest facility to be saturated with walking wounded before the first ambulance leaves the scene.
Convergent responders taking patients ad hoc
No transport officer, or nobody obeying one
Establish the role early and route everything through it.
Green area unattended
Sorted and then forgotten
Assign someone. Occult injuries and deterioration happen there, and patients wander off unaccounted for.
Children triaged on adult criteria
START applied to a pediatric scene
Use JumpSTART. Adult respiratory thresholds mislabel normal children as Immediate and miss the ones who need rescue breaths.
Contaminated patients moved before decontamination
Urge to treat overrides the hazard
Contamination spreads to the receiving hospital and can close it. Decontaminate first.
Nobody knows who is where
Tracking never started
Tag numbers recorded at transport. Family reunification is a real and large part of the response.
CPR started on a pulseless patient
Ordinary practice applied to an extraordinary situation
In an MCI, a pulseless traumatic arrest is Black or Expectant. One CPR attempt consumes the responders who could sort thirty people.

blocks.html:
• Account for everyone — tag numbers, destinations, and the Green area. Reunification and identification begin immediately and take far more effort than anyone expects.
  • Hand over triage categories and their reasoning to receiving facilities, and tell them the total scene picture — a hospital that knows forty more are coming behaves differently from one that does not.
  • Debrief the responders, properly and more than once. The expectant decisions are what people carry, and the effect is delayed. Make specific offers of support rather than general ones, and repeat them weeks later.
  • Review honestly. Over- and under-triage rates, time to first transport, distribution across hospitals, and where the process broke. Every MCI review finds the same three things — communications, tracking, and distribution — which means they are fixable in advance.
  • Drill it. Triage decisions are made under conditions that make deliberation impossible, so the algorithm has to be automatic. A card in a pocket is not a substitute for having done it.

Sort, do not treat. The pull to stay with the first critical patient is the failure mode that costs the most lives, and knowing that in advance is the only defense.

The voice sort does most of the work. Two shouted sentences categorize most of a scene before you touch anyone.

Go to the quiet one. Noise means an airway and perfusion.

Over-triage is not the safe option. Tagging everyone Red degrades care for the people who actually need it.

Children need JumpSTART — different rates, and rescue breaths before you call an apneic child Black.

Only four interventions during the sort: airway, hemorrhage, decompression, antidote. Nothing else.

Expectant is resource-relative and reversible. Reassess when help arrives, and give comfort care when you can spare it.

Don't send everyone to the nearest hospital — the walking wounded have already filled it.

Say your tag out loud. It gives command a running count and catches your own errors as you go.

Re-triage. One pass is not triage; it is the first pass.

Scene safety first. Secondary devices target responders.

procedures.title: Arterial Line Placement During Resuscitation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Real-time hemodynamic monitoring when non-invasive measurement isn't keeping up with how fast the patient is changing.
procedures.description: Real-time hemodynamics when non-invasive monitoring lags.

blocks.html:
• Any patient on a vasoactive infusion. A cuff cycling every three minutes cannot titrate a drug whose effect changes in thirty seconds — and in low-flow states the cuff is not merely slow, it is wrong.
  • Shock of any cause where the trend between cuff readings is the information you need
  • Frequent blood gases — ventilated patients, DKA, toxic ingestions, post-arrest care
  • During CPR — a genuinely different indication with genuinely different value; see §08. It lets you measure whether your compressions are generating perfusion and detect ROSC without pausing.
  • Titrating blood pressure to a tight target — aortic dissection, post-arrest neuroprotection, intracranial hemorrhage, permissive hypotension in trauma
  • Dynamic preload assessment (pulse pressure variation) in the appropriate ventilated patient

• Infection, burn, or trauma over the site — choose another artery.
  • Known vascular compromise or a previous surgical or interventional injury to that vessel — prior radial harvest for CABG, an AV fistula in that arm, a vascular graft.
  • Raynaud phenomenon, thromboangiitis obliterans, or severe peripheral vascular disease at the intended site.
  • End arteries without collateral supply. The brachial artery is the notable one — it is effectively the sole supply to the forearm, and thrombosis there threatens the whole limb. The median nerve runs alongside it. Prefer radial, femoral, or axillary.
  • Coagulopathy is relative — but it makes site choice matter. Radial is superficial and compressible; femoral bleeding can dissect into the retroperitoneum if the puncture is above the inguinal ligament.

On the Allen test: it has been shown repeatedly to predict neither ischemic complications nor their absence, and a “failed” Allen test in a patient who needs a line should not stop you. Its residual value is as a prompt to look at the hand and think about collateral flow before and after. It is not a gate.

• Catheter. 20 G, 4.5–5 cm for radial — either a plain catheter-over-needle or an integrated-guidewire kit. 18 G, 10–16 cm for femoral, placed by Seldinger technique. Pediatric radial: 22–24 G.
  • Ultrasound, linear probe, sterile sheath. Ultrasound guidance improves first-pass success and reduces attempts, and its advantage is largest in precisely the patients you are placing the line in — hypotensive, edematous, pulseless. Default to it.
  • Transducer set: pressure tubing (short and stiff — see §07), transducer, three-way stopcock, cable to the monitor.
  • Flush bag under a pressure bag at 300 mmHg, delivering roughly 3 mL/h continuously. Check the pressure bag is actually inflated — a deflated bag is a common cause of a line that clots and a trace that damps.
  • Lidocaine 1% for any patient with perception. A small wheal also reduces arterial spasm.
  • Arm board, rolled gauze or a 500 mL bag, and tape for radial positioning.
  • Clear labeling — red-striped tubing, an ARTERIAL label on the stopcock, and no injection ports that can be mistaken for an IV.

sections.title: Choosing the Site — and the Radial-to-Femoral Gradient

rows: Radial
Superficial, compressible, good collateral via the palmar arches, lowest complication rate, keeps the groin free
Small and spasm-prone. Under-reads central pressure in shock (see below). Hardest exactly when you need it most.
Femoral
Large, easy to find with ultrasound even when pulseless, accurate in shock, stays patent when radial arteries have clamped down. Often the right first choice in profound shock.
Groin contamination and higher infection risk. Retroperitoneal bleed if punctured above the ligament. Competes with ECMO/REBOA access.
Axillary
Central pressures, large vessel, good collateral through the scapular network. Underused.
Brachial plexus adjacent. Not compressible. Requires ultrasound.
Dorsalis pedis / posterior tibial
Available when arms are burned, injured, or occupied
Small, distal, and systolic pressure is markedly amplified — often 10–20 mmHg above central. MAP remains usable.
Brachial
Large, easy to palpate
End artery with the median nerve alongside. Reserve for when nothing else is available.

blocks.title: The radial line may be lying to you in vasopressor shock
blocks.html: In distributive shock on high-dose vasopressors, peripheral vasoconstriction creates a real pressure gradient between the aorta and the radial artery. Radial MAP can read 10–30 mmHg below simultaneous femoral MAP. The failure mode is specific and dangerous: the radial number looks inadequate, so the norepinephrine goes up, so the gradient widens, so the number still looks inadequate. If a patient is on escalating pressors and the radial trace looks disproportionately bad for how they appear, place or compare against a femoral line before climbing further.

steps.title: Position — extended, not hyperextended
steps.html: Rolled gauze or a small fluid bag under the wrist, arm on a board, palm up. Extend to about 30–45° and tape the thumb down in gentle traction to stabilize the vessel. Hyperextension flattens the artery and reduces flow — a wrist bent back as far as it goes is a common and self-inflicted reason a line will not thread. If the pulse weakens as you extend, back off.

steps.title: Map it with ultrasound before you prep
steps.html: Short axis, just proximal to the wrist crease. Identify the radial artery: round, pulsatile, non-compressible, with the two small venae comitantes flanking it. Note the depth (usually 2–5 mm) and the course — if it dives or branches, move proximally to a straighter segment. A palpable pulse tells you nothing about whether the vessel runs straight.

steps.title: Prep, drape, and wheal
steps.html: Chlorhexidine and dry. A small lidocaine wheal for anyone with perception — it also blunts the spasm that follows a painful first pass.

steps.title: Enter at 30–45°, then go flat
steps.html: Puncture the skin, then advance slowly toward the vessel. Flash means the needle tip is in the lumen — not the catheter. Drop the hub toward the skin to about 10–15° and advance the whole assembly a further 1–2 mm so the catheter's leading edge crosses the arterial wall. Only then advance the catheter alone. Skipping this is the single commonest reason a line flashes beautifully and then will not thread.

steps.title: Ultrasound: walk the tip down, don't chase the shaft
steps.html: In short axis, what you see is a cross-section of the needle — and a bright dot may be the shaft, not the tip. Use dynamic needle tip positioning: advance the needle a millimeter, slide the probe a millimeter forward, re-find the bright dot, repeat. You are always looking at the tip because you keep moving the probe past it. Alternatively use long axis in-plane, which shows the whole needle at once and is excellent for a straight superficial radial — at the cost of needing to hold the probe exactly in the vessel's plane.

steps.title: If it won't thread: transfixion
steps.html: A legitimate rescue, not a failure. Deliberately pass through both walls, remove the needle, then withdraw the catheter slowly until pulsatile flow returns — you are now in the lumen from behind. Advance. With an integrated-wire kit, thread the wire at the moment of pulsatile return instead. Transfixion punctures the back wall, so expect a little more bruising.

steps.title: Connect, flush, secure
steps.html: Occlude the artery proximally with a fingertip while you disconnect the needle — it keeps the field clean and loses less blood. Connect the primed transducer tubing, flush, and secure with a sutureless device or a suture. Keep the wrist in gentle extension in the final dressing; a line that works on the arm board and damps when the wrist flexes is positional, not broken.

blocks.html: Femoral arterial line

Same Seldinger sequence as a central line, with the target switched: the artery is lateral to the vein (NAVEL, lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics). Puncture 1–2 cm below the inguinal ligament, measured from the ASIS–pubic tubercle line rather than the skin crease. Enter at 45°, take pulsatile return, thread the wire with no resistance, nick, dilate shallowly, and advance an 18 G, 10–16 cm catheter.

Two things differ from the venous version. Above the ligament, an arterial bleed is retroperitoneal — unrecognizable and uncompressible. And if ECPR or REBOA is on the table, this is the vessel those teams need; place it on the side they are not planning to use, and tell them it is there.

sections.title: Zeroing, Leveling, and Why the Number Is Wrong

blocks.html: Two different actions that get conflated, and one of them has to be repeated all day.

Zeroing tells the monitor which pressure is atmospheric. Open the stopcock to air at the transducer, press zero, close it. Done once at setup and after any disconnection or suspicion of drift.

Leveling tells you what you are measuring. The transducer must sit at the phlebostatic axis — fourth intercostal space, mid-axillary line. This must be re-checked every time the bed height or the patient's position changes, which in a busy unit is many times a day and is the most frequently skipped step in arterial monitoring.

The number that makes it concrete: every 10 cm of vertical offset is a 7.4 mmHg error. A transducer taped to the bed rail 13 cm below the patient's chest reads about 10 mmHg too high — more than enough to justify not escalating a pressor on a patient who needs one. Above the axis, it under-reads by the same rule.

For cerebral perfusion — post-arrest care, traumatic brain injury, stroke — some units level to the external auditory meatus (approximating the circle of Willis) instead, which reads lower than the phlebostatic axis by the height difference. Know which convention your unit uses and make sure everyone at the bedside is using the same one; two teams levelling differently on the same patient will disagree about the MAP by 10–15 mmHg and never work out why.
The trace carries more information than the three numbers next to it.

The fast-flush (square wave) test — do this before you believe any arterial number. Pull the flush tab for about a second and release. The trace squares off at the flush pressure, then snaps back. Count the oscillations after release:

  • 1–2 oscillations, then a clean return to baseline — optimally damped. Trust all the numbers.
  • Fewer than 1 — sluggish, rounded return: over-damped. The trace loses its dicrotic notch and looks flattened. It under-reads systolic and over-reads diastolic. Causes: air bubbles anywhere in the circuit, a clot or fibrin at the tip, a kink, the wrist flexed, compliant or over-long tubing, too many stopcocks, a flush bag below 300 mmHg, or arterial spasm.
  • More than 2–3 oscillations — a whippy, spiky trace: under-damped (hyper-resonant). It over-reads systolic by as much as 20–30 mmHg and under-reads diastolic. Causes: long stiff tubing, tachycardia, high contractility, catheter whip. A damping device or a shorter tubing run fixes it.

The rule that saves you in both cases: MAP is the robust number. Mean arterial pressure survives damping error far better than systolic or diastolic, because it is an integrated area rather than a peak. When the waveform is imperfect and you cannot fix it immediately, titrate to MAP, not to systolic.

What else the shape tells you:

  • Upstroke slope — steepness tracks contractility and the rate of ventricular ejection. A slurred, slow upstroke suggests poor contractility or aortic stenosis.
  • Dicrotic notch position — a notch sitting low on the downstroke suggests low systemic vascular resistance (sepsis, vasodilation). High on the limb suggests a vasoconstricted, high-resistance state.
  • Narrow pulse pressure — hypovolemia, tamponade, or a failing ventricle. Wide — vasodilation, aortic regurgitation, or a stiff aorta.
  • Pulse pressure variation (PPV) — respiratory swing in pulse pressure. >13% predicts fluid responsiveness, but only in a patient in sinus rhythm, fully mechanically ventilated with no spontaneous effort, at a tidal volume of at least 8 mL/kg, with a closed chest and no severe right heart failure. Outside those conditions it is not interpretable — and it is quoted outside those conditions constantly.
  • Pulsus paradoxus — an inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mmHg, visible directly on the trace. Points to tamponade, severe asthma, or massive pulmonary embolism.
  • Pulsus alternans — alternating strong and weak beats. Severe left ventricular dysfunction.
This is the use that changes management most, and it is the least familiar.

During cardiac arrest the arterial line stops being a monitor and becomes a feedback device on the quality of your resuscitation.

  • Diastolic pressure is the number that matters, because coronary perfusion happens in diastole. Target an arterial diastolic above roughly 25–30 mmHg during compressions. Below about 20 mmHg, ROSC becomes very unlikely.
  • A low diastolic is actionable in two directions: change the compressor or fix the mechanics (rate, depth, recoil, hand position), or give a vasopressor. It converts “are these compressions any good?” from an argument into a reading.
  • ROSC is detectable without pausing. An abrupt rise in diastolic and the appearance of an organized native waveform between compressions signals return of circulation — so you can confirm it without the interruption in flow that a pulse check costs.
  • Use it alongside end-tidal CO2, not instead of it. ETCO2 reflects pulmonary blood flow, arterial diastolic reflects coronary perfusion pressure; they answer adjacent questions and together they cover most of what you want to know.
  • Post-ROSC it is immediately useful for titrating to a MAP target without waiting on a cuff that will not cycle usefully in a poorly perfused patient.

In a prolonged code, particularly one heading toward ECPR, a femoral arterial line is worth the two minutes it costs — and it is often being placed by the same team, at the same time, in the same groin as the rest of the cannulation plan. Coordinate that.

rows: Flash, then the catheter won't advance
Needle tip in the lumen, catheter tip still in the wall
Drop to 10–15° and advance the whole assembly 1–2 mm before sliding the catheter. Then transfixion if needed.
Pulse disappeared during positioning
Wrist hyperextended, flattening the artery
Relax to 30–45°. Re-palpate or re-image.
Artery visible but keeps rolling away
Not enough skin tension; approach angle too shallow
Tension the skin distally with the non-dominant hand. Enter directly over the vessel center in short axis.
Trace flattens and numbers drift low
Over-damping: air, clot, kink, flexed wrist, or a deflated pressure bag
Square-wave test. Check the pressure bag is at 300 mmHg, hunt for bubbles at stopcocks, straighten the wrist, gently aspirate then flush. Do not flush forcefully against resistance.
Systolic reads absurdly high, trace looks spiky
Under-damping / resonance
Shorten the tubing, remove extra stopcocks, add a damping device. Meanwhile titrate to MAP.
Arterial MAP much lower than the cuff, on high-dose pressors
Radial-to-central gradient in vasoconstricted shock
Compare against a femoral line or a manual cuff before escalating pressors further. Do not chase the radial number upward.
Cannot aspirate, cannot flush
Clotted or the tip is against the wall
Reposition the limb and retry gently. If truly occluded the line is finished — remove it. Forcing a flush risks retrograde embolization.
Hand or fingers pale, cool, painful
Thrombosis or embolism distal to the catheter
Remove the line. Assess perfusion, warm the limb, get vascular input. Do not wait to see if it improves with the line in.
Expanding pulsatile swelling at an old site
Pseudoaneurysm
Ultrasound and vascular referral. Do not aspirate it.
Trace is fine, numbers implausible for the patient
Transducer not level — bed raised or lowered
Re-level to the phlebostatic axis and re-zero. Remember 10 cm = 7.4 mmHg.
Blood in the tubing, slowly backing up
Pressure bag deflated or empty
Re-inflate to 300 mmHg, refill. Then check the line has not clotted.

blocks.title: Never inject into an arterial line
blocks.html: Inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes intense vasospasm, distal thrombosis, and tissue necrosis — it has ended in amputation. The defenses are physical and procedural, not vigilance: red-striped tubing, an ARTERIAL label at every stopcock, no needleless injection ports on the arterial circuit, and stating “that's the art line” out loud at every handover. If it happens: stop immediately, leave the catheter in place, and involve vascular surgery — the catheter is the route for any attempted treatment.

• Temporary radial artery occlusion — not rare, and usually asymptomatic because of palmar arch collateral. Permanent ischemic injury is well under 1%. Risk rises with catheter size relative to vessel, dwell time, repeated attempts, and vasopressor use.
  • Distal ischemia — the complication that matters. Check the hand or foot at least every shift and document it; the first sign is often mottling or delayed capillary refill rather than pain.
  • Hematoma and bleeding, particularly on removal or with coagulopathy. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a high femoral puncture.
  • Pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula — femoral more than radial; consider in any new pulsatile mass or bruit at an old site.
  • Infection — lower than central venous catheters but not negligible; femoral highest.
  • Nerve injury — median nerve at the brachial site, brachial plexus at the axillary site.
  • Retrograde cerebral embolization — forceful flushing of a radial line with as little as 2 mL can drive air or clot retrograde into the subclavian and then the carotid circulation. Flush gently and in small volumes.
  • Forearm compartment syndrome — rare, from a large hematoma in an anticoagulated patient.
  • Blood loss from sampling — a real and cumulative cause of anemia in a long ICU stay. Use a closed conservation system and question each draw.

• Re-level at every position change, and square-wave test at the start of each shift and any time the numbers surprise you.
  • Document distal perfusion each shift — color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation.
  • Keep the pressure bag at 300 mmHg and the flush bag full. Most “the art line died overnight” events start here.
  • Remove it when the indication ends. The line is there for pressor titration or frequent gases; when neither is true, it is only accumulating risk and drawing blood.
  • On removal: hold direct pressure for a full 5 minutes at a radial site, longer with coagulopathy or antiplatelet therapy, and 10–20 minutes for femoral. Do not occlude so hard that you obliterate distal flow for the entire period. Then apply a pressure dressing and re-check the site and the distal pulse 15 and 60 minutes later — late re-bleeding after an apparently dry site is the usual pattern.

Square-wave test before you believe the number. Four seconds, and it tells you whether the systolic in front of you is real.

When the waveform is imperfect, trust the MAP. Damping distorts systolic and diastolic far more than the mean.

Flash is the needle, not the catheter. Drop the angle and advance 1–2 mm more. This single habit fixes most failed radial attempts.

Don't hyperextend the wrist. You flatten the artery you are trying to cannulate.

Ten centimeters is 7.4 mmHg. A transducer that has drifted off the phlebostatic axis is the commonest reason a stable patient appears to have changed.

In vasopressor shock the radial under-reads. Compare against femoral before you escalate on a number you do not trust.

In arrest, watch diastolic. Above 25–30 mmHg during compressions, or change something. It also shows you ROSC without a pause.

PPV needs four conditions. Sinus rhythm, fully controlled ventilation, tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg, closed chest. Outside those, it is a number, not information.

Label it, and never inject into it. The safeguards have to be physical — red tubing and no injection ports — because attention fails.

Check the hand. The complication that costs a patient something is distal ischemia, and it is found by looking.

procedures.title: Central Line Placement Under Arrest Conditions
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Femoral-first access during active resuscitation — landmark or ultrasound-guided, without interrupting compressions.
procedures.description: Femoral-first access without interrupting compressions.

blocks.html:
• Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest where peripheral and intraosseous access are inadequate, failed, or unavailable
  • Vasopressor infusion that will run for hours, at doses or concentrations you do not want in a peripheral vein
  • Volume — but only if you place a large-bore introducer sheath. A triple-lumen is worse than a good peripheral for flow (see §03)
  • Anticipated ECPR, transvenous pacing, or a pulmonary artery catheter — access you will need regardless of how this code ends
  • Post-ROSC, when the line placed under compressions needs to become the line you can keep

What it is not indicated for: getting drugs in faster than an IO. An intraosseous line is already running, already works for every arrest drug, and does not require someone to stop resuscitating and start a sterile procedure. Central access during arrest is for the things IO cannot do — sustained pressors, large-bore volume, a pacing wire, a monitoring column.

blocks.title: Below the diaphragm, drugs take longer
blocks.html: A standard 20 cm femoral catheter sits in the iliac vein or low IVC. During CPR, forward flow from below the diaphragm is poor and drug transit to the central circulation is slower than from an upper-body line or a proximal humeral IO. It still works — but every drug gets a 20 mL flush and the leg gets raised. If you have a choice of sites and no reason to avoid the chest, an upper-body line delivers faster.

• A groin you are going to need for ECMO. If ECPR is on the table — even as a maybe — do not put a resuscitation line in the groin the cannulation team wants. Right femoral vessels are conventionally preferred for VA-ECMO cannulation. Use the left groin, or go above the diaphragm. A triple-lumen in the right femoral vein at minute 12 can cost the cannulation at minute 25, and nobody will remember to tell the ECMO team it is there.
  • Vascular injury, graft, or known thrombus at the intended site. A femoral line above a pelvic fracture or an IVC injury delivers drug into the retroperitoneum.
  • Infection or burn over the site — choose another.
  • Subclavian in severe coagulopathy — the site is not compressible. In a coagulopathic bleeding patient, femoral or IJ are the compressible options.
  • Coagulopathy generally is relative, not absolute, in arrest. So is the absence of full sterile barrier. Both are reasons to plan an exchange later, not reasons to withhold access now.

sections.title: Which Catheter — and Why It Is Usually the Wrong One

blocks.html: The kit you grab determines what the line can do. This decision is made before you scrub, and it is frequently made wrong.

rows: 7 Fr triple-lumen, 20 cm
~25–50 mL/min through the distal lumen
Multiple simultaneous infusions, pressors, monitoring. Not volume.
8.5 Fr introducer sheath (“Cordis”), 10 cm
Hemorrhage and volume. Also the conduit for a transvenous pacing wire or a PA catheter.
16 G peripheral, 1.25 in
~200 mL/min
Reference point — it beats a triple-lumen, because flow falls with catheter length and rises with the fourth power of radius.

blocks.html:
Everything else you need:

  • Ultrasound, linear probe, sterile sheath and gel. In arrest this is not an optional refinement — it is the only reliable way to tell artery from vein when there is no pulse and no color difference. Prepare it while you prep the skin, not after.
  • Chlorhexidine, full barrier drape, gown and gloves — use what the situation allows, and document what it did not.
  • Seldinger components: introducer needle, guidewire, scalpel, dilator, catheter, suture or securement device.
  • Saline flushes for every lumen, and a primed extension set.
  • A pressure transducer or a length of sterile IV tubing (for the manometry check — §06).

rows: Femoral — the default
Does not compete with the airway or the compressor. Compressible. Easy landmarks and easy ultrasound. Can be done by one person in a crowded room.
Slower drug transit during CPR. Highest infection rate. May consume the ECMO groin.
Subclavian

Above the diaphragm, so faster drug delivery. Stays out of the way of both the head and the groin. Best long-term infection profile. Landmarks survive when the vein is empty — it is tethered open by surrounding tissue.
Not compressible. Pneumothorax risk in a patient already being ventilated. Chest wall is moving under compressions.
Internal jugular
Above the diaphragm, compressible, excellent ultrasound target.
Directly contests the airway. Head-of-bed is the busiest square meter in the room. Realistic mainly post-ROSC or when someone else fully owns the airway and the bed can be turned over to you.

blocks.html:
The practical rule: during active compressions, femoral — unless ECPR is a possibility, in which case femoral on the left, or subclavian. After ROSC, when the room calms and the bed is yours, the decision reverts to the usual one.

Say out loud which groin you are taking. Two operators independently deciding “femoral” and arriving at the same groin, or the ECMO team arriving to find both groins used, are avoidable and entirely typical failures.

steps.title: Claim the space and set up on the correct side
steps.html: Announce it: “I am taking the left femoral vein.” Sit or kneel at the groin, outside the compressor's arc. Have the whole kit open and the wire loosened from its dispenser before you start — you will not be able to fish for components one-handed with a needle in a vein that is moving with every compression.

steps.title: Find the inguinal ligament, not the skin crease
steps.html: Draw the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle — that is the inguinal ligament. Puncture 1–2 cm below it. In an obese patient the skin crease can sit several centimeters distal to the ligament and using it as the landmark puts you too low, in the branching femoral vessels. Puncturing above the ligament is worse: that bleed is retroperitoneal, not compressible, and silent.

steps.title: Put the probe on — short axis first
steps.html: Lateral to medial the structures run NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics. The vein is medial to the artery. On ultrasound, the artery is round, thick-walled and resists compression; the vein is more oval and collapses. Be warned: in arrest, an empty artery compresses too, and during compressions the vein can transmit pulsation. Do not rely on pulsatility or on blood color — deoxygenated arterial blood in arrest is dark. Use position and wall thickness, and then use the wire (step 7).

steps.title: Prep and drape as fully as the clock allows
steps.html: Chlorhexidine, let it dry if you can, full drape if someone can hand it to you. If a step gets skipped, skip it deliberately and say so — it goes in the note and it sets up the exchange decision later.

steps.title: Needle in at 30–45°, aspirating continuously
steps.html: Aim just medial to the artery, along the vessel's axis, advancing under constant negative pressure on the syringe. Compressions do not stop. Expect the target to move a centimeter with each one — advance between compressions if you can time it, and accept that this is harder than an elective line. Flash is dark and often non-pulsatile even from an artery, because there is no pulse.

steps.title: Drop the angle, thread the wire, and never let go of it
steps.html: Flatten the needle toward the skin before feeding the wire so it turns up the vessel rather than through the back wall. The wire should pass with no resistance at all. A hand is on the wire at every instant from the moment it leaves the dispenser until it is withdrawn — a wire released during chest compressions embolizes. Do not advance more than about 20 cm.

steps.title: See the wire in the vein. This is the step that prevents the disaster.
steps.html: Turn the probe to long axis over the vein and identify the echogenic wire lying inside it. If you cannot see the wire in the vein, you do not have a venous wire. Slide the probe proximally and confirm it stays in the venous channel. Dilation is the point of no return — ten seconds of ultrasound before the dilator is the cheapest insurance in the procedure.

steps.title: Nick and dilate — shallow
steps.html: Scalpel blade against the wire, cutting away from the wire, just through dermis. Then pass the dilator over the wire only far enough to open the tract — typically 2–3 cm. The dilator is a tissue dilator, not a vessel dilator; burying it perforates the posterior wall.

steps.title: Catheter over wire — wire out the hub first
steps.html: Thread the catheter until the wire emerges from the distal hub, then advance it into the vessel. Femoral catheters sit at roughly 20–25 cm at the skin. Remove the wire and confirm it is intact and whole when it is out.

steps.title: Aspirate every lumen, flush every lumen, secure
steps.html: Every port must draw blood back and flush freely. Suture or use the securement device — a line that is only taped will be removed by the transfer to CT. Then announce it: “Left femoral central line is in and working.”

sections.title: Confirming It Is Venous — When Every Normal Clue Has Failed

blocks.html: In arrest, all three of the usual reassurances are unreliable at once.

• Pulsatility: useless. There is no pulse — and compressions make everything pulsatile.
  • Color: useless. Arterial blood in arrest is desaturated and dark.
  • Ease of flow / low resistance: useless. There is no arterial pressure to push back.

What actually works, in order of usefulness during CPR:

  • 1. Ultrasound of the wire, long axis. The definitive bedside test, available before dilation, and the only one that is fully reliable during compressions. Make it a habit, not a tiebreaker.
  • 2. Transduce the needle or catheter. Connect to a pressure transducer and read the waveform. Post-ROSC this is decisive. During compressions it is muddied — compression-generated arterial waveforms can be substantial — but a clearly arterial trace is still an answer.
  • 3. Manometry. Attach sterile IV tubing to the needle hub, fill it, and hold it vertically. A venous column rises a few centimeters and stops; an arterial column climbs and swings. Interpretable post-ROSC; confounded during compressions.
  • 4. Blood gas from the catheter. Slow, and in arrest the arteriovenous difference narrows — a last resort, not a plan.
  • 5. Post-procedure imaging. Chest film for upper-body lines to confirm tip position and exclude pneumothorax. It answers a question you needed answered twenty minutes earlier — useful for documentation and tip position, not for preventing arterial dilation.

blocks.title: If you dilated an artery — leave the catheter in
blocks.html: A large-bore catheter that has been dilated into the femoral or subclavian artery is tamponading its own hole. Pulling it produces uncontrolled arterial bleeding, and in the subclavian position that bleeding is into a space you cannot compress. Leave it in place, leave it clamped, and call vascular surgery or interventional radiology now. This instinct — not to pull — is counterintuitive and has to be pre-loaded, because in the moment every reflex says remove it.

rows: No flash anywhere
Vein is empty and collapsed — the commonest problem in arrest
Use ultrasound to find the vein rather than hunting. Withdraw slowly under aspiration — the back wall is often transfixed on the way in and the flash appears coming out.
Flash obtained, wire will not pass
Bevel against the wall, or needle tip only partly in the lumen
Do not force — forcing dissects. Drop the angle a few degrees, rotate the needle 90°, re-confirm aspiration, retry. If it still won't pass, start over.
Wire passes but resistance partway
Valve, tortuosity, or the wire has gone up a tributary
Withdraw a few centimeters and re-advance. Confirm position on ultrasound. Never push a wire that resists.
Cannot tell artery from vein
Arrest physiology — all the usual discriminators have failed
Ultrasound the wire in long axis before dilating. If you still cannot say, do not dilate.
Bright pulsatile blood after ROSC
Arterial cannulation, unmasked by return of a pulse
If it is a needle — remove and compress 10 min. If it has been dilated and catheterized — leave it in and call vascular surgery.
Catheter in, no blood returns from any port
Tip against a wall, kinked at the skin, or not in the vessel
Withdraw 1–2 cm, reposition the limb, reattempt aspiration. If it flushes but will not draw, treat it as unverified until imaged.
Groin swelling during resuscitation
The line is extravascular, or an arterial puncture is bleeding
Stop infusing through it. Compress. Reassess with ultrasound. A retroperitoneal bleed from a high puncture will not show as groin swelling.
Wire disappeared
Released during compressions — embolized
Do not chase blindly. Immediate imaging and interventional radiology for retrieval.
Sudden hypoxia / hypotension after a subclavian or IJ attempt
Pneumothorax — or tension, under positive pressure
Clinical diagnosis and needle or finger decompression. Do not wait for a film in a deteriorating patient.
ECMO team arrives, both groins used
Nobody said which side they were taking
Preventable only in advance: declare the side, and preserve the right groin whenever ECPR is conceivable.

blocks.html:
• Arterial puncture and arterial cannulation — the defining risk of this procedure in arrest, because every normal discriminator fails simultaneously. Needle punctures compress; dilated catheters do not come out at the bedside.
  • Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a femoral puncture above the inguinal ligament. Not compressible, not visible, and presents as unexplained shock after an apparently uneventful line.
  • Guidewire embolization — rare, entirely preventable, and specifically more likely here because compressions jostle the operator's hands.
  • Pneumothorax and hemothorax — subclavian and IJ. In a ventilated patient a simple pneumothorax can tension quickly.
  • Air embolism — upper-body lines, especially on chest recoil. Keep the hub occluded.
  • Vessel perforation and cardiac tamponade — from over-advancing a dilator or a stiff wire.
  • Arrhythmia from a wire in the right atrium or ventricle. Irrelevant in arrest; genuinely dangerous peri-arrest. Limit the wire to ~20 cm.
  • Infection — elevated, because barrier precautions were compromised. Femoral is the highest-risk site. Plan the exchange; see §09.
  • Thrombosis — femoral lines in an immobile ICU patient.

• Re-verify the line now that there is a pulse. Transduce it. Draw a gas from it if there is any doubt. A line that was “probably venous” during compressions gets a definitive answer within minutes of ROSC, because the answer is now easy to obtain.
  • Image it. Chest film for any upper-body line — tip at the cavoatrial junction, no pneumothorax. Femoral lines do not need a film for position but do need a documented function check.
  • Flag it as an emergent line, explicitly, in the chart and at handover. Write down which barrier precautions were and were not used. Lines placed without full sterile technique should be removed or replaced as soon as the patient is stable, generally within 24–48 hours — and the only way that happens is if the next team knows.
  • Reassess whether you still need it. The indication was arrest. If the patient now needs only maintenance fluids and a single infusion, the line's risk has outlived its purpose.
  • Tell the ECMO, IR, and surgical teams which vessels are occupied. Access planning downstream depends on it.

See the wire before you dilate. If you take one thing: long-axis ultrasound confirming the wire inside the vein, every time, before the dilator. Everything else in arrest lies to you.

Protect the right groin if ECPR is possible. The line you place in minute 12 can cost the cannulation in minute 25.

If you dilated an artery, do not pull it. The catheter is plugging the hole. Clamp it, leave it, call vascular surgery.

Grab the right kit. A triple-lumen is not a volume line. If you need blood to move, that is an 8.5 Fr introducer — or a short 14 G peripheral, which beats the triple-lumen anyway.

Puncture below the inguinal ligament, judged from bone landmarks, not the skin crease. Above it, the bleed is retroperitoneal and silent.

The vein is empty, so hunt with the probe, not the needle. And watch for the flash on withdrawal — you transfix the back wall more often than you think.

A hand on the wire at all times. Compressions are shaking the field; this is exactly where wires get let go.

Flush hard and raise the leg after every drug through a femoral line during CPR.

An IO already in and working beats a central line you are still placing. Place this line for what only it can do, not for speed.

Say which side you are taking, out loud. Most access collisions are communication failures, not technical ones.
