procedures.title: ECMO Cannulation Prep & Activation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Peripheral VA/VV cannulation framework, from activation call to first flow — and the timing discipline that drives ECPR outcomes more than technique does.
procedures.description: VA/VV framework from activation call to first flow.

blocks.html: VA-ECMO — circulatory support

• Refractory cardiogenic shock — infarction, myocarditis, decompensated cardiomyopathy, post-cardiotomy
  • ECPR — refractory cardiac arrest with a plausibly reversible cause
  • Massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic collapse
  • Severe hypothermic arrest — ECMO is both the support and the rewarming method, and outcomes here are far better than for other arrest etiologies
  • Refractory arrhythmia; massive poisoning with cardiotoxic drugs; peripartum cardiomyopathy
  • Bridge to recovery, to a durable device, to transplant — or to a decision
VV-ECMO — respiratory support

• Severe refractory hypoxemic respiratory failure — typically P/F <80 for more than 6 hours, or <50 for more than 3 hours, despite optimized ventilation, proning, and neuromuscular blockade
  • Refractory hypercapnia with pH <7.20 despite optimal settings
  • Inability to ventilate within lung-protective limits — severe asthma, airway obstruction, bronchopleural fistula

VV-ECMO supports gas exchange; it does nothing for the circulation. A hypoxemic patient who is also in shock from right heart failure is a VA or VAV question, not a VV one.

blocks.title: Activation delay is the biggest modifiable factor — by a wide margin
blocks.html: For ECPR, survival is driven by time from arrest to flow far more than by any technical detail of the cannulation. Every additional interval of conventional CPR before flow costs outcome. The target is flow within about 60 minutes of arrest, which means the call goes out when ECMO first becomes a real possibility — not once every other option has visibly failed. An activation that turns out to be unnecessary costs almost nothing. One that comes twenty minutes late costs everything.

Favorable ECPR criteria (thresholds are institutional — know yours):

  • Witnessed arrest with immediate bystander CPR — short or no no-flow interval
  • Initial shockable rhythm, or a clearly reversible cause such as hypothermia, poisoning, or massive PE
  • Low-flow time under roughly 60 minutes with high-quality, minimally interrupted compressions
  • Age within the program's limit, commonly under 65–70
  • ETCO2 above about 10 mmHg during CPR — a marker of both compression quality and residual viability
  • Signs of life during resuscitation, intermittent ROSC, or preserved neurologic signs
  • No known terminal illness, and an acceptable baseline functional state

Contraindications: unwitnessed arrest with prolonged downtime and poor CPR; an irreversible or non-survivable underlying condition; severe pre-existing multi-organ failure; known severe aortic regurgitation or aortic dissection (for VA); uncontrolled hemorrhage or recent intracranial hemorrhage (relative, and dependent on a source-control plan); severe peripheral vascular disease precluding femoral cannulation; and no institutional capacity to manage the patient afterwards.

Hypothermic arrest deserves separate mention: the usual downtime limits do not apply, neurologically intact survival is documented after hours of CPR, and ECMO is the definitive rewarming modality. Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead — and ECMO is how they get warm.

rows: Peripheral VA
21–25 Fr multistage, femoral vein → cavoatrial junction
15–19 Fr, femoral artery (retrograde)
Fastest to establish. Retrograde aortic flow is the source of most of its specific problems — see §06.
Peripheral VV
23–25 Fr, femoral vein
19–21 Fr, internal jugular
Separate the tips to limit recirculation.
VV, dual-lumen
Single cannula via right IJ, spanning SVC to IVC with the return port aimed at the tricuspid valve
One site, permits mobility. Requires echo or fluoroscopic guidance — malposition is easy and consequential.
VAV
Adds a jugular return limb to a VA circuit
The answer to differential hypoxia (§06).

blocks.html:
• Size by the vessel, not by the patient. Measure the femoral artery with ultrasound. A common rule is that the arterial cannula's outer diameter should not exceed about two-thirds to three-quarters of the vessel's internal diameter — oversizing is how limbs are lost.
  • Flow follows the fourth power of the radius and falls with length. Full support is roughly 60–80 mL/kg/min. Drainage is almost always the limiting side, so do not undersize the venous cannula to save time.
  • A distal perfusion catheter — 5–7 Fr, antegrade into the superficial femoral artery, connected to the arterial limb. Plan it at cannulation. See §06.
  • Ultrasound for access, and TEE or fluoroscopy for wire and cannula tip confirmation.
  • Primed, de-aired circuit — pump, oxygenator, tubing, heater-cooler.
  • Heparin, and ACT or anti-Xa monitoring.
  • A mechanical CPR device for ECPR. It makes cannulation during ongoing compressions genuinely feasible, and it frees a person.
  • NIRS probes for the calves, for limb monitoring.

steps.title: Activate early, and run everything in parallel
steps.html: Call the moment ECMO is plausible. Circuit priming is frequently the rate-limiting step, not the cannulation — so perfusion starts priming at minute one, while access is being obtained. Two operators work the two vessels simultaneously. Resuscitation does not pause for any of it.

steps.title: Assign the roles out loud before anyone touches the groin
steps.html: Venous operator, arterial operator, perfusionist, airway and compressions, drugs, and a scribe on the clock. ECPR fails on choreography more often than on technique.

steps.title: Ultrasound-guided access to the common femoral vessels
steps.html: Below the inguinal ligament, above the bifurcation — the same narrow window as any femoral access, and it matters more here because the sheath is enormous. Measure the artery before you choose the cannula. Vein and artery on the same side is conventional; using opposite groins is an option when anatomy demands it.

steps.title: Confirm both wires before any dilation
steps.html: The venous wire must be seen in the right atrium or IVC, and the arterial wire in the descending aorta — on TEE or fluoroscopy. Serial dilation over a misplaced wire creates a hole the size of the dilator in a structure that cannot tolerate one. This is the single most important safety step in the procedure, and under ECPR time pressure it is the one most likely to be skipped.

steps.title: Place the distal perfusion catheter now
steps.html: Antegrade into the superficial femoral artery distal to the arterial cannula, before the leg is committed. Doing it at cannulation takes a few minutes; doing it later means doing it on a leg that is already ischemic, and limb complications are among the commonest serious harms of peripheral VA support.

steps.title: Dilate serially and place the cannulae
steps.html: Step up in sequence, keeping a hand on the wire throughout. Venous cannula tip at the cavoatrial junction; arterial cannula to the institutional depth. Confirm both positions before connecting.

steps.title: Connect wet-to-wet, and hunt every bubble
steps.html: Make each connection with both ends flooded. Air on the arterial side goes to the brain and the coronaries. Clamp, connect, de-air, unclamp — deliberately, in that order, spoken aloud each time.

steps.title: Start low and climb
steps.html: Begin at low revolutions and increase while watching circuit pressures, the drainage line for chatter, the arterial waveform, and the patient. Line chatter means the drainage cannula is sucking against a wall or the patient is underfilled — reduce flow and give volume rather than driving the pump harder.

steps.title: Anticoagulate, image, and hand over properly
steps.html: Heparin per protocol once bleeding risk is assessed — commonly a bolus at cannulation then an infusion to ACT or anti-Xa targets, and sometimes deliberately withheld initially after traumatic or surgical ECPR. Secure the cannulae to the skin robustly. Chest film, echo, lactate, and limb checks. Then drop the ventilator to rest settings — the lungs have just stopped being the priority.

sections.title: Two Problems Unique to Peripheral VA

blocks.html:
Differential hypoxia (“harlequin” or north–south syndrome). Retrograde ECMO flow from the femoral artery meets antegrade native output from a recovering heart somewhere in the aorta — the “watershed.” If the lungs are still bad, that native blood is poorly oxygenated, and it is the blood supplying the aortic root and arch: the coronaries and the brain. The lower body is pink on ECMO blood while the heart and brain are hypoxic.

  • Monitor the right radial artery — it arises most proximally and best reflects what the brain is receiving. A pulse oximeter on the right hand is the cheap version of the same idea.
  • The fix: improve native lung function and ventilation, reduce flow competition, add a jugular return limb (VAV), or move to a central or axillary arterial return.
  • Paradoxically, a recovering heart is what causes this, so it appears just as things seem to be improving.

Left ventricular distension. Retrograde flow raises afterload on a ventricle that may not be able to eject against it. The LV dilates, the aortic valve stops opening, pulmonary edema develops, and stasis risks intracardiac thrombus.

  • Recognize it: a flat, non-pulsatile arterial waveform; worsening pulmonary edema on the film; frank pulmonary hemorrhage; and on echo, a dilated LV with an aortic valve that is not opening and spontaneous contrast.
  • Vent it: inotropic support, reduced ECMO flow, an intra-aortic balloon pump, an Impella, atrial septostomy, or a surgical vent. Pulsatility on the arterial trace is the bedside sign to protect — losing it is the warning.

rows: Everyone waiting for a decision
Delayed activation — the dominant failure
Call it. An unnecessary activation is cheap; a late one is not.
Cannulae in, circuit not ready
Priming started too late
Perfusion primes from minute one, in parallel. Never sequentially.
Drainage line chattering, flow dropping
Hypovolemia, or the cannula tip against a wall
Reduce revolutions and give volume. Increasing pump speed makes suction worse and hemolyzes blood.
Low flow despite high revolutions
Undersized or kinked drainage cannula; tamponade; obstruction
Check the tubing, image the tip, echo for tamponade. Drainage is usually the limit.
Right hand or right radial desaturating
Differential hypoxia
Optimize ventilation; consider VAV or a different return site. Do not be reassured by a good saturation from the left side or a foot.
Arterial waveform flattens
LV distension — the ventricle has stopped ejecting
Echo now. Vent the LV: inotrope, reduce flow, IABP, Impella, septostomy.
Frothy pink secretions from the tube
Pulmonary edema from LV distension
Same answer, urgently.
Leg mottled, cool, NIRS falling
Limb ischemia from the arterial cannula
Distal perfusion catheter now if not already placed. Vascular surgery. This is limb-threatening and common.
Good circuit saturations, patient still hypoxic (VV)
Recirculation — oxygenated blood being drained straight back
Separate the cannula tips; reposition under echo; reduce flow. High premembrane saturation with a hypoxic patient is the signature.
Dark blood post-oxygenator, rising pressure gradient
Oxygenator failing or clotting
Post-membrane gas, trend the gradient, plan a circuit change before it fails outright.
Pink plasma, rising free hemoglobin
Hemolysis — usually excessive negative drainage pressure or pump thrombus
Reduce suction, give volume, inspect the pump head.
Falling platelets with clotting
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Send the assay, change anticoagulant.
New unexplained shock or a falling hematocrit
Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a high puncture
Image it. Cannulation site bleeding is the commonest complication of all.

blocks.html:
• Bleeding — the most frequent complication overall: cannulation sites, retroperitoneum, gastrointestinal, and intracranial hemorrhage, which is among the most feared and carries very poor outcomes.
  • Limb ischemia distal to the arterial cannula, up to and including amputation. Preventable, mostly, by a distal perfusion catheter placed at cannulation.
  • Vessel injury — dissection, perforation, retroperitoneal hemorrhage — usually from dilating over an unconfirmed wire.
  • Air embolism, catastrophic on the arterial limb.
  • Differential hypoxia and LV distension (§05).
  • Stroke, both ischemic and hemorrhagic; and watershed injury from the arrest itself.
  • Hemolysis, and acquired von Willebrand syndrome from shear across the circuit.
  • Thrombosis — circuit, oxygenator, or intracardiac — and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
  • Infection, and acute kidney injury frequently requiring renal replacement integrated into the circuit.
  • Recirculation in VV, limiting effective oxygen delivery.
  • A bridge to nowhere — support established in a patient with no recovery, no device candidacy and no transplant route. This is a real and foreseeable harm, and the way to avoid it is to ask what the bridge leads to before cannulating.

• Chest film and echo. Cannula positions, LV function and distension, valve opening, tamponade.
  • Rest the lungs. Lung-protective or rest settings, low driving pressure, modest PEEP. The ventilator is no longer doing the work and continuing aggressive settings adds injury.
  • Check the limb and set up monitoring for it — pulses or Doppler, NIRS, hourly documented assessment.
  • Follow lactate, urine output, and mixed venous saturation as the markers of whether flow is adequate.
  • Right radial arterial line or right-hand oximetry for VA, so differential hypoxia is detectable.
  • Treat the underlying cause. ECMO buys time and treats nothing — coronary angiography, thrombolysis or embolectomy for PE, rewarming, antidote, source control.
  • Set the exit strategy explicitly, and write it down. Recovery, durable device, transplant, or a defined time-limited trial with agreed criteria. Answering this on day four is far harder than answering it on day zero.
  • Talk to the family early about what the support does and does not do.

Call early. Time from arrest to flow is the outcome variable. Nothing about the technique matters as much.

Prime in parallel. The circuit, not the cannulation, is usually the bottleneck.

Confirm both wires before you dilate. The most important safety step, and the first one sacrificed to urgency.

Place the distal perfusion catheter at cannulation — not when the leg is already turning.

Measure the artery and size to the vessel. Oversizing costs limbs.

Drainage is the limit. Chatter means give volume, not more revolutions.

Watch the right hand. Differential hypoxia appears exactly when the heart starts recovering.

Protect pulsatility. A flattening arterial trace means the LV has stopped ejecting and needs venting.

Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead — and in hypothermic arrest, ECMO is how they get warm.

Know what the bridge leads to before you build it.

procedures.title: Intraosseous Access
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites — the fastest reliable vascular access when peripheral IV attempts have failed or time doesn't allow for them.
procedures.description: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites.

blocks.html:
• Cardiac arrest, any age, when a peripheral IV is not already running
  • Shock of any cause where access is the rate-limiting step — hemorrhagic, septic, anaphylactic, cardiogenic
  • Two failed peripheral attempts, or a patient in whom you can see at a glance that attempts will fail (burns, IV drug use, obesity, profound vasoconstriction, hypothermia)
  • Status epilepticus, status asthmaticus, hypoglycemia with altered mental status — time-critical drug delivery in a moving target
  • Pre-hospital and austere settings where ultrasound-guided peripheral or central access is not available
  • As a bridge during RSI when you need induction drugs now and the line you have is unreliable

blocks.title: What the 2025 trials actually showed
blocks.html: Two large randomized trials of out-of-hospital arrest — PARAMEDIC-3 and IVIO — found that an IO-first strategy did not improve survival over an IV-first strategy, and PARAMEDIC-3 found lower rates of ROSC in the IO-first arm. This does not make IO a bad route. It means IO is the answer to “I cannot get a vein,” not a shortcut to be reached for reflexively when a vein is available. If a peripheral IV will be in within about 90 seconds, place the IV. If it won't, drill.

Absolute — pick a different bone:

  • Fracture in that bone, at or proximal to the site. Infusate leaks out the fracture; a tibial IO above a tibial fracture perfuses the hematoma, not the patient.
  • Previous IO attempt in the same bone within 48 hours, successful or not. The old cortical hole is a vent — the new line will run straight out of it into the soft tissue. Cross to the other side or another site.
  • Orthopedic hardware, prosthetic joint, or prior surgery at the site (knee replacement, IM nail, shoulder arthroplasty).
  • Infection, burn, or cellulitis over the insertion point. Seeding the marrow through infected skin produces osteomyelitis. Burned skin over an otherwise good site is not an absolute bar in extremis — but choose unburned skin if any exists.

Relative:

  • Osteogenesis imperfecta, osteopetrosis, severe osteoporosis — fragile or sclerotic bone. Osteopetrotic bone may simply not be penetrable.
  • Landmarks you cannot confidently palpate. Body habitus that defeats palpation is a reason to change sites or use ultrasound, not a reason to guess. A blind drill into soft tissue is the commonest cause of a failed IO.
  • Sternal IO: add prior sternotomy, sternal fracture, and small children to the exclusion list.
A powered driver with the wrong needle in it fails exactly like no driver at all.

• Powered driver (battery drill-type) or manual driver. Check the battery indicator at the start of any shift you might need it. A driver that stalls partway through the cortex leaves a needle you must remove and a site you can no longer use.
  • Needle sets — three lengths, and the length is the decision. The color codes below are the widely used EZ-IO convention; confirm against the set in your own kit.
    • 15 mm (pink): 3–39 kg
    • 25 mm (blue): ≥3 kg — the adult tibial default
    • 45 mm (yellow): ≥40 kg, or any site with heavy overlying tissue. The proximal humerus in an adult is a 45 mm needle, always — the deltoid is thicker than people estimate, and a 25 mm needle in a humerus is the single most common cause of an IO that “placed fine” and then infiltrated.
  • Chlorhexidine or whatever prep is within reach. In arrest this is one pass, not a scrub.
  • Extension set with a Luer lock, primed. Prime it — pushing the air column in the tubing into the marrow first is both wasted time and extra pain.
  • Two 10 mL syringes: one of normal saline for the flush, one for aspiration.
  • Preservative-free 2% lidocaine (cardiac lidocaine) for any patient with a pulse and any perception. This is not optional comfort care — see §09.
  • Pressure bag or infusion pump. Gravity through an IO delivers roughly a milliliter a minute. Without pressure you have access that does nothing.
  • Securement dressing (the winged stabilizer in the kit, or a bulky dressing and tape).

blocks.title: The 5 mm rule
blocks.html: Seat the needle through the skin until the tip touches bone, then look at the hub. At least one black depth marking must be visible above the skin. If no line shows, the needle is too short to cross the cortex and still sit in the marrow — swap up a size before you pull the trigger. Checking this takes two seconds and prevents the failure you won't detect until you flush.

rows: Proximal humerus
~5 L/hr
Volume resuscitation; drugs you want centrally fast; awake patients (least painful site)
Displacement with any arm movement — secure the arm to the torso. Not during unmechanized CPR on that side.
Proximal tibia
~1 L/hr
Default in arrest with ongoing compressions; easiest landmarks; pediatrics
Slowest flow. Posterior extravasation is invisible — you must palpate the calf.
Distal femur
~1 L/hr
Infants and small children — wide, flat, forgiving target
Growth plate. Leg must be straight.
Distal tibia
~1 L/hr
Second-choice extremity site; useful when the knee is involved
Thin cortex — easy to go through and through.
Sternum (manubrium)
High
Military/tactical, dedicated device, bilateral extremity trauma
Dedicated device only. Competes with pad and compression placement.

blocks.html:
The default pairing worth committing to memory: humerus for flow and speed to the central circulation, tibia for a moving resuscitation. Humeral flow is roughly five times tibial, and drug transit to the central compartment is faster — which matters for adenosine and for arrest drugs. But the humeral needle sits in a bone attached to a limb that everyone in the room will move, and it dislodges.

In a running code with manual compressions, the tibia is usually the right call: nobody is near it and nothing displaces it. If you place a humeral IO in that setting, tape the arm down across the abdomen and tell the team it is there.

sections.title: Proximal Humerus — The One People Miss

blocks.html: Almost every humeral failure is a positioning failure, and it happens before the drill comes out.

blocks.alt: Proximal humerus intraosseous access in two steps. First, internal rotation: the arm is adducted with the palm on the umbilicus and the elbow pointing backward, which swings the greater tubercle forward into the operator's target line. Second, the angle: the needle enters the most prominent point of the greater tubercle, one to two centimeters above the surgical neck, and is driven at forty-five degrees toward the elbow. A needle driven straight in instead travels medially through the humeral head into the glenohumeral joint space.
blocks.caption: Internal rotation and the 45° caudad angle are the two things that make this line work, and neither is visible once the drill is in your hand. A needle driven perpendicular to the skin travels medially through the head and into the glenohumeral joint — it will stand up convincingly, flush poorly, and infiltrate.

steps.title: Position the arm — this is the procedure
steps.html: Adduct the arm tight to the chest wall, then internally rotate so the palm rests on the umbilicus and the elbow points posteriorly. If you can, have someone hold it. Internal rotation is what swings the greater tubercle anteriorly into your target line and moves it clear of the acromion. Without it you are drilling into the joint capsule or the deltoid.

steps.title: Find the golf ball on the tee
steps.html: Place the heel of your hand on the anterior shoulder and slide your thumb up the anterior humeral shaft. You will feel the shaft narrow — that notch is the surgical neck — and then a broad, round prominence above it. That prominence is the greater tubercle: the ball sitting on the tee. The target is the most prominent point of that ball, roughly 1–2 cm above the surgical neck. If you never felt a narrowing, you have not found the neck, and your landmark is a guess.

steps.title: Angle 45° down and back
steps.html: Enter perpendicular to the surface of the tubercle, which means aiming roughly 45° caudad (toward the elbow) and slightly posteromedial. Straight-in aiming at the ceiling walks you into the joint space. Think of the needle as pointing at the opposite hip.

steps.title: Push to bone, then check the line
steps.html: Push the needle through the skin and soft tissue manually until the tip stops on bone. Now look: at least one black depth line must be showing. In an adult humerus this should be a 45 mm needle. Only then squeeze the trigger.

steps.title: Let the drill do the work — then feel the change
steps.html: Apply steady, gentle axial pressure and let the driver cut. Leaning on it stalls the motor. You are drilling through a thicker cortex than the tibia, so it takes longer and the “pop” is less obvious. The endpoint is a sudden loss of resistance and a change in the driver's pitch as it unloads, or the hub reaching the skin. Stop there. Continuing drives the needle out the far cortex.

steps.title: Uncouple, unscrew, secure
steps.html: Hold the hub and pull the driver straight off — do not let it torque the needle. Remove the stylet by turning counterclockwise. Attach the primed extension set. Then tape the arm to the torso. A humeral IO not secured to the body has an hourly dislodgement rate that makes it unreliable exactly when you stop watching it.

blocks.alt: Proximal tibial intraosseous landmarks, anterior view of the right knee. The tibial tuberosity is the reference bump. The adult target lies two centimeters medial and one centimeter proximal to it, above the tuberosity. The pediatric target lies one centimeter medial and one to two centimeters distal to it, below the tuberosity, so that it stays clear of the open proximal tibial growth plate. The two targets sit on opposite sides of the tuberosity.
blocks.caption: The tuberosity is the reference, not the target. Adult goes proximal to it; a child goes distal — opposite directions, for the one reason shown here. Getting them backwards in a child puts the needle through an open physis.

steps.title: Find the tuberosity, then move off it
steps.html: Run a finger up the shin to the bony bump below the patella — the tibial tuberosity. You are not drilling into it. Adult: about 2 cm medial and 1 cm proximal to the tuberosity, on the flat anteromedial face of the tibia. Child: about 1 cm medial and 1–2 cm distal — distal, to stay clear of the proximal tibial physis. In an infant, one finger-breadth below and medial.

steps.title: Support the knee, don't suspend the leg
steps.html: Put a rolled towel under the knee so it rests in slight flexion on a solid surface. A leg that bounces on the mattress absorbs the drill and turns a clean insertion into a wandering one.

steps.title: Perpendicular — 90° to the flat surface
steps.html: Unlike the humerus, the tibial approach is straight in, 90° to the flat medial surface. Angling drags the needle toward the thin cortex and out the side.

steps.title: Drill to the give
steps.html: The tibial cortex is thin and the pop is distinct — often the first clear tactile landmark a trainee ever gets. Stop at the pop. In a child the cortex is thinner still and the marrow cavity is shallow; a through-and-through insertion is the classic pediatric error. Feather the trigger rather than holding it down.

steps.title: Stylet out, extension on, palpate the calf
steps.html: After the flush, put your hand behind the calf. The tibia extravasates posteriorly where you cannot see it, and the first sign of a failed tibial IO is often a firm posterior compartment rather than a visible bulge.

blocks.html: Alternate sites

Distal femur (pediatric): leg straight, patella identified. Insert 1 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella and 1–2 cm medial to the midline, aiming straight back (slightly cephalad if anything). Wide target, thick marrow, forgiving — a good choice in a small child when the tibia has failed.

Distal tibia: 2 cm proximal to the most prominent point of the medial malleolus, on the flat medial surface, perpendicular. Thin cortex — easy to over-drill.

Sternum: device-specific (FAST1 / FASTResponder and similar), targeting the manubrium about 1.5 cm below the sternal notch via the device's own locating collar. Fixed depth, no freehand angle to judge. Do not improvise a sternal IO with an extremity needle.

sections.title: Confirming You Are in the Marrow

blocks.html: Four checks, in order. Only one of them is decisive.

• 1. The needle stands unsupported. Let go. A correctly seated IO is held rigidly by cortical bone and stands like a flagpole. One that wobbles, leans, or falls is in soft tissue. This is a fast and powerful negative test.
  • 2. Loss of resistance was felt. Corroborative, not proof — in the humerus it can be subtle, and in osteoporotic bone it can be absent entirely.
  • 3. Marrow aspirates. Nice when it happens. Its absence proves nothing — a substantial fraction of correctly placed IOs never yield aspirate, particularly in arrest. Do not pull a good needle because nothing came back.
  • 4. The flush runs without swelling. This is the test that decides. Push 10 mL of saline briskly in an adult (2–5 mL in a child) while watching and feeling the limb. Free flow with no swelling, no boggy tissue, no resistance building under your thumb — you are in. Anything else means stop.

blocks.title: The flush is not a confirmation step — it is part of the insertion
blocks.html: The marrow cavity is a sponge of trabecular bone and fat, not an open tube. Without a forceful flush the space does not open and nothing will infuse afterward, no matter how perfectly the needle sits. The commonest complaint about IO access — “it's in but it won't run” — is nearly always an under-flushed line. Push it hard, and push it again if flow is sluggish.

sections.title: Lidocaine, Pressure, and What Can Go Through It

blocks.html:
Lidocaine — the sequence matters more than the dose. The saline flush into a conscious patient's marrow is described by patients as among the worst pain in medicine. Lidocaine must go in before the flush, not after.

  • Adult: preservative-free 2% lidocaine, 40 mg (2 mL) slowly over about 120 seconds → let it dwell 60 seconds → flush 5–10 mL saline → a further 20 mg (1 mL) over 60 seconds.
  • Pediatric: 0.5 mg/kg, max 40 mg, same dwell-then-flush sequence.
  • Repeat doses are appropriate for ongoing pain during infusion. Account for the total in any systemic lidocaine ceiling.
  • This is for any patient with a pulse and any plausible perception. It is not indicated in arrest — and if they wake up, give it then.

Pressure. Gravity produces roughly 1 mL/min through an IO. Every infusion that needs to be fast needs a pressure bag at 300 mmHg or a pump. If a resuscitation is running slowly through an IO, check the pressure bag before you blame the needle.

What can go through it: everything. Crystalloid, blood and all components, vasopressors, induction and paralytic agents, antibiotics, TXA, sodium bicarbonate, hypertonic saline, contrast for CT. Onset and peak levels approximate IV. There is no drug class that is IV-only. The proximal humerus is preferred for adenosine and other agents whose effect depends on a tight, fast bolus.

Labs from the aspirate: the first aspirate can be sent for type and screen, chemistry, lactate and blood gas, and correlates acceptably for most. It is unreliable for platelet and white cell counts, and marrow will clog an automated analyzer. Call the lab and the blood bank before you send it — some will not accept it, and you need to know that before it is the only sample you have.

rows: Needle bounces off, drill bogs down
Leaning on the driver and stalling the motor; or a dead battery; or sclerotic bone
Ease the axial pressure and let it cut. Swap batteries. If two attempts stall, change sites.
Drove it in, no pop, hub at skin
Needle too short — it never crossed into marrow
Remove. Re-site on the other limb with the next size up. Do not redrill the same bone.
Needle wobbles / falls over
In soft tissue, or through-and-through out the far cortex
Remove and re-site on a different bone. Hold pressure.
No marrow aspirate
Normal — common in low-flow states
Ignore it. Confirm with the flush instead.
Flush meets hard resistance
Tip against cortex, or the lumen is plugged with a marrow core
One firm attempt to clear. If still blocked, it is a failed line — remove.
Limb swells / calf firms up on flush
Extravasation
Stop immediately. Remove. New site on a different bone. Mark the limb and reassess for compartment syndrome hourly.
Ran fine, then stopped
Dislodgement (classically humeral, with arm movement), or clotting from an inadequate initial flush
Re-flush firmly. Check the needle is still rigid. If it now wobbles, it has moved — replace it.
Correct position but flow is slow
Running on gravity
Pressure bag to 300 mmHg, or a pump. Re-flush.
Awake patient screams on infusion
Lidocaine omitted, or given after the saline flush
Stop the infusion. Give lidocaine, dwell 60 seconds, then restart.
Second IO in the same bone won't hold pressure
The earlier cortical hole is venting the marrow space
Expected and unfixable. Use a different bone — this is why the 48-hour rule exists.

blocks.html:
• Extravasation → compartment syndrome. The complication that matters, and it is essentially always a recognition failure rather than a technique failure. The tibia is the highest-risk site because leakage tracks posteriorly and stays invisible. Any IO limb gets a documented baseline and scheduled re-checks while it is running.
  • Through-and-through penetration — classically the pediatric tibia, from holding the trigger through the marrow cavity and out the far cortex. Presents as a needle that stands but will not flush.
  • Fracture — excess force in osteoporotic or pediatric bone, or a manual needle levered sideways.
  • Osteomyelitis — well under 1%, and rises with dwell time and with insertion through non-prepped or infected skin.
  • Growth plate injury — the reason pediatric tibial landmarks sit distal to the tuberosity and femoral landmarks sit proximal to the patella.
  • Fat and marrow embolization — demonstrable, but not associated with clinically meaningful harm in humans. It is not a reason to withhold or under-flush an IO.
  • Skin necrosis from vesicant or vasopressor extravasation into soft tissue — a downstream consequence of a missed infiltration, not a separate event.

24 hours is the ceiling under most manufacturer instructions, and sooner is better. IO is a bridge. Once the patient is stabilized and a peripheral or central line is in, the IO comes out — leaving it “just in case” accumulates infection risk for access you are not using.

Removal: attach a Luer-lock syringe to the hub (a slip-tip will pull off). Rotate clockwise while drawing straight out along the needle's axis. Do not rock, lever, or bend. Side-loading can shear the needle and leave a fragment in the bone — a problem that becomes an orthopedic consult. Dress the site; it will ooze a little.

Document: site, needle size, time in, time out, lidocaine given, and the limb assessment. If the patient goes to CT or the OR, tell the receiving team the IO is there — humeral needles under a gown are easy to miss and easy to knock out.

Flush like you mean it. If you remember one thing: the marrow cavity does not open until you force it open. Almost every “the IO doesn't work” complaint is an under-flushed line.

The needle stands up or it isn't in. Letting go of the hub is a free, instant, highly specific test, and it is the one people skip in a hurry.

No aspirate is not a failure. More correctly placed IOs yield nothing back than most clinicians expect. Confirm with the flush, not the syringe.

The humerus needs the long needle and the right rotation. Hand on the belly, 45° toward the elbow, 45 mm needle. Get those three and the humerus is the best line in the room; miss any one and it fails quietly.

Secure the arm. A humeral IO not taped to the torso will be pulled out by someone doing something reasonable.

Pressure bag, every time. Access without pressure is not resuscitation.

Never re-drill the same bone. Within 48 hours, the previous hole vents everything you put in. Cross to the other side.

IO is not a second-class line. Every drug, blood product, and contrast agent that goes IV goes IO. Treat it as full access — and then replace it within 24 hours.

procedures.title: Junctional Tourniquet Application
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Hemorrhage control at the junctional zones — groin, axilla, pelvis — where a standard limb tourniquet has no purchase.
procedures.description: Hemorrhage control at groin, axilla, pelvis.

blocks.html:
• Life-threatening hemorrhage in a junctional zone — the groin and inguinal region, the axilla and shoulder girdle, the gluteal region, the perineum, and the base of the neck. Anatomy where there is no cylindrical limb for a standard tourniquet to squeeze.
  • Traumatic proximal amputation — a high thigh or shoulder-level amputation leaves no residual limb above the injury to place a limb tourniquet on
  • Junctional bleeding that continues despite correct wound packing and sustained direct pressure
  • As a bridge while a limb tourniquet is converted, or while proximal surgical control is arranged
  • Abdominal aortic occlusion (specific devices only) as a non-invasive analogue of Zone 3 REBOA in pelvic and high junctional hemorrhage

• None absolute in life-threatening junctional hemorrhage.
  • Bleeding a limb tourniquet can reach. If there is a cylinder of limb above the wound, use a standard tourniquet — it is faster, better understood by everyone downstream, and does not require the specific device knowledge these do.
  • Pelvic fracture, for abdominal aortic compression devices. An inflatable wedge pressed onto a disrupted pelvis can displace the fracture and is generally avoided; a pelvic binder plus a groin-targeted device is the better combination.
  • Abdominal aortic occlusion in penetrating abdominal trauma or suspected abdominal injury — you are compressing bowel and a possibly injured aorta against the spine.
  • Pregnancy, for abdominal devices.
  • Any device you have not used before, if manual pressure is working. A fist held correctly on the femoral artery beats forty seconds spent reading a label.
Unlike limb tourniquets, these share almost no technique. This table is the reason this entry exists.

rows:
CRoC
Combat Ready Clamp
A rigid C-clamp bolted to a base plate, driving a pressure disc down onto the vessel by a threaded handle
Inguinal; axilla with repositioning
Needs a firm surface under the patient. Slow to assemble. Very effective once seated, and the pressure is directly and continuously adjustable.

JETT
Junctional Emergency Treatment Tool
A belt with two screw-down pressure pads
Bilateral inguinal simultaneously
The only common device designed for both groins at once — the reason it exists is bilateral proximal amputation. Not for axilla.
SAM Junctional TQ
Pelvic belt with an inflatable Target Compression Device (one or two)
Inguinal, axillary; the belt doubles as a pelvic binder
Inflate to hemorrhage control. Cleared for up to 4 hours. The dual-purpose pelvic function is genuinely useful in blunt trauma.

AAJT-S
Abdominal Aortic and Junctional TQ
Inflatable wedge over the abdomen compressing the aorta against the spine
Distal aorta (at the umbilicus); also axilla and groin
Abdominal application is limited to about 60 minutes — this is whole-body distal ischemia, functionally non-invasive Zone 3 REBOA. Avoid with pelvic fracture, abdominal injury, or pregnancy.

blocks.title: Know the device in your bag, today
blocks.html: Limb tourniquets are close enough to one another that skill transfers. These do not. A CRoC and an AAJT share no motions, no landmarks, and no endpoints. The failure mode is specific and predictable: an operator meets an unfamiliar device during the two minutes it was bought to save, and reads the instructions while the patient exsanguinates. Find out which one your service stocks and put your hands on it before you need it. If you are improvising because you don't know the device, go back to a fist on the ramus.

sections.title: Before the Device: the Things That Work Immediately

blocks.html:
Every junctional device takes time to deploy. The bleeding does not pause for it, so something has to hold the line first — and these techniques are not a lesser substitute, they are the opening move.

  • A fist, a knee, or a heel on the femoral artery. Press at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament — halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle — driving straight down so the artery is compressed against the superior pubic ramus. Use body weight through a straight arm or a knee. This works, it works instantly, and it holds while everything else is organized. It is also exhausting, so rotate people.
  • Pack the wound at the same time (see the wound packing entry). Packing and a junctional device are complementary: the pack controls what is bleeding in the wound, the device controls inflow from above. A device applied over an unpacked cavitating wound often fails.
  • Axillary compression — push the axillary artery against the humeral head, or reach higher and compress the subclavian downward behind the clavicle against the first rib.
  • Abdominal aortic compression by fist — a closed fist or the heel of the hand pressed hard just left of the umbilicus, directed posteriorly toward the spine, with the operator's weight over it. A crude and short-lived measure that can buy minutes in catastrophic pelvic or high groin bleeding.
  • Analgesia. All of this is savagely painful. Ketamine, early.

steps.title: Manual pressure first, and keep it there
steps.html: One person holds the femoral artery against the pubic ramus and does not let go until the device is tightened and has taken over. Deploying a device while nobody is compressing means the patient bleeds throughout the assembly.

steps.title: Expose fully and pack the wound
steps.html: Cut the clothing away to bare skin — a pad over fabric slides. Pack the wound cavity firmly while pressure is maintained proximally.

steps.title: Place the pad over the artery, not over the wound
steps.html: The target is proximal inflow: the femoral artery at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, where it can be pressed onto the superior pubic ramus. This is the single most common misapplication — the pad is instinctively centered on the injury, which compresses a hole rather than the vessel feeding it. Find the landmark by bone, not by the wound.

steps.title: Anchor the belt around the pelvis and tension it
steps.html: Belt-based devices need a firm circumferential anchor before the pad can generate force. Seat the belt, remove the slack, then apply pressure through the pad.

steps.title: Tighten to hemorrhage control — that is the endpoint
steps.html: Screw down, ratchet, or inflate until bleeding stops. Unlike a limb tourniquet, you cannot rely on loss of a distal pulse: the collateral circulation around the pelvis and shoulder is rich, and a palpable distal pulse does not mean the device has failed. Watch the wound, not the foot.

steps.title: Verify after every movement
steps.html: Recheck after each log-roll, lift, and transfer. These devices slip — they sit on a mobile, conical, blood-slick surface, and a pad that has migrated a couple of centimeters off the artery is doing nothing while looking correct.

steps.title: Write the time on the patient
steps.html: On the skin and on the device, in marker. Say it at handover. Ischemic time drives every downstream decision and is the number most often lost.

blocks.html:
Harder than the groin, and less often practiced. The axillary artery has no convenient flat bone beneath it and the shoulder girdle is mobile.

  • Target the axillary artery against the humeral head with the arm adducted, or reach proximally and compress the subclavian artery downward behind the clavicle onto the first rib.
  • Anchor over the opposite shoulder — axillary applications need a counter-anchor across the torso, because there is no circumference to grip. A belt that simply encircles the chest will ride.
  • Pack the wound as well, always. Axillary bleeding has substantial collateral supply through the scapular anastomosis, and inflow control alone often leaves brisk back-bleeding.
  • Watch the airway and breathing. A device anchored across the chest restricts ventilation, and high axillary wounds are close enough to the pleura that a pneumothorax should be actively excluded.
  • Brachial plexus injury is a real consequence of sustained axillary compression. It is accepted in exchange for survival, and it is documented.

sections.title: Abdominal Aortic Occlusion — and Its Clock

blocks.html:
An inflatable wedge placed over the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus, compressing the infrarenal aorta against the vertebral column. Functionally a non-invasive Zone 3 REBOA: it stops inflow to the pelvis and both legs without any vascular access at all.

  • Indication: catastrophic pelvic, perineal, or high bilateral groin hemorrhage not controllable by any other means.
  • Do not use with pelvic fracture, suspected abdominal injury, penetrating abdominal trauma, or pregnancy.
  • Time limit is approximately 60 minutes, and it is a hard limit. Everything below the device is ischemic from the moment it is inflated, and the reperfusion load on release is the same problem REBOA has: potassium, acid, and vasoplegia arriving at once.
  • Announce the clock the way you would for a balloon. Inflation time called out loud, repeated every five minutes, written down.
  • Prepare for release exactly as for REBOA deflation — blood running, pressors connected, calcium drawn up, and a surgeon present. Release gradually, not by opening the valve.
  • Confirm effect by loss of femoral pulses bilaterally and a rise in proximal blood pressure. If neither happens, the device is malpositioned or under-inflated — or the bleeding is above it.

rows: Device on, still bleeding briskly
Pad centered on the wound instead of on the proximal artery
Move the pad to the bony landmark — midpoint of the inguinal ligament, onto the ramus. Check this before anything else.
Still bleeding, pad correctly placed
Insufficient pressure, or the wound cavity is bleeding independently
Increase pressure to the device's limit. Pack the wound if you have not. Reassess for a second site.
Bleeding controlled, then restarts
Device migration — almost always after a move
Re-seat and re-tension. Re-verify after every transfer, every time.
Distal pulse still present
Normal — collateral flow around the pelvis and shoulder
Not a failure. The endpoint is a dry wound, not an absent pulse. Do not over-tighten chasing the pulse.
Device will not seat / keeps sliding
Applied over clothing, or blood-slick skin, or no firm surface beneath
Strip to skin and dry it. Rigid clamp devices need a hard backboard under the patient.
Patient fighting, unmanageable
Pain — these are excruciating
Ketamine. An incompletely applied device because the patient could not tolerate it is a preventable failure.
Bilateral groin wounds, one device
Only JETT covers both simultaneously
Manual pressure on the second side, or a second device. Do not let one side go untreated while perfecting the other.
Abdominal device on, pressure unchanged
Under-inflated, malpositioned — or bleeding above the level of occlusion
Inflate further and confirm both femoral pulses are gone. If still no response, look above the diaphragm.
Collapse when the device comes off
Reperfusion washout
Re-apply. Calcium, product, pressors. Release slowly and only with a surgeon present.
Nobody knows when it went on
Time not recorded
Preventable only up front — marker on skin, spoken at handover, written in the note.

blocks.html:
• Ischemia distal to compression, scaling with dwell time — and with abdominal application, that means the pelvis, both legs, and the pelvic viscera.
  • Reperfusion injury on release — hyperkalemia, acidemia, vasoplegia, arrhythmia and arrest. Identical in kind to REBOA deflation, and prepared for the same way.
  • Compartment syndrome of the compressed limbs after reperfusion. Serial checks; low threshold for fasciotomy.
  • Nerve injury — femoral nerve in the groin, brachial plexus in the axilla. Frequently accepted deliberately.
  • Pressure necrosis of skin and underlying soft tissue at the pad.
  • Bowel injury and aortic injury from abdominal compression, particularly in an already injured abdomen.
  • Ventilatory restriction from abdominal or thoracic-anchored devices.
  • Fracture displacement where a device is applied over an unstable pelvis.
  • Incomplete control creating false reassurance — a device that is on and visible is easy to mistake for a problem solved.

• Name the device. The receiving team may never have seen it. “Junctional tourniquet” is not enough information to release one safely.
  • Give the application time — written on the patient, not only spoken.
  • Say what is packed underneath, and how many rolls or sponges.
  • Say what has already failed, so nobody repeats it.
  • These come off in an operating room, with proximal control obtained and the team ready for reperfusion — not in a resuscitation bay to see whether the bleeding has stopped.
  • For abdominal aortic devices, state the clock as a deadline, not as an elapsed time: “inflated at 14:32, off by 15:32.”

A fist on the ramus works right now. Start there, keep it there, and let the device take over — never the other way around.

The pad goes on the artery, not on the wound. Find it by bone: midpoint of the inguinal ligament, onto the superior pubic ramus.

Pack the wound too. Inflow control and cavity control are different problems and you usually have both.

The endpoint is a dry wound, not an absent pulse. Collateral flow means the pulse can persist with the device working perfectly.

Know your device before the day you need it. Nothing transfers between a CRoC, a JETT and an AAJT except the intent.

Re-check after every move. These slip, and a slipped device looks applied.

Abdominal aortic occlusion has a one-hour clock — treat it exactly like a Zone 3 balloon, including how you come off it.

Give ketamine.

Write the time on the skin.

procedures.title: Lateral Canthotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Emergent decompression of orbital compartment syndrome — a vision-saving procedure with a narrow therapeutic window.
procedures.description: Vision-saving orbital compartment decompression.

blocks.html: The orbit is a closed cone with one soft wall. Cutting that wall is the entire procedure.

• Orbital compartment syndrome — a tense, proptotic orbit with threatened vision, from retrobulbar hemorrhage or any rapidly expanding orbital process
  • After orbital or facial trauma, especially with a fracture and an anticoagulated patient
  • Iatrogenic retrobulbar hemorrhage — after a retrobulbar or peribulbar block, blepharoplasty, or orbital surgery
  • Spontaneous retrobulbar hemorrhage — anticoagulation, vascular malformation, Valsalva
  • Rapidly expanding orbital emphysema, abscess, or edema with the same physiology

The mechanism: the orbit is bone on four sides. The only structure that can give is the front — the orbital septum, held in place by the medial and lateral canthal tendons. Blood accumulating behind the globe pushes it forward until those tendons tether it, at which point pressure rises steeply, the central retinal artery perfusion pressure is overcome, and the retina becomes ischemic. Canthotomy and cantholysis release the anterior tether. Nothing else available at the bedside does.

blocks.title: This is a clinical diagnosis and a 90-minute problem
blocks.html: Retinal ischemia becomes irreversible somewhere around 90 to 120 minutes, and there are reports of loss sooner. Do not send the patient to CT to confirm it. Do not wait for ophthalmology to arrive from home, and do not wait for a formal visual acuity. The diagnosis is made with a light, a hand, and a tonometer if one is nearby, and the treatment takes about two minutes. Vision is lost to delay in recognition, essentially never to technical difficulty.

sections.title: Making the Diagnosis in Ninety Seconds

rows: Proptosis
Look from above and behind the patient's head, down across both eyes — asymmetry is obvious from this angle and easy to miss from the front
May be masked by massive lid swelling.
Resistance to retropulsion
Gentle pressure on the closed lid with a thumb. A normal globe gives slightly; this one feels like a marble set in concrete
The most useful bedside sign, and the fastest. Do not press hard.
Relative afferent pupillary defect
Swinging flashlight test
The key objective sign of optic nerve compromise. Present early.
Reduced visual acuity
Counting fingers, hand motion, light perception — whatever they can manage
Document it. It is the number everyone will ask about afterwards.
Intraocular pressure
Tono-Pen or equivalent
Normal 10–21 mmHg. Above 40 with visual compromise is decompression territory. A tonometer is helpful, not required — its absence is not a reason to wait.
Pain, ophthalmoplegia, chemosis
Examination
Severe deep orbital pain out of proportion is typical.
Fundus
Ophthalmoscope, if there is time
Retinal arterial pulsations or a pale retina are late. Their absence reassures you about nothing.

blocks.html:
Globe rupture. A ruptured globe has already decompressed itself; there is no compartment to release, and manipulating the orbit risks extruding intraocular contents. Look for it before you cut:

  • Teardrop or peaked pupil pointing toward the rupture
  • Extruded dark uveal tissue at the limbus or under the conjunctiva
  • Seidel sign — aqueous streaming through fluorescein
  • Shallow or flat anterior chamber, hyphema, marked hypotony
  • 360° bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage, or a visible full-thickness laceration

If the globe is ruptured: rigid shield, no pressure, no further examination, antiemetics, analgesia, antibiotics, and ophthalmology now. A patient can have both a ruptured globe and a tense orbit — that is a specialist decision, not a bedside one.

Not contraindications: anticoagulation, thrombocytopenia, an uncooperative patient, or the absence of an ophthalmologist. Each of these is a reason to proceed more carefully, not to wait.

• Local anesthetic with epinephrine — 1–2 mL of lidocaine 1–2% with 1:100,000 epinephrine. The vasoconstriction genuinely helps in a field that will bleed.
  • Straight scissors — iris scissors, tenotomy scissors, or straight Mayo. Curved scissors make the cantholysis harder to direct.
  • Toothed forceps — Adson or similar. You need to grip and pull the lid firmly; smooth forceps will slip.
  • A straight hemostat — for the crush step, which both reduces bleeding and marks the line.
  • Gauze, saline, and a rigid eye shield for afterwards.
  • Tonometer if available, before and after.
  • Nothing else. This does not need a tray, an operating room, or sterile drapes. A prepped skin surface and clean instruments are sufficient.

steps.title: Document vision, pupil and pressure — fast
steps.html: Acuity at whatever level they can give, the presence of an afferent defect, and IOP if a tonometer is at hand. Thirty seconds, not five minutes. These numbers establish both the indication and the response.

steps.title: Infiltrate laterally, away from the globe
steps.html: Inject 1–2 mL into the lateral canthus, directing the needle laterally toward the orbital rim, never medially toward the eye. Adding anesthetic adds volume to a compartment that is already over-pressurized, so use the smallest volume that will work.

steps.title: Crush with the hemostat for 30–60 seconds
steps.html: Clamp from the lateral commissure horizontally out to the orbital rim, and hold. This crushes the tissue you are about to cut, which reduces bleeding into a field you need to see — and it leaves a visible blanched line that is exactly your incision. Optional in principle; worth the minute in practice.

steps.title: Canthotomy — cut horizontally to the rim
steps.html: Place one blade in front of and one behind the lateral canthus, and cut full thickness, horizontally, about 1–2 cm out to the lateral orbital rim. Skin, muscle, conjunctiva — all of it. This step alone relieves almost nothing. It is the exposure, not the treatment.

steps.title: Cantholysis — this is the procedure
steps.html: Grasp the lower lid at its cut edge with toothed forceps and pull it anteriorly and superiorly, away from the face. That tension puts the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon on stretch. Point the scissors inferiorly and slightly posteriorly — toward the patient's chin, roughly 45° — and strum the tissue with the blade tips. You will feel a taut band like a guitar string. Cut it. There is a distinct release, and the lower lid becomes completely floppy.

steps.title: Test the release before you stop
steps.html: Pull the lower lid away from the globe. If it comes freely, with no tethering at all, the crus is divided. If anything still holds it back, you have not cut the tendon — go back and strum again. Failing to complete the cantholysis is the classic technical error, and it leaves an orbit that has been cut but not decompressed.

steps.title: Reassess — and release the superior crus if needed
steps.html: Recheck pressure, proptosis, and vision. If improvement is inadequate, release the superior crus using the same technique with the upper lid, scissors pointing superiorly. Do this without hesitation — the risk is ptosis from levator injury, which is trivial against blindness.

steps.title: Still tense? Keep going.
steps.html: If both crura are released and the orbit is still hard, the septum may need dividing (septolysis), or the hematoma may need direct drainage. Get ophthalmology or oculoplastics now — but do not stop at a half-measure while waiting.

steps.title: Shield it, and recheck the vision
steps.html: Saline gauze and a rigid shield — not a pressure patch, which is the opposite of what this orbit needs. Then document acuity, pupil and pressure again. Serial checks, because a hemorrhage can continue and re-tension the orbit.

blocks.html: Medical adjuncts — alongside, never instead: head of bed up 30–45°, acetazolamide 500 mg IV, mannitol 1–2 g/kg IV, and a topical agent such as timolol. Reverse anticoagulation where relevant. Each of these lowers pressure by a modest amount over tens of minutes. None of them opens a closed compartment. Start them on the way to the cut, not as an alternative to it.

rows: Cut made, orbit still hard
Cantholysis not completed — only the skin was divided
Test the lid: it must be completely floppy. If it tethers, the crus is intact. Go back, tension the lid, and strum for the band.
Cannot feel the tendon
Not enough tension on the lid, or the scissors are pointing the wrong way
Pull the lid firmly anteriorly and superiorly. Aim the scissors toward the chin, not laterally. The band appears under tension and vanishes without it.
Inferior crus released, still tense
Inadequate release
Take the superior crus. Then consider septolysis. Do not stop halfway.
Field filling with blood
Expected — this is a vascular area
Use the crush step. Pressure with gauze between cuts. Do not abandon the procedure for bleeding; it settles.
Improved, then tense again an hour later
Ongoing hemorrhage
Serial checks exist for this. Re-examine, reverse anticoagulation, escalate to ophthalmology for drainage.
Vision does not improve after good release
Ischemia already established, or a different diagnosis
Optic nerve injury, traumatic optic neuropathy, or central retinal artery occlusion. The decompression was still correct. Ophthalmology, and imaging now that the emergency is treated.
Peaked pupil noticed after the incision
Unrecognized globe rupture
Stop. Shield, no pressure, antiemetics, antibiotics, ophthalmology immediately.
Nobody willing to do it
Unfamiliarity — the real failure mode
It is two cuts with straight scissors, it takes about two minutes, and the wound heals remarkably well. The alternative is a blind eye.

blocks.html:
• Incomplete decompression — by a wide margin the most important, and always from stopping at the canthotomy.
  • Bleeding at the incision — common, self-limiting, and mitigated by the crush step.
  • Injury to the globe or lateral rectus — avoided by directing the scissors away from the eye and staying at the rim.
  • Lacrimal gland injury with superior crus release.
  • Ptosis from levator damage during superior cantholysis — an accepted trade.
  • Ectropion, lid malposition, or scarring, usually correctable later.
  • Infection — uncommon; the periorbital blood supply is excellent.
  • Cutting an eye that did not need it — a small harm, and a far better error than the other one.

• Do not suture it acutely. The wound is left open and heals by secondary intention with surprisingly good cosmetic results. Formal canthoplasty, if wanted, happens later and electively.
  • Rigid shield, never a pressure patch.
  • Serial visual acuity, pupil and pressure checks — hourly at first. Re-accumulation happens.
  • Ophthalmology review for every patient, regardless of how well it went.
  • CT orbits now, once the emergency is treated — for fracture, foreign body, and the extent of the hemorrhage.
  • Reverse the anticoagulation where one is responsible, and stop antiplatelet agents pending review.
  • Antibiotics in the setting of trauma or fracture; tetanus.
  • Document the before-and-after numbers. Acuity, afferent defect, and IOP at both time points, with times. This is the record that shows the procedure was both indicated and effective.

The canthotomy is the exposure; the cantholysis is the treatment. If you stop after the skin incision you have done nothing for the pressure.

The endpoint is a floppy lid. Pull it away from the globe — if it tethers at all, the crus is still intact.

Pull the lid up and out, and point the scissors at the chin. The tendon only becomes findable under tension.

Do not go to CT first. This is a clinical diagnosis with a ninety-minute clock.

Retropulsion is the fastest sign. A globe that feels like a marble is the whole examination when time is short.

Look for a ruptured globe before you cut. Teardrop pupil, extruded uvea, Seidel sign.

Acetazolamide and mannitol are adjuncts. They do not open a closed compartment.

If one crus is not enough, take the other. Ptosis is a trivial price.

Leave it open. It heals well and it is not a repair you make at 3 a.m.

Recheck it in an hour. Hemorrhage can continue.

Lima V, Burt B, Leibovitch I, Prabhakaran V, Goldberg RA, Selva D. Orbital compartment syndrome: the ophthalmic surgical emergency. Surv Ophthalmol. 2009;54(4):441–449.
Roberts JR, Custalow CB, Thomsen TW, eds. Roberts and Hedges' Clinical Procedures in Emergency Medicine and Acute Care, 7th ed. Elsevier; 2019 — Lateral Canthotomy.
