procedures.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol Activation & Sequencing
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Getting blood products moving before the lab catches up — ratio-based transfusion as a bridge to definitive hemorrhage control.
procedures.description: Ratio-based transfusion sequencing and logistics.

blocks.html: The protocol exists to be pulled early. Over-activation costs product; under-activation costs the patient.

Activate on any of these — do not wait for a lab value:

  • Critical Administration Threshold (CAT+): ≥3 units of red cells in any 60-minute period. This is the most useful real-time trigger — it is the one you can recognize while it is happening.
  • ABC score ≥2 (one point each): penetrating mechanism · SBP ≤90 · HR ≥120 · positive FAST.
  • Shock index (HR ÷ SBP) >1.0, and especially >1.4.
  • Anticipated ≥10 units in 24 h or ≥4 units in 1 h — the classic definitions, useful for audit, too slow to be a bedside trigger.
  • Clinical gestalt. A ruptured AAA, a mangled pelvis, a boggy uterus that will not contract, or bright blood filling a chest tube is enough. Pulling the trigger on a patient who turns out not to need it is a recoverable error.

Non-trauma activations matter just as much: obstetric hemorrhage, upper GI variceal bleeding, ruptured aneurysm, and post-operative surgical bleeding all belong here.

• None absolute in the presence of major hemorrhage.
  • Documented refusal of blood products. Follow the patient's stated wishes and your institution's policy. Have the alternative plan ready before you need it — cell salvage, TXA, fibrinogen concentrate, factor concentrates, and aggressive surgical control. Know which of these an individual patient does and does not accept; the categories are not uniform.
  • Uncontrolled surgical bleeding is not a transfusion problem. Product buys time to get to the OR, angiography suite, or the balloon. If activation is being used as a substitute for source control, the protocol will fail no matter how well it is run.
  • Futility. Massive transfusion in a patient with unsurvivable injury consumes a finite regional blood supply. This is a judgment call made early and explicitly, not one drifted into.

• The activation mechanism itself — one phone number or one order. Know it before the day you need it. The commonest delay in a massive transfusion is not the blood bank; it is the four minutes spent working out who to call.
  • Rapid infuser with integrated warmer (Belmont, Level 1, or equivalent) — capable of 500–1000 mL/min at 38 °C. A blood warmer on a gravity line is not a rapid infuser.
  • Two large-bore access points. Flow scales with the fourth power of radius and inversely with length: a short 14–16 G peripheral outperforms a long triple-lumen central line for volume. If central access is needed, use an introducer sheath (8.5 Fr), not a multi-lumen.
  • Forced-air warmer, warmed room, warmed fluids — hypothermia is generated by the resuscitation itself.
  • Point-of-care testing: blood gas with ionized calcium, lactate, hemoglobin; and viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) if available.
  • A whiteboard and a scribe. Product counts, time of activation, and calcium doses are all lost in real time without someone writing them down.
Ratios are prescribed so nobody has to calculate during the event.

rows: Red cells
6 units
Uncrossmatched O to start. O-negative for females of childbearing potential; O-positive is acceptable for males and post-menopausal females and protects a scarce O-neg supply.
Plasma (FFP / thawed)
6 units
Thawing takes 20–30 min unless pre-thawed plasma is stocked — this is the usual reason pack 1 arrives red-cell-heavy.
Platelets
1 apheresis unit
One apheresis unit ≈ 6 pooled units — this is what makes a 6:6:1 pack a “1:1:1” ratio. Miscounting this is how platelets get under-given.
Cryoprecipitate
Often not in pack 1
Must usually be asked for. See §06 — fibrinogen falls first and is the thing most often missed.
Whole blood (LTOWB)
Increasingly pack 1
Low-titer group O whole blood delivers the balanced ratio in a single bag with one venipuncture-equivalent of dilution. Where stocked, it is the simplest way to get the ratio right.

blocks.html: What PROPPR actually showed. 1:1:1 versus 1:1:2 produced no difference in 24-hour or 30-day all-cause mortality. What it did show: more patients achieved anatomic hemostasis, and fewer died of exsanguination in the first 24 hours, with 1:1:1. That is the basis for the default — a reasonable empiric starting ratio, not a proven mortality intervention. It is a bridge to goal-directed therapy, and should be abandoned for viscoelastic guidance as soon as you have data.
Pediatric dosing

• Red cells: 10–20 mL/kg per round
  • Plasma: 10–20 mL/kg
  • Platelets: 10–15 mL/kg
  • Cryoprecipitate: 5–10 mL/kg
  • Pediatric massive transfusion is commonly defined as >40 mL/kg of any product in 24 h, or >half the estimated blood volume in 3 h.
  • Children tolerate the citrate and potassium load of rapid transfusion worse than adults, not better. Calcium and potassium need checking sooner.

sections.title: Drugs That Go With the Blood

blocks.html: These are the doses. They are forgotten more often than the blood is.

rows: Tranexamic acid — trauma
1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h
Within 3 hours of injury. Beyond 3 hours CRASH-2 showed a signal of harm — check the clock, not just the bleeding. Rapid push causes hypotension.
Tranexamic acid — postpartum
1 g IV over 10 min; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24 h
WOMAN trial. Same 3-hour window from onset of bleeding.
Tranexamic acid — pediatric
15 mg/kg (max 1 g) over 10 min, then 2 mg/kg/h
Extrapolated dosing; confirm locally.
Calcium chloride 10%
1 g (10 mL) = 13.6 mEq elemental Ca

Roughly 1 g per 4 units of product, or empirically with pack 1. Three times the elemental calcium of gluconate per gram. Sclerosant — prefer a central or large vein, but do not withhold it for that reason in exsanguination.
Calcium gluconate 10%
3 g (30 mL) = 13.6 mEq elemental Ca
Peripheral-friendly equivalent. Requires hepatic metabolism to liberate calcium — less reliable in the shocked, acidotic liver.
Calcium — pediatric
CaCl 20 mg/kg or Ca gluconate 60 mg/kg
Same trigger: ionized calcium, or empirically per pack.
Fibrinogen (cryoprecipitate)
10 pooled units (raises fibrinogen ~50–100 mg/dL)
When fibrinogen <150 mg/dL, or <200 in obstetric hemorrhage. See §06.
Fibrinogen concentrate
Where stocked — no thaw time, no ABO matching, smaller volume.
Anticoagulant reversal
Agent-specific
Ask about DOACs and warfarin on every bleeding patient. Reversal is a separate decision tree — see the anticoagulant reversal protocol; do not improvise doses here.

blocks.title: Hypocalcemia is the fourth point of the diamond
blocks.html: Every unit of product carries citrate, which chelates ionized calcium. Ionized calcium <0.9 mmol/L on arrival independently predicts mortality and the need for massive transfusion. Calcium is required for platelet function and for nearly every step of the coagulation cascade — you cannot clot without it, and no amount of plasma substitutes for it. It is also negatively inotropic when low. Give calcium with the first pack and recheck the ionized level every 30 minutes; target >1.1–1.2 mmol/L.

rows: Ionized calcium
>1.1–1.2 mmol/L
<1.1 — and empirically with pack 1 regardless
Fibrinogen
>150 mg/dL (>200 obstetric)
<150 → cryoprecipitate or concentrate
Platelets
>50 ×10<sup>9</sup>/L; >100 with TBI or ongoing bleeding
<50, or <100 with head injury
INR / PT ratio
>1.5 → plasma (slow signal — viscoelastic is faster)
Temperature
Always — warm everything, all the time
pH / base deficit
pH >7.2
Worsening base deficit means ongoing bleeding, not a bicarbonate problem
Potassium
<5.5 mmol/L
Rising with rapid transfusion of older units — especially in children
Blood pressure (pre-control)
Except TBI or spinal cord injury: SBP ≥110, MAP ≥80

blocks.html:
Reading viscoelastic tests quickly. The point of TEG/ROTEM here is not elegance — it is that each abnormality maps to one bag.

  • Prolonged R time (TEG) / CT (EXTEM) → not enough clotting factors → plasma (or PCC in the anticoagulated).
  • Narrow alpha angle, prolonged K / low FIBTEM A10 → not enough fibrinogen → cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.
  • Low MA (TEG) / low EXTEM A10 with normal FIBTEM → not enough platelets → platelets.
  • LY30 >3% / increased maximum lysis → hyperfibrinolysis → TXA.

Permissive hypotension until hemorrhage is controlled: a clot formed at SBP 85 survives; the same clot is blown off at SBP 140. The exceptions are absolute — a brain or cord that is also injured needs perfusion pressure more than it needs a protected clot.

Crystalloid is not resuscitation. Keep it under 1 L before blood arrives, and ideally near zero. It dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis, drops the temperature, and raises pressure enough to displace clot — four harms, no benefit.

steps.title: Activate out loud, and name the person
steps.html: “I am activating massive transfusion. [Name], you are calling the blood bank.” Undirected instructions in a full room get executed by nobody. State the location, the patient identifier, and that this is an MTP activation.

steps.title: Assign the four jobs
steps.html: Blood bank liaison (the only person who talks to blood bank, and who keeps the runner moving) · Rapid infuser operator (does nothing else) · Scribe (units in, times, calcium doses, labs sent) · Team leader (source control and the decision to keep going). One person cannot hold two of these.

steps.title: Start uncrossmatched now, send the type and screen simultaneously
steps.html: Do not hold the first unit waiting for a crossmatch. Send the sample at the same moment the emergency-release blood is hung, so the switch to type-specific product is ready when the initial supply runs down.

steps.title: Give TXA and calcium with pack 1
steps.html: Both are time-sensitive and both are the things that get remembered at minute 40. Check the injury clock for the 3-hour TXA window before giving it.

steps.title: Warm everything
steps.html: Infuser warmer on and verified at temperature, forced-air blanket over whatever is not exposed, room heat up, wet clothing cut off and removed. Hypothermia here is iatrogenic and it is the leg of the lethal triad you have the most direct control over.

steps.title: Get labs at activation and every 30–60 minutes
steps.html: Blood gas with ionized calcium, CBC, fibrinogen, PT/INR, and viscoelastic if available. Fibrinogen specifically — it is not on a standard coagulation panel at many sites and it is the first thing to fail.

steps.title: Drive toward source control the whole time
steps.html: OR, interventional radiology, endoscopy, balloon tamponade, a binder, a tourniquet, uterotonics. Every round of product is a question about why the bleeding has not stopped. If the answer is “we are still waiting for the OR,” escalate that instead of hanging another unit.

steps.title: Deactivate explicitly, and return the cooler
steps.html: Call blood bank and say the protocol is off. Unopened coolers go back promptly — units held at the bedside past their window are destroyed, and a regional supply is finite. This step is skipped constantly.

rows: Product arrives but nothing is going in fast
Access is the limit — long, narrow catheters
Place a short large-bore peripheral or an 8.5 Fr introducer. Not a triple lumen.
Pack 1 is all red cells, no plasma
Plasma is still thawing
Expected. Ask whether pre-thawed plasma or LTOWB exists. Do not slow the red cells waiting.
Bleeding from every puncture site and mucosa
Established coagulopathy — usually fibrinogen and calcium
Cryoprecipitate and calcium now, do not wait for the panel. Send viscoelastic.
Pressure won't come up despite volume
Ongoing bleeding you have not found — or a non-hemorrhagic cause
Reassess the four spaces (chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long bones and the floor). Rule out tension pneumothorax and tamponade — both mimic refractory hemorrhagic shock.
Sudden arrest mid-transfusion
Hyperkalemia or profound ionized hypocalcemia from rapid product delivery
Calcium immediately. Treat hyperkalemia. This is more common with older units, rapid central infusion, and children.
Widening QRS, peaked T waves
Hyperkalemia from stored red cells
Calcium, insulin/dextrose, consider washed or fresher units for continued transfusion.
Temperature falling despite a warmer
Warmer not at temperature, or bypassed by a side line
Verify the warmer is actually in circuit and the display is at target. Cover everything else.
Hypotension right after TXA
Pushed too fast
TXA goes over 10 minutes. Slow it.
Hypoxia and infiltrates within 6 h
TRALI or TACO
Supportive care and respiratory support; distinguish by volume status and response to diuresis. Report the reaction — it changes future product selection.
Blood bank says they are out
Regional supply limit reached

This is a command decision, not a clinical one: escalate to the blood bank medical director and consider transfer, damage-control surgery now rather than later, and an explicit goals-of-care conversation.

blocks.html:
• Hypothermia — worsens platelet function and enzyme kinetics. Largely iatrogenic and largely preventable.
  • Ionized hypocalcemia — citrate-driven; causes coagulopathy, hypotension, and arrest. The single most under-treated complication of massive transfusion.
  • Hyperkalemia — potassium leaks from stored red cells; risk scales with unit age, infusion rate, and inversely with patient size.
  • Dilutional coagulopathy — from crystalloid and from red-cell-heavy ratios.
  • Metabolic alkalosis — a late effect as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate.
  • TRALI (within 6 h, non-cardiogenic infiltrates) and TACO (volume overload) — both present as post-transfusion hypoxia and are distinguished mainly by volume status.
  • Acute hemolytic reaction — rare with emergency-release O product; the real risk is a mislabeled sample. Two-person identity verification does not stop during a resuscitation.
  • Transfusion-associated immunomodulation and infection risk — dose-dependent, and a reason to stop when bleeding stops.
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome after large-volume resuscitation — measure bladder pressure if the abdomen becomes tense and oliguria or high airway pressures develop.

Three units in an hour is your trigger. Of all the scores, CAT+ is the one you can actually notice in real time.

Calcium with the first pack, every time. It is the most commonly omitted and most rapidly lethal deficiency in the whole protocol, and it is one syringe.

Check the clock before giving TXA. Within 3 hours it helps; beyond it, the trial data point the other way. Bleeding alone is not the indication — timing is.

One apheresis platelet equals six units. Miscount this and your “1:1:1” is a 6:6:6 — wildly over-plateleted — or you give six pooled bags thinking you are behind.

Fibrinogen fails first and is measured last. Order it explicitly; it is absent from many default coagulation panels.

Short and fat beats long and central. A 14 G peripheral moves more blood than a triple-lumen. If you want central, place an introducer sheath.

Keep the pressure low until the bleeding stops — unless the brain or cord is injured, where perfusion wins.

Every unit is a question about source control. The protocol is a bridge to an operation, an embolization, or a balloon. It is not a destination.

Deactivate and send the cooler back. Unglamorous, constantly forgotten, and the difference between a functioning regional blood supply and a depleted one.

items.html: Holcomb JB, Tilley BC, Baraniuk S, et al. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(5):471–482.

CRASH-2 Collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage: a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9734):23–32.
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Effect of early tranexamic acid administration on mortality, hysterectomy, and other morbidities in women with post-partum haemorrhage. Lancet. 2017;389(10084):2105–2116.
Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma, 6th edition. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):80.
Nunez TC, Voskresensky IV, Dossett LA, Shinall R, Dutton WD, Cotton BA. Early prediction of massive transfusion in trauma: simple as ABC? J Trauma. 2009;66(2):346–352.
American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma. Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual, 10th ed. ACS; 2018.
Your institution's own MTP pack composition, activation number, and deactivation procedure. These vary substantially — confirm the local specifics before you need them.

procedures.title: Pelvic Binder Placement
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Circumferential stabilization at the level of the greater trochanters — closing volume in an unstable pelvic ring fracture before hemorrhage becomes uncontrollable.
procedures.description: Circumferential stabilization at the greater trochanters.

blocks.html:
• Any hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient with a mechanism that could break a pelvis. This is the important one — it is an empiric indication, applied before imaging and before examination confirms anything.
  • Clinical signs of pelvic ring disruption: instability felt on a single gentle examination, leg-length discrepancy, external rotation of a limb, perineal or scrotal hematoma, blood at the urethral meatus, an open perineal wound
  • Radiographic pelvic ring disruption on a trauma film or CT, if one is not already on
  • Traumatic arrest or peri-arrest from blunt mechanism — part of the same reflex as bilateral thoracostomies
  • During transfer or extrication of any patient with a suspected pelvic injury, whether or not they are currently unstable

A binder costs almost nothing to apply and almost nothing to be wrong about. The asymmetry is the whole argument: binding a pelvis that turns out to be intact is a non-event; failing to bind one that is disrupted is a preventable death.

• None absolute in suspected pelvic disruption with shock.
  • It will not help an isolated hip dislocation, an isolated femoral neck fracture, or an acetabular fracture with an intact ring. A binder closes a ring; if the ring is not open, there is nothing to close.
  • Lateral compression (LC) patterns are already internally rotated, so a binder adds little and could theoretically over-compress. In practice this is not distinguishable at the bedside or in the field, and current guidance is to bind anyway — the theoretical harm has not materialized in the literature, and the cost of withholding in an open-book injury is very real.
  • Vertical shear patterns will not be reduced by circumferential compression alone; they need longitudinal traction and definitive fixation. Bind anyway, but know the binder is not the answer.
  • Skin already compromised at the level of the trochanters — degloving, burn, open fracture. Apply anyway if the patient is bleeding, and flag it loudly for early removal.

• A commercial binder — SAM Pelvic Sling, T-POD, Prometheus, or your service's equivalent. The advantage is not the fabric; it is that these devices self-limit tension at approximately 180 N, which is enough to close a ring and not enough to cause pressure injury quickly. A buckle that clicks and stops is doing something a sheet cannot.
  • A folded bed sheet as the improvised version — effective, universally available, and with one real drawback: you cannot control or reproduce the tension. Fold to about 20–25 cm wide, cross the ends, and secure with clamps or a tied knot.
  • Tape or a triangular bandage to bind the knees and ankles together — this is part of the procedure, not an optional extra (see §05).
  • Trauma shears. Everything comes off from under the binder first; see the warning below.
  • A marker for the application time.

blocks.title: Empty the pockets before you close the binder
blocks.html: A phone, a set of keys, a belt buckle, a holster, or a wallet trapped under a binder at the trochanter becomes a focal pressure point on a shocked, hypoperfused, immobile patient. Pressure necrosis over that object can begin within a couple of hours and will not be found until the binder comes off. Cut the clothing away and sweep the field with your hand before you tighten.
The most common application error, and it is not a small one.

A binder works by internally rotating both hemipelves around the femoral heads, which closes an opened symphysis, reduces pelvic volume, and lets a tamponading hematoma reach a pressure at which it stops growing. That rotation is generated by squeezing at the widest transverse point of the pelvis — the greater trochanters.

Placed at the iliac crests instead, the binder squeezes above the axis of rotation. It does not close the symphysis — and it can lever the ring further open. It also sits on bone with almost no soft-tissue cover, so it produces skin injury faster while achieving less. A binder at the belt line looks correct in a photograph and does nothing.

How to find the level without thinking: the greater trochanters sit roughly in line with the pubic symphysis, which is far lower than instinct suggests — about the level of the front trouser pocket, not the waistband. Palpate the bony prominence on the lateral hip and put the middle of the binder there.

rows: APC — anteroposterior compression (“open book”)
Symphysis sprung open, volume increased
Yes — this is the pattern it is designed for. Reduces volume and restores tamponade.
LC — lateral compression
Hemipelvis driven inward, already internally rotated
Limited mechanical benefit. Bind anyway — you cannot tell the patterns apart at the bedside and the harm is theoretical.
VS — vertical shear
Hemipelvis displaced cephalad
Partially. Needs traction and external fixation. Bind, but escalate.
Combined
Mixed
Bind.

steps.title: Examine the pelvis once, gently — or not at all
steps.html: One careful assessment, and only if it will change what you do. Never spring the pelvis, and never re-check it. Repeated manipulation shears the clot that is the only thing containing a pelvic venous hemorrhage. If a binder is going on regardless — which for an unstable patient it is — the examination adds risk and no information. Assess once, bind, then leave it alone.

steps.title: Strip and sweep the field
steps.html: Cut clothing away from the hips. Sweep with your hand for phones, keys, buckles, and debris. Log-roll only if necessary and only once — or slide the binder under the natural hollow at the knees and walk it up beneath the buttocks, which avoids rolling entirely.

steps.title: Position at the greater trochanters
steps.html: The middle of the binder sits over the trochanters, level with the pubic symphysis. Check both sides — a binder that is correct on one hip and rides up on the other is applying an asymmetric force. If the device has a marked center, put it on the symphysis.

steps.title: Internally rotate the legs and tie them together
steps.html: Bring the legs into slight internal rotation — toes pointing at each other — and bind the knees and ankles with tape or a bandage before tightening. The femurs are levers on the femoral heads; internal rotation at the feet closes the ring from the other end. This step takes fifteen seconds, contributes real reduction, and is skipped almost every time.

steps.title: Tighten to the device's stop — not to maximum force
steps.html: Pull the straps evenly from both sides and let the buckle click. Snug and symmetric, not crushing. Over-tightening does not close the ring any further once it is reduced; it just injures skin and, in lateral compression patterns, risks over-reduction. With an improvised sheet you have no stop, so aim for firm and even, and re-check the skin more often.

steps.title: Leave a window for the groin — deliberately
steps.html: This patient will very likely need femoral arterial or venous access, and may need a REBOA sheath or angiography. Position the binder so the femoral triangles remain reachable, and say out loud that it is in place, because the next person to look will find the landmarks covered and lose time working out why.

steps.title: Check distal perfusion, then write the time on it
steps.html: Pulses, color, capillary refill in both legs. Then write the application time on the binder itself in marker. The dwell-time clock has started and nobody downstream will know when unless you record it now.

sections.title: What the Binder Actually Stops — and What It Doesn't

blocks.html:
Most pelvic bleeding is venous and cancellous bone — the presacral venous plexus and the raw fracture surfaces. That bleeding is low-pressure and self-tamponading if the pelvic volume stays small enough for a hematoma to build pressure. This is exactly what a binder restores, and it is why a binder works at all.

Arterial bleeding does not care about a binder. A torn internal iliac branch bleeds at systemic pressure into a space the binder has narrowed but not closed. If the patient remains unstable after the binder is on and other sources are excluded, the binder has done its job and reached its ceiling.

The escalation ladder from there:

  • Angiography and embolization — the definitive answer for arterial pelvic bleeding where it is available quickly
  • Preperitoneal pelvic packing — surgical, fast, and the better option where angiography is slow or the patient cannot survive the trip. The binder stays on for it.
  • External fixation — mechanical stability, usually alongside one of the above
  • REBOA Zone 3 — infrarenal occlusion as a bridge, sparing the kidneys and gut
  • Massive transfusion and TXA running throughout

The practical point: a binder that is on and correct, in a patient who is still unstable, is not a reason to reapply the binder. It is the signal to move to the next rung.

rows: Binder on, no improvement in pressure
Placed at the iliac crests, not the trochanters
Look at the level. This is the first thing to check and the most likely error. Reposition once, correctly.
Correctly placed, still unstable
Arterial pelvic bleeding, or a second source entirely
Binder has reached its ceiling. Escalate (§06). Re-examine chest, abdomen, and long bones — and the floor.
Binder keeps riding upward
Applied over clothing, or the patient is being moved a lot
Strip to skin. Re-seat at the trochanters and secure the legs together, which helps hold it.
Asymmetric, tight on one side
Uneven pull during tightening
Release and re-tension evenly from both sides simultaneously. Asymmetric force can displace a fracture.
Skin blistering under the binder
Pressure injury — or an object trapped underneath
If an object: it must come out. Otherwise this is a hard prompt to get to definitive fixation and off the binder.
Team asks to remove it for CT
Misconception — it stays on
Do not remove a binder for imaging. Scan through it. A reduced pelvis on CT is the expected appearance and the radiologist should be told a binder is on.
Cannot find the femoral pulse for access
Binder covering the groin
Reposition slightly caudad or use ultrasound through the available window. Plan the window when you apply it.
Blood at the meatus, urine needed
Possible urethral injury
Do not force a urethral catheter. Urology input; suprapubic drainage if needed.
Fracture looks worse on the post-binder film
Almost always an LC pattern being over-compressed — rare
Discuss with orthopedics before loosening anything. Do not loosen a binder in an unstable patient on imaging appearance alone.

blocks.html:
• Pressure necrosis over the trochanters and sacrum — the dominant complication. In a shocked, hypothermic, immobile patient, skin injury can begin within 2–3 hours. Objects trapped underneath accelerate it dramatically.
  • Ineffective reduction from incorrect level — not a complication of the device so much as of its application, and the commonest reason a binder fails.
  • Over-compression of a lateral compression fracture — theoretical, rarely demonstrated, and not a reason to withhold.
  • Delayed recognition of ongoing arterial bleeding, because the binder is on and looks like an intervention that should have worked.
  • Obscured vascular access and delayed femoral cannulation.
  • Missed injuries under the binder — open perineal wounds and degloving are hidden the moment it goes on, which is an argument for a quick look before tightening.
  • Clot disruption from repeated pelvic examination — a complication of the assessment, not the binder, and entirely avoidable.

• It stays on until orthopedics or trauma surgery removes it — through the trauma bay, through CT, through transfer, and into the operating room. Nobody loosens it “to have a look.”
  • Target removal or conversion to definitive fixation within about 24 hours, and sooner in a patient who is hypoperfused, since that is the window in which skin injury accumulates.
  • Inspect the skin at the first safe opportunity, in a controlled setting, with orthopedics present and the ability to re-apply.
  • Handover the application time explicitly. Written on the binder, stated out loud, and in the note. A binder whose start time is unknown gets managed as if it has been on longer than it has, or worse, shorter.
  • Tell the receiving team it is on at all. Under a blanket, on a shocked patient in a busy resuscitation, a correctly applied binder is genuinely easy to miss.

Greater trochanters, level with the symphysis. Lower than instinct says. This single fact accounts for most binder failures.

Bind empirically. Unstable, blunt, plausible mechanism — that is enough. Do not wait for a film.

Examine once, then never again. Springing a pelvis buys no information and shears the clot holding the patient together.

Tie the knees and ankles. Fifteen seconds, real reduction, almost always skipped.

Sweep the pockets. A phone under a binder is a pressure ulcer with a start time.

Snug, not crushing, and symmetric. The commercial devices stop at the right tension on purpose.

Leave the groin reachable. This patient is going to need femoral access, and probably angiography.

Do not take it off for the CT.

Still unstable with a correct binder means escalate, not retighten. Angiography, packing, external fixation, Zone 3.

Write the time on it.

procedures.footer: Built for rapid recall under pressure, not as a substitute for institutional protocol or real-time specialist consultation during a live event. Verify technique and equipment against your own institution's protocol before clinical use.

procedures.title: Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Zone selection, balloon inflation, and the discipline of treating occlusion time as a hard clock. A bridge to hemorrhage control, not a treatment in itself.
procedures.description: Zone 1/3 aortic occlusion for non-compressible torso hemorrhage.

blocks.html:
• Non-compressible torso hemorrhage — pelvic, junctional, or intra-abdominal — with shock refractory to initial resuscitation
  • Peri-arrest from suspected sub-diaphragmatic bleeding: SBP <70–80 mmHg despite product, or a patient losing their pulse in front of you with a mechanism that fits
  • Bridge to definitive control in a patient who will not survive transport, induction of anesthesia, or the walk to CT without proximal aortic control
  • An alternative to resuscitative thoracotomy in a patient who still has a rhythm and a blood pressure — it achieves aortic occlusion without opening the chest
  • Non-trauma uses: ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm as a bridge to repair, and refractory postpartum hemorrhage (Zone 3), where it is an established adjunct in some centers

blocks.title: Survival benefit is not established — this is a bridge, not a proven mortality intervention
blocks.html: The 2023 UK-REBOA trial randomized exsanguinating trauma patients to standard care with or without REBOA and found no survival benefit, with numerically higher mortality in the REBOA arm. Earlier support came almost entirely from registry data (AAST AORTA) and non-randomized comparisons, which carry real selection bias — the patients who die fastest never reach REBOA at all, which flatters its apparent outcomes.

• Suspected thoracic aortic injury or dissection proximal to the intended zone. A balloon inflated in a dissected aorta can extend the dissection or rupture it.
  • Hemorrhage above the diaphragm. Occluding below a thoracic source does not control it — it raises the pressure driving it, and it costs you the minutes in which you might have found it. A chest that is bleeding gets a thoracostomy and a thoracotomy, not a balloon.
  • Cardiac arrest from a non-hemorrhagic cause. REBOA does not replace compressions, defibrillation, or reversing the cause.
  • Prolonged arrest with no signs of life and no realistic path to control — the same futility judgment that governs thoracotomy.
  • No obtainable common femoral access — bilateral vascular injury or destroyed groins.
  • No definitive control available. If there is no OR, no interventional radiology, and no transfer plan, the balloon buys ischemic time for no purpose. Do not inflate a balloon you have no plan to deflate.
  • Pediatric patients — not established; catheter and sheath sizes do not fit small vessels.

• REBOA catheter. Current low-profile systems (ER-REBOA and partial-occlusion variants) run through a 7 Fr sheath and carry an integrated distal pressure port — a significant advantage, because it lets you transduce proximally and distally without a second line. Older compliant occlusion balloons need 11–12 Fr, which changes the access and closure problem entirely.
  • Sheath matched to the catheter. Note the length — the sheath length counts against your insertion depth measurement.
  • Ultrasound with a linear probe. The access is the procedure; see §05.
  • Guidewire (0.035″ for most systems), and a stiffer exchange wire if you plan to upsize.
  • Two transducers — proximal (the catheter's own port, or a radial line) and distal (the sheath side-arm). The proximal/distal pressure pair is how you know the balloon is working, and it is what makes partial occlusion possible.
  • Saline for inflation — or dilute contrast if fluoroscopy is available. Never air. An air-filled balloon that ruptures embolizes air into the aorta and onward to brain and coronaries; a saline balloon that ruptures does nothing.
  • Syringes with fine graduations (a 20 mL syringe, ideally a Luer-lock) — balloon volumes are small and the difference between occlusion and over-inflation is a couple of milliliters.
  • Plain radiograph capability or fluoroscopy for position confirmation. A portable chest or abdominal film in the resuscitation bay is usually achievable and is worth taking.
  • A visible clock or timer, started at inflation. See §07.
  • Cutdown tray as the access backup — and as what you will need at the end to take the sheath out.

blocks.alt: The three REBOA aortic zones. Zone 1 runs from the origin of the left subclavian artery down to the celiac axis and is used for intra-abdominal bleeding or peri-arrest, with a target occlusion time of thirty minutes or less, measured externally to the sternal notch at roughly forty-five to fifty centimeters. Zone 2 runs from the celiac axis to the lowest renal artery and is a no-fly zone, because a balloon there crosses the celiac, superior mesenteric and renal origins without the benefit of proximal control. Zone 3 runs from the lowest renal artery to the aortic bifurcation and is used for pelvic or junctional bleeding and postpartum hemorrhage, tolerating up to sixty minutes, measured externally to the umbilicus at roughly twenty-seven to thirty centimeters.
blocks.caption: Zone 1 buys the most pressure at the highest cost: every abdominal organ, both kidneys and the cord sit downstream. Zone 3 spares all of them. If the proximal pressure does not rise on inflation, the balloon is under-inflated, malpositioned — or the bleeding is above it.

rows: Zone 1 (supraceliac)
Origin of the left subclavian → celiac axis
Intra-abdominal hemorrhage; peri-arrest from any sub-diaphragmatic source. The functional equivalent of a cross-clamp at thoracotomy.
Aim ≤30 min; 15–20 is better. Every abdominal and pelvic organ plus both kidneys is downstream.
Zone 2 (visceral)
Celiac axis → lowest renal artery
Nothing. This is the “no-fly” zone. A balloon here occludes across the origins of the celiac, SMA, and renal arteries without the benefit of full proximal control.
Zone 3 (infrarenal)
Lowest renal artery → aortic bifurcation
Isolated pelvic or junctional hemorrhage; postpartum hemorrhage. Spares the kidneys, gut, liver, and cord.
Substantially longer — up to 60 min, and beyond with care. Only the pelvis and legs are ischemic.

blocks.html:
Choosing between them. Zone 3 is safer and should be used whenever the source is clearly pelvic — an unstable pelvic fracture with a binder on and a negative FAST. Zone 1 is for an intra-abdominal source, an uncertain source in extremis, or a patient who is arresting. Zone 1 buys more pressure at much higher cost.

Getting the depth. External measurement is the usual method in a resuscitation bay. Lay the catheter on the patient from the access site and read off the target landmark:

  • Zone 1: to the sternal notch / manubrium — roughly 45–50 cm in an adult
  • Zone 3: to the umbilicus (or just above it) — roughly 27–30 cm

Protocols vary in which landmark they cite, and body habitus shifts both. Confirm the position radiographically whenever you can — on a plain film, the balloon in Zone 1 should sit at the level of the mid-to-lower thoracic vertebrae, and in Zone 3 below the renal arteries around L2–L3. Treat the external measurement as the starting estimate and the pressure response as the functional check.
Access is the procedure. Everything that follows is quick; the femoral artery is where REBOA succeeds or fails.

steps.title: Get the arterial line in before you need the balloon
steps.html: The highest-value operational habit in REBOA has nothing to do with the balloon. Place a common femoral arterial line early in any shocked trauma patient — it gives you real-time pressure you need anyway, and if REBOA becomes necessary it converts a difficult new puncture in a pulseless patient into a straightforward wire exchange and upsize. Teams that do this reliably get balloons up in a few minutes; teams that don't spend those minutes hunting a femoral pulse that no longer exists.

steps.title: Target the common femoral artery, under ultrasound
steps.html: Puncture below the inguinal ligament but above the bifurcation into superficial and profunda femoris. A sheath in the superficial femoral artery is too big for the vessel and produces limb ischemia and thrombosis. Above the ligament, a failed puncture bleeds into the retroperitoneum. That is a narrow window, and in a pulseless patient ultrasound is the only way to find it — look for the vessel before it divides, image the bifurcation and come up from it.

steps.title: If ultrasound access fails, cut down early
steps.html: Set a limit in advance — two or three passes, or 90 seconds — and then convert to a femoral cutdown. The commonest way REBOA fails is not a technical error at the balloon but ten minutes burned on percutaneous attempts in a vessel with no pressure in it. Decide the escalation point before you start, out loud.

steps.title: Sheath in, transduce the side-arm
steps.html: Place the sheath over the wire. Connect the side-arm to a transducer — this is your distal pressure, and it will be the thing that tells you the balloon is occluding and, later, the thing that lets you run partial occlusion.

steps.title: Measure, then advance to the zone
steps.html: Choose the zone (§04), measure externally from the access site, and mark the catheter. Advance smoothly — it should pass with no resistance. Resistance means the wire or catheter has found a branch vessel or a dissection plane. Stop, withdraw, reassess. Do not push through resistance in an aorta.

steps.title: Inflate slowly, watching two numbers
steps.html: Inflate with saline in 1–2 mL increments while watching the proximal pressure rise and the distal waveform flatten. Typical volumes: Zone 1 ≈ 8–10 mL, Zone 3 ≈ 2–6 mL — but the endpoint is the pressure response, not the volume. Stop at the minimum volume that achieves occlusion. Over-inflation risks aortic injury and rupture, and the aorta of a young exsanguinating trauma patient is small and empty.

steps.title: Confirm, and start the clock out loud
steps.html: Occlusion is confirmed by a rising proximal MAP and loss of the distal arterial waveform and femoral signal. Then say it to the room: “Balloon up at 14:32, Zone 1. I will call it out every five minutes.” Write it on the board. The clock is the safety system — see §07.

steps.title: Go to definitive control now
steps.html: The moment the balloon is up, the only remaining question is where the bleeding gets stopped and how soon. OR, angiography suite, pelvic packing, preperitoneal packing. Every minute of inflation should be a minute of movement toward that. A stable patient with a balloon up is not a stable patient; they are an ischemic patient with a normal-looking monitor.

blocks.html:
Complete occlusion maximizes proximal pressure and maximizes distal ischemia. The refinement that has come out of the last decade is to give up some of the first to buy a great deal of the second.

  • Partial REBOA (pREBOA): deflate back from full occlusion until a small amount of distal flow returns — titrating to a target such as a proximal MAP around 80–90 mmHg, or a measurable distal systolic pressure. Distal perfusion continues at a reduced rate, the acid and potassium load accumulates more slowly, and the safe dwell extends substantially. This requires a distal transducer and continuous attention: a partial balloon drifts, and one that drifts closed is a full occlusion nobody is timing.
  • Intermittent REBOA (iREBOA): cycles of inflation and deflation. Simpler to do without a distal transducer, but each deflation produces a hemodynamic swing and can dislodge fresh clot. Generally the less favored of the two.
  • Purpose-built partial-occlusion catheters exist and make the titration far more controllable than throttling a standard compliant balloon by hand.

If your service is going to do REBOA at all, partial occlusion with distal pressure monitoring is the version most likely to do more good than harm — but it demands a dedicated person watching two pressures and nothing else.
Deflation is more dangerous than inflation, and it is the part people prepare for least.

blocks.title: Inflation time is the entire safety margin
blocks.html: Everything distal to the balloon is ischemic from the second it goes up, and the reperfusion injury is proportional to the dwell. Zone 1: target under 30 minutes, and treat 15–20 as the aspiration. Zone 3 is far more forgiving — up to an hour and sometimes beyond — because only the pelvis and legs are at stake. Announce the time every five minutes. Nobody should be surprised at minute 30, and in practice they are, because in a busy resuscitation nobody owns the clock unless someone is told to.

Before you deflate, have all of this ready:

  • The surgeon present and the source controlled or controllable
  • Blood products running, not ordered
  • Vasopressors drawn up and connected
  • Calcium ready — the reperfusion washout carries potassium and acid, and calcium is both the antiarrhythmic and the inotrope for that moment
  • Consideration of sodium bicarbonate for the acid load
  • A current potassium if you can get one

Then deflate in 1–2 mL increments, over minutes, watching the pressure. If the pressure falls, stop — and re-inflate if it collapses. You can go back up. The washout of lactate, potassium, and inflammatory mediators from ischemic viscera and limbs can cause profound vasoplegia, arrhythmia, and arrest, and the magnitude scales with how long the balloon was up and how fast you let it down. A fast deflation after a long Zone 1 occlusion can kill a patient whose bleeding you have just successfully stopped.

rows: No femoral pulse to puncture
Profound shock — expected, not a reason to stop
Ultrasound. If two or three passes fail, cut down rather than continuing to probe.
Wire or catheter meets resistance
Branch vessel, tortuosity, or a dissection plane
Stop. Withdraw and redirect. Never force a wire in an aorta.
Balloon inflated, proximal pressure does not rise
Three possibilities, in order: under-inflated; malpositioned (too low, or in an iliac); or the bleeding is above the balloon

Add 1–2 mL. Check distal waveform is truly lost. Confirm position on film. If pressure still doesn't rise, strongly consider a thoracic source — reassess the chest, get a film, and think about thoracotomy.
Distal waveform persists after inflation
Incomplete occlusion, or the balloon is in an iliac with flow down the other side
Verify position. A balloon in one iliac occludes one leg and nothing else.
Proximal pressure rises then falls again
Balloon migration, a leak, or continued bleeding outrunning the occlusion
Check the inflation volume has held; re-transduce; get a film. Consider that the source is above.
Sudden loss of balloon resistance / syringe empties
Balloon rupture
This is why you inflate with saline. Do not inflate further. Withdraw the catheter as a unit. Decide immediately whether to replace it or convert to thoracotomy.
Collapse during deflation
Reperfusion washout — potassium, acid, vasodilatory mediators
Re-inflate. Give calcium, product, pressors. Then come down more slowly.
Leg mottled and pulseless after the sheath is in
Sheath thrombosis or SFA placement
Vascular surgery now. This is limb-threatening and it is a common REBOA complication, not a rare one.
Anuria and a rising creatinine post-procedure
Renal ischemia from Zone 1 occlusion, plus rhabdomyolysis
Expected consequence to monitor for, not a surprise. Check CK and potassium; support the kidneys.
Tense, painful legs hours later
Reperfusion compartment syndrome
Serial compartment checks are mandatory after any lower-body ischemic interval. Low threshold for fasciotomy.

blocks.html:
• Ischemia–reperfusion injury — the dominant harm, proportional to dwell time and zone. Acute kidney injury, gut ischemia, hepatic injury, rhabdomyolysis, spinal cord ischemia with Zone 1, and a systemic inflammatory response that outlasts the procedure by days.
  • Limb ischemia, thrombosis, and amputation — from the sheath itself, from a superficial femoral puncture, or from the occlusion interval. Reported in a meaningful fraction of cases; the larger the sheath, the higher the rate.
  • Access-site complications — pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, dissection, retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a high puncture.
  • Aortic injury or rupture from over-inflation, particularly in a small, empty, young aorta.
  • Balloon rupture or migration.
  • Reperfusion arrest on deflation — hyperkalemia, acidemia, and vasoplegia arriving together.
  • Compartment syndrome of the legs after reperfusion.
  • Missed proximal injury — the most consequential cognitive error. Occluding below an undiagnosed thoracic source delays the correct operation while the patient keeps bleeding.
  • Sheath removal problems — a 7–12 Fr arterial sheath is not pulled at the bedside and forgotten. It needs a closure device or surgical repair, and a plan made in advance.

• The sheath needs an owner and a plan. Percutaneous closure device or open repair, by vascular or trauma surgery. Document who is responsible and when it comes out. Sheaths left in overnight because nobody owned them are a recognized source of limb loss.
  • Hourly limb assessment — pulses (Doppler if not palpable), color, temperature, capillary refill, and compartment tension in both legs. An ankle-brachial index once the patient is stable.
  • Serial potassium, lactate, creatinine, CK, and blood gas. Hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis are expected after a substantial ischemic interval, not incidental findings.
  • Urine output and color — pigmented urine means myoglobin; start fluids and follow CK.
  • Record the occlusion interval precisely — zone, inflation time, deflation time, partial-occlusion periods. Every downstream team needs this number and it cannot be reconstructed later.
  • Watch for delayed gut and cord injury after Zone 1 — abdominal examination, lactate trend, and a neurologic assessment of the legs once sedation allows. Paraplegia after Zone 1 occlusion is rare but real.

Put a femoral arterial line in early. The single change that makes REBOA achievable is having the access already there, so the balloon is an upsize and not a puncture.

If the proximal pressure doesn't rise, suspect a chest. A correctly placed, properly inflated balloon raises pressure. When it doesn't, the most important possibility is that you are occluding below the bleeding.

Zone 3 whenever the source is pelvic. It costs you less pressure and buys a far longer safe window.

Zone 2 is a no-fly zone. All of the visceral cost, none of the proximal benefit.

Saline, never air. A ruptured saline balloon is an inconvenience; a ruptured air balloon is an arterial air embolism.

Inflate to the pressure, not to the volume. Stop at the least volume that occludes. The published volumes are a range, not a target.

Own the clock out loud. Zone 1 under 30 minutes, called every five. This is a communication task, and it is the one that fails.

Deflation needs more preparation than inflation. Blood up, pressors connected, calcium drawn, surgeon present, and come down a milliliter at a time.

Cut down early rather than probe long. Set the escalation point before you start.

Somebody owns the sheath. Name them before you leave the resuscitation bay.

A balloon buys time and nothing else. The moment it is up, the only meaningful activity in the room is getting to definitive control.

procedures.title: Wound Packing with Hemostatic Agents
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Direct pressure taken to its logical extreme — packing the wound cavity itself, not just covering the surface.
procedures.description: Direct pressure taken into the wound cavity itself.

blocks.html:
• Junctional hemorrhage — groin, axilla, gluteal, perineum, base of the neck. The anatomy where a limb tourniquet has nothing to squeeze against.
  • Deep or cavitating extremity wounds where surface pressure closes the skin but not the vessel underneath
  • Bleeding that continues past a correctly applied limb tourniquet — packing is an adjunct, not a competitor
  • A mangled or traumatically amputated limb stump, packed above the tourniquet line
  • Scalp and facial wounds that bleed briskly and are hard to compress against a curved skull

The common thread is a wound with a floor you can reach. Packing works by putting material in direct contact with a torn vessel and holding it against something solid. If you cannot get to the vessel, packing will not find it for you.
This is the section that matters most, and it is the one usually reduced to “none absolute.”

• An open chest wound. There is nothing to tamponade against — the pleural space is not a cavity that packing can fill, and pushing gauze into it drives air and material toward the lung. An open chest wound gets a vented chest seal and a plan for decompression, not a pack.
  • An abdominal wound or evisceration. The peritoneum is a non-compressible space. Packing achieves nothing, and gauze forced through the wall can perforate bowel. Cover eviscerated contents with a moist dressing and move toward an operating room.
  • The eye or the orbit.
  • An open skull fracture with visible brain. Packing raises intracranial pressure and can drive fragments inward. Cover only.
  • Wounds where the source is clearly proximal and unreachable — a groin wound whose vessel has retracted under the inguinal ligament. Packing the visible hole while the bleeding happens above it wastes the minutes you needed for a junctional device or proximal manual compression.

Relative: a neck wound can be packed, but never wrap the neck circumferentially — you will obstruct the airway and the contralateral carotid. Pack, then hold with a hand or secure over the shoulder and under the opposite axilla.

sections.title: Equipment — and Which Agents Are Obsolete

blocks.html:
• Kaolin-impregnated gauze (Combat Gauze and equivalents) — the current first-line hemostatic dressing in Tactical Combat Casualty Care. Kaolin activates factor XII and the contact pathway. Non-exothermic.
  • Chitosan-based gauze (Celox Gauze, ChitoGauze) — an accepted alternative. Chitosan works by a charge-based mucoadhesive mechanism that is largely independent of the clotting cascade, which makes it a rational choice in a patient who is anticoagulated or profoundly coagulopathic.
  • Compressed expanding sponges (XStat) — injectable mini-sponges for narrow-tract junctional wounds that a hand cannot reach into. Each sponge carries a radiopaque marker, and the count must travel with the patient.
  • Plain gauze — entirely acceptable. A correctly packed plain-gauze wound under sustained pressure outperforms a hemostatic dressing packed badly. Do not delay packing to hunt for the good stuff.
  • Analgesia. Packing a deep wound in a conscious patient is among the most painful things done in prehospital care. Ketamine is the usual answer because it preserves airway and pressure. Plan it before you start, not after the patient fights you.
  • Pressure dressing (elastic wrap or purpose-built) and a marker.

What is no longer recommended: granular and powder agents poured into a wound. The first-generation zeolite products were strongly exothermic and caused full-thickness burns in the wound and to the hands applying them. Granules also migrate, embolize, and are extremely difficult for a surgeon to debride. If a powder is what is in the bag, it is better than nothing — but gauze is the modern form factor for a reason.

sections.title: Find the Source Before You Fill the Hole

blocks.html:
The single conceptual error in wound packing is treating it as filling a cavity. It is not. It is putting a thumb on a specific torn vessel and then wedging the wound full so the thumb can leave.

  • Expose completely. Cut the clothing away. A wound you are packing through a trouser leg is a wound you cannot see.
  • Sweep out pooled blood and loose clot with a gloved hand. Established clot sitting in the cavity holds your packing away from the vessel and hides the jet you are looking for.
  • Look for the jet, then put a finger on it. Pulsatile bleeding localizes itself if you clear the pool for a second and watch. Once you have it, keep a finger there while you bring the gauze in with the other hand.
  • Expect the wound to be deeper than it looks. Skin defects are small; tracts are long. Your finger goes in to the knuckles, not to the fingernail.

steps.title: Start at the source, not at the skin
steps.html: Drive the first few inches of gauze directly onto the bleeding vessel with your fingertip, replacing your finger with the gauze in the same spot. This first contact is what stops the bleeding; everything after it is scaffolding that holds the contact in place.

steps.title: Pack against bone wherever the anatomy allows
steps.html: A vessel compressed between gauze and bone is occluded; a vessel compressed between gauze and soft tissue is merely pushed aside. See §07 for the specific targets — femoral against the superior pubic ramus, axillary against the humeral head or first rib.

steps.title: One continuous strip, fed in hard, no dead space
steps.html: Feed the roll in progressively, using your fingers to ram each bight firmly into a corner before bringing in the next. This is not gentle. A loose pack with air in it is functionally an unpacked wound — and it looks fine from the outside while the patient bleeds into the dressing. Use as many rolls as the cavity takes.

steps.title: Fill to just proud of the skin
steps.html: The last of the packing should sit slightly above the skin surface so the dressing on top transmits pressure into the wound rather than bridging across it.

steps.title: Three minutes of hard, uninterrupted pressure
steps.html: Both hands, body weight over the wound, no peeking. See §06 — this is the step people get wrong.

steps.title: Pressure dressing over the top, then watch it
steps.html: Apply an elastic pressure dressing over the pack, firm enough to maintain compression. Then look at it again in a few minutes — and keep looking. Mark the time and the number of rolls used on the dressing and on the patient.

blocks.title: If it fails, remove and repack — do not pile on top
blocks.html: This is the opposite of the rule for a soaked-through dressing, and the difference matters. A dressing is reinforced. A failed pack is removed and replaced, because its failure means the gauze never reached the bleeding vessel — and adding more material on top of a pack that missed just raises the pile. Pull it, find the source again, and pack it properly with fresh material.

Three minutes of continuous direct pressure, timed on a clock, without lifting to look. Current TCCC guidance specifies a minimum of three minutes for hemostatic dressings; some chitosan products and some coagulopathic patients warrant five. Check the packet of what you are actually using.

Why it is non-negotiable: a clot takes minutes to form and seconds to shear off. Lifting the pack at ninety seconds to see how it is going destroys everything the ninety seconds achieved and resets the clock — and it is the commonest reason a correctly packed wound appears to keep bleeding. The urge to check is strongest at exactly the moment checking is most destructive.

Have someone time it out loud. Three minutes with your weight on a wound feels far longer than three minutes, and untimed holds are consistently short. This is the same failure as the REBOA clock: a task nobody owns is a task that does not happen.

Use the time. It is three minutes in which the person holding pressure can do nothing else — so everyone else gets access, blood, TXA, and the transport decision moving.

rows: Groin / inguinal
Common femoral
Superior pubic ramus, at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
The highest-yield target in junctional bleeding. A fist or a knee works while a device is found.
Axilla
Axillary
Humeral head, or the first rib higher up
Deep and awkward. Drive the pack toward the chest wall, not toward the arm.
Neck
Carotid / jugular / subclavian
Cervical transverse processes
Never circumferential. Consider an occlusive layer — a large open venous injury here can entrain air.
Proximal thigh
Femoral
Femur shaft
Pack toward the bone posteriorly, not just downward.
Gluteal / buttock
Superior gluteal
Ilium and sacrum
A deep and notoriously difficult pack; often needs angiography.
Scalp
Superficial temporal, occipital
Skull
Galeal vessels retract into the scalp — sutures or staples through the galea often beat packing.
Bleeding continues around the pack
Dead space — the pack is not in contact with the vessel
Remove it. Find the source with a finger. Repack from the source outward, harder.
Bleeding stopped, then restarted in transit
Clot sheared by movement, or the hold was too short
Direct pressure again for a full timed three minutes. Secure better before the next move.
Wound is too narrow for a hand
A deep tract with a small skin defect
Expanding sponges if you have them. Otherwise extend the skin opening — you cannot pack what you cannot reach.
Groin pack fails repeatedly
The vessel has retracted proximal to the inguinal ligament
Stop packing. Proximal compression at the ramus, then a junctional device. This needs a surgeon.
Patient fights you
Untreated pain, or agitation from shock
Ketamine. An incompletely packed wound because the patient could not tolerate it is a preventable failure.
Oozing everywhere despite good packing
Coagulopathy — hypothermia, acidosis, dilution, anticoagulants
Packing cannot fix a clotting problem. Warm them, give TXA, activate massive transfusion, consider a chitosan agent that does not depend on the cascade.
Neck pack, patient now stridulous
Expanding hematoma or circumferential compression
Secure the airway early — it will only get harder. Never wrap the neck all the way around.
Packed limb now pale and pulseless
Pressure dressing applied as a tourniquet
If it is a tourniquet, make that a deliberate decision and mark it. If not, loosen the circumferential wrap while maintaining direct pressure over the pack.

blocks.html:
• Ongoing occult hemorrhage beneath an intact-looking dressing — the failure mode of a loose pack, and the reason a packed wound gets looked at repeatedly rather than dressed and forgotten.
  • Retained packing material — a foreign body and an infection source. Count and document.
  • Wound infection and tissue necrosis from prolonged tight packing.
  • Nerve injury from sustained pressure, particularly axillary and inguinal packs.
  • Thermal injury — historical, from first-generation exothermic granular agents.
  • Distal ischemia if the overlying pressure dressing becomes an unintended tourniquet.
  • Airway compromise from a neck pack or a developing hematoma.
  • Air embolism from an open large vein in the neck or axilla — an argument for an occlusive layer over a neck pack.

• Say what is in the wound and how much. Agent, number of rolls or sponges, time packed. Write it on the dressing and on the patient's skin — verbal handover in a trauma bay is lost.
  • Expanding sponges must be counted, and the count must be spoken to the surgeon. They are radiopaque for exactly this reason, but a film is a slower way to learn a number you already had.
  • Do not unwrap it to show anyone. The receiving team does not need to see the wound; they need to know what you found and what you did. The pack comes out in an operating room.
  • Flag coagulopathy and anticoagulants explicitly — a pack in a patient on a DOAC is holding a line that will not hold itself.

Pack onto the vessel, not into the hole. The first inch of gauze does the work; the rest holds it there.

Compress against bone. Soft tissue on both sides means the vessel just moves.

Three minutes, timed out loud, no peeking. The urge to check peaks exactly when checking is most destructive.

A failed pack is removed and replaced — not reinforced. Opposite rule to a soaked dressing, and the distinction is the whole point.

Never pack a chest or an abdomen. Seal the chest, cover the abdomen, and go.

Never wrap a neck circumferentially.

Plain gauze packed well beats hemostatic gauze packed badly. Do not spend thirty seconds hunting for the right packet.

Give ketamine before you start. This hurts more than almost anything else you will do to a conscious patient.

Count what goes in, and say the number out loud at handover.
